text:
My mother says I dance like someone apologising. She said it the first week, standing in the doorway of the bedroom while I tried to hold my wrist in the shape the video showed, and she has said it in some form every week since, and I have never once agreed with her, and I still do not.

The festival was in August, in the community hall behind the Sikh temple on Fenton Road, and I did not want to go. I want to be honest about that because the version of this story where I discovered my heritage and wept into a dupatta is not the version that happened. I did not want to go because I had been going since I was six and every year it was the same folding chairs, the same aunties asking which university, the same three uncles arguing about the sound system. My mother wanted me to perform. Not attend - perform. Giddha, with the group of women she has known since she came here in 1998. She said, you are seventeen, next year you will be somewhere else, do this one thing.

So I learned. Six weeks, four evenings a week, in the bedroom with the door shut because the living room had my brother in it. My mother taught me the boliyan first, the couplets you call out, and this was the beginning of the argument. She wanted me to shout them. Not sing - shout, the way you would shout across a field to a woman working three rows over. I could not do it. I could get my voice to about half the volume she wanted and then something in my throat would close. She would say louder and I would say I am being loud and she would say no, that is your school voice.

Here is what I think and what I have not been able to make her understand. She grew up where the dance was the ordinary way a person moved. I grew up where it is a thing you take out of a box. When I shout the boliyan in a bedroom in a semi-detached house on a Tuesday, I am not doing what she did at nineteen. I am performing what she did at nineteen. The shame in my throat is not shame about being Punjabi. It is the shame of being watched doing something I have not earned. She hears that as a smaller version of the same thing. She hears rejection. And I cannot get the distinction across without it sounding like an excuse, which possibly it is.

I danced at the festival. I was fine. The clapping was the clapping you get for a seventeen-year-old who tried. Afterward she pressed her hand flat against my back, which is what she does instead of hugging, and she said, better. Not good. Better.

We had the argument again in November. We will have it again. I have started to think this is not a problem I am supposed to solve, that some inheritances arrive as arguments rather than as objects, and that the argument is the inheritance. I do not know if she would accept that. She would probably say I am making a theory out of not practising enough. She might be right. I still cannot shout the boliyan properly, and I still do not think it is because I am ashamed.

meta.topic: learning traditional dance for a festival they did not want to attend
meta.prompt: Some students have a background, identity, interest, or talent that is so meaningful they believe their application would be incomplete without it. If this sounds like you, then please share your story.

text:
There is a mug on the windowsill in our kitchen that leans about four degrees to the left. My dad drinks out of it on purpose, which I think is a joke and also isn't. It was the eleventh mug I made and the first one that held water.

The wheel came off Gumtree for forty pounds, from a woman in Sale whose mother had died. It's a Shimpo, or it was, in about 1980. The pedal sticks. And the head - the metal disc the clay sits on - has a wobble. Not a big one. If you spin it empty and put a pencil next to it you can watch the gap open and close, maybe two millimetres. The woman didn't mention it. I don't think she knew.

Nobody taught me. There's no pottery at my school and the studio in town charges thirty-five an hour, so it was YouTube and a bucket and the shed. And for about four months I was completely, spectacularly bad.

Here is what happens. You centre the clay - you push it down and in with the heel of your hand until it stops fighting you and just sits there spinning as if it isn't moving at all. Then you open it, you pull the walls, you get a cylinder. Except my clay would never quite stop moving. There'd always be this slow lurch, a pulse, once per rotation. And every video I watched said the same thing: if it's off-centre, you haven't centred it. Push harder. Brace your elbow on your thigh. Breathe out.

So I assumed it was me. For four months I assumed it was me. I have a whole cardboard box of collapsed walls in the shed, every one of them lurching in the same direction, and I sat there taking it personally.

The thing that fixed it wasn't insight, it was boredom. I was waiting for the shed to warm up one Saturday and I spun the empty head and watched it, and I saw the gap between the head and the splash pan open and close. Once per rotation. Same rhythm as the lurch.

It wasn't me. It was never entirely me.

I want to be careful, because the tidy version of this is that I learned to stop blaming myself, and that's not right either. Some of it was me. My hands were weak and my clay was too dry and I was rushing the pull. The honest version is messier: the machine was broken and I was bad, at the same time, and I couldn't tell the two apart because I had no one to ask.

That's the real answer to what teaching yourself shows you. Not persistence. Not resourcefulness. It's that without a teacher you have no way of knowing which of your failures are diagnostic. A teacher would have spun that head in ten seconds. Instead I spent a third of a year building a very confident theory about my own hands.

I never fixed the wobble properly. I shimmed it and it's better and it's still there. What I did instead was learn to throw with it - to feel the pulse coming and let my fingers give slightly on that quarter of the turn, which is apparently not a technique anyone teaches, because why would you.

So the mug leans. Four degrees, always the same direction, because I was compensating for a machine and slightly overdid it. My dad says it's the best one.

meta.topic: learning to make pottery on a wheel that wobbled
meta.prompt: What is something you have taught yourself, and what did learning it without a teacher show you?

text:
My mother thinks that what I did last year was kind. We have been going round this for eight months and neither of us has moved.

I was a scribe. There is a boy in the year below me, Tomas, who is blind, and for two terms I sat in exams and in some lessons and wrote down what he said. Nobody trained me. There was supposed to be a training session and it was cancelled twice and then term started. So what I know about scribing I taught myself, in the room, while doing it, which is not a good way to learn anything and is how most people learn most things.

The first thing I learned was that I did not know what a scribe was for. I had assumed I was a pen. He would say words and the words would appear on the page and my job was to be transparent. That lasted about forty minutes. Because he would say a sentence and then stop and say "no, wait," and I would have written half of it, and now there was a decision to make about what to cross out that he could not see me making. Or he would spell a word and the spelling would be wrong and I would have to decide, in a fraction of a second, whether correcting it was help or cheating. There is no manual for that. Or if there is, it was in the training session that got cancelled.

I built my own rules. That is the honest version of "taught myself." I decided that I would read back everything, always, even when it was slow, even when he was impatient, because the alternative was that my version of his answer would go in and he would never know. I decided I would not fix spelling unless he asked, and that I would ask once at the start of every session whether he wanted me to. I decided that when he paused I would say "you're at, and therefore the pressure" and let him hear where he was, rather than waiting silently, because silence made him rush.

None of those rules were obvious. I got them wrong first. In the November mock I "helped" - he was going nowhere on a question and I read the question back with a slightly different emphasis, and the emphasis was a hint, and he took it. He got a better mark than he had earned. I have never told anyone that except my mother, and here.

Which is where the disagreement is.

My mother says I am being hard on myself. She says the whole point of an access arrangement is that the boy should not be disadvantaged, that a sighted student would have reread the question with their own emphasis anyway, that I am inventing a crime. She says this in the voice she uses when she has decided the conversation is finished. And she says the larger thing, which is that it was generous of me to do it at all, that most seventeen-year-olds would not have given up their frees, and that I should let myself have that.

I do not think it was generous. I think that is the part she will not hear. It was interesting. I wanted to be in the room. There is something in the mechanics of it - the exact latency between his sentence and my hand, the fact that a comma is a decision somebody has to make and normally the writer makes it and here it was me - that I found more absorbing than any lesson I sat in that year. That is not kindness. That is curiosity wearing a volunteer's badge, and being praised for it makes me feel like a fraud in a way I cannot explain to her without it sounding like fishing.

And the emphasis thing was real. She calls it a nothing. It was not a nothing to me because I felt the moment I did it - I felt myself decide to be liked rather than be accurate, which is exactly the failure mode a scribe has to not have.

We are not going to resolve it. I have stopped raising it. She thinks I have come round. What I have actually concluded is narrower: that the only reliable thing I learned without a teacher was where my own hand wants to go when nobody is checking, and that knowing that is not the same as being able to stop it. Tomas has a different scribe this year. She was trained. I hope she was told about the pause.

meta.topic: working as a scribe for a blind student
meta.prompt: What is something you have taught yourself, and what did learning it without a teacher show you?

text:
Room 9 is not a nice room. It is the small one off the maths corridor with a whiteboard that keeps a ghost of everything ever written on it and a radiator that comes on in June. Tuesday and Thursday, half three to half four, I sit in there with between two and five students from Year Nine and Ten who are failing maths, and that is the place where I feel most like myself.

It was not supposed to be that. I need to say that clearly, because the version where I have always wanted to teach is not true.

I started because I needed something for the personal statement. That is the entire reason. Mrs Kaur put a sign-up sheet on the noticeboard for peer tutors and I wrote my name on it in October thinking it would be an hour a week of feeling clever in front of people who were worse at something than me. I am not proud of that sentence but it is what I thought.

And the first term was awful. Not dramatic - just awful in the way that a thing is awful when you are bad at it and cannot see why. I would explain fractions. I would explain fractions again, more slowly, in the same words, which is the single most useless thing a person can do. I had a boy called Ryan who would go completely still when I started talking, and I read that as not caring, and I got quietly annoyed with him for weeks.

The moment I changed my mind was in January and it was about ten seconds long.

I had asked Ryan to do something with negative numbers and he had done it wrong, and instead of explaining I asked him - mostly out of tiredness - how he'd got that. And he told me. He had a whole method. It was internally consistent. It was wrong in exactly one place, near the beginning, and everything after that was correct reasoning built on a broken step. He had not been failing to think. He had been thinking hard, the whole time, in a direction nobody had checked.

I remember feeling something reorganise itself. I had assumed that failing maths meant an absence - an empty space where understanding should be, which I could fill by pouring in explanation. It is not an absence. It is a structure. There is always a structure, and it is doing its best, and it is usually broken somewhere small and load-bearing.

After that the job became interesting in a way it had not been. Not rewarding, exactly. Interesting. Because now the work was diagnostic: get them talking, find the one wrong beam, and everything above it fixes itself faster than you would believe. Ryan got a five in the summer. I would like to claim that but honestly I think most of it was that somebody finally asked him what he was doing rather than telling him what to do.

So Room 9. Bad chairs, terrible radiator. I feel most myself there because it is the only place in my week where I am not performing understanding, I am investigating somebody else's. Nobody is marking me. There is no correct method to demonstrate. There is just a person and a wrong answer and the question of where the wrong answer came from, and I find that I could do that for a very long time without getting bored.

I came for the personal statement. I stayed because January.

meta.topic: tutoring maths to students who were failing it

text:
I spent a month on Ward 12 when I was fifteen, and the belief I challenged was mine, and I got it wrong in a way I am still working out.

The belief was that being ill was a period of suspension. Real life was outside, at school, in the group chat, and the ward was a waiting room I would eventually be released from back into the actual world. I held this so completely that I did not think of it as a belief. It was just the shape of things. So I did the logical thing: I brought my textbooks in, I asked my mother for the GCSE past papers, and I set out to make the month not count. I worked through chemistry on a bed-tray with a cannula in my left hand. I was, I thought, being admirable.

There was a woman opposite me called Pat who had been in for eleven weeks. She did the crossword slowly. She talked to the healthcare assistants about their children by name. I thought she had given up. That is the honest word for what I thought. I had a private, entirely unearned sense that I was doing it correctly and she was doing it wrong, and I never said it, and I am fairly sure she knew.

What I got wrong was the arithmetic. I assumed that time spent in the ward was subtracted from my life and time spent on chemistry was added back. But I was not learning any chemistry. I was reading the same page while a machine beeped. Nothing went in. Meanwhile Pat, who I had written off, knew that the physiotherapist came Tuesdays and that if you asked on Monday you could get an earlier slot, and she told me, and it was the single most useful piece of information anyone gave me that month.

She was not passing time. She was living somewhere, competently, that I had refused to admit was a place.

I went home in April. The belief did not collapse dramatically; it eroded over the following year, mostly at odd moments - realising I could not remember one thing from those textbooks but could remember the exact sound of the drug trolley.

What I think now is that "real life" is not a location you get returned to. It is wherever you actually are, and treating a month of it as a waiting room does not preserve that month, it just wastes it while making you feel virtuous.

I still catch myself doing it. Every time a queue is long, or a lesson is dull, I feel the old subtraction start. I have not fully stopped. But I notice, which I did not before, and I think of Pat and her crossword and the fact that she was better at being alive on that ward than I was.

meta.topic: a hospital stay that lasted a month
meta.prompt: Reflect on a time when you questioned or challenged a belief or idea. What prompted your thinking? What was the outcome?

text:
I sang in the church choir for five years without believing a word of it, and for most of that time I thought this made me a hypocrite. The moment I stopped thinking so happened in a rehearsal in a cold building in February, and it changed more than my opinion of myself.

The facts first. St Cuthbert's, second row, alto. I joined at twelve because my mother sang there and because they paid the choral scholars four pounds a service, which at twelve is real money. I stayed because I liked it. By fourteen I had stopped believing in God, quietly and without drama, the way you stop believing in a rumour when nobody produces evidence. I did not tell anyone. I kept turning up, and I kept singing about a resurrection I did not think had happened, and I felt like a fraud every single Sunday.

I had a private argument running in my head for about three years. It went: these words are claims. To sing a claim is to assert it. To assert something you think is false is to lie. Therefore I am lying, beautifully, in four-part harmony, for four pounds.

Then February. We were learning the Allegri Miserere, which is too hard for a parish choir, and we had been on the same eight bars for forty minutes. Sylvia, who directs, stopped us because the altos were flat on a suspension. She said something I have thought about ever since. She said: you are not holding that note for yourself, you are holding it so the sopranos have something to be dissonant against.

That is a technical instruction, about tuning. But I sat there with my folder open and understood, suddenly and physically, that I had been wrong about what I was doing.

A suspension only exists as a relationship. My note, alone, is neither right nor wrong. It becomes something when it rubs against the note above it and then resolves. Nobody in the building can hear my line as a line. What they hear is the whole chord, which is made of four people each holding something incomplete.

I had been treating singing as a series of statements I personally issued. It is not. It is a structure that four people build together, and the alto part is not a sentence I say, it is a piece I carry so that the thing can stand up. Whether I believe the words is a question about me. Whether the chord tunes is a question about us.

I am not claiming this solved theology. I still do not believe in God, and I do not think singing solves anything about that. What changed was my understanding of participation. I had assumed you could only legitimately take part in something you privately endorsed, that sincerity was the entry requirement for everything. But most of the things human beings do together are not like that. You hold a line so that someone else's line means something. That is not fraud. That is how a chord works, and, I have come to think, how quite a lot else works too.

After that I stopped apologising to myself on Sundays.

I sang my last service in December. Sylvia gave me a pencil, because I had never once brought one in five years. The new thing I understand about myself is that I do not need to agree with a room in order to be honestly of use to it, and I learned that from being flat on a suspension in a freezing church.

meta.topic: the church choir they sang in but did not believe in

text:
My sister Nadia thinks I should have stayed. This is a live argument in our house, still, fourteen months on, and I have not won it and neither has she.

I volunteered at Brackenridge Animal Rescue for eleven months and I was bad at it. Not bad in the way people mean when they are being modest. Bad. Nadia had been going for three years and got me in, and she is very good - she once spent forty minutes lying flat on a concrete floor with her hand out for a lurcher called Bess who would not come near anyone. I could not do any of that. Dogs got worse around me. I would go into a kennel to do enrichment and the animal would go rigid, and I would go rigid because it had gone rigid, and we would stand there feeding each other's fear until somebody senior came and did it properly in ninety seconds.

The belief I had, and it is a very ordinary belief, is that caring about something makes you good at it. I did care. So I assumed competence would arrive with hours logged, and that anything else was a failure of commitment.

I gave it eleven months. What I eventually had to accept is that the thing I was missing was not commitment, it was a particular stillness - the ability to be calm in a way that is not performed, because a frightened dog is not reading your face, it is reading your whole body, and mine was telling the truth.

So I stopped. And I went and did the other thing instead, which is the part Nadia objects to. Brackenridge had a grant application half-finished and a foster-placement spreadsheet nobody had updated since 2022, and I am good at that. I rebuilt the records. I wrote the funding bid that got them the second van.

Nadia's argument is this: I quit the hard part. She says that anyone can do admin, that I chose the version of helping where nothing frightening happens, and that I let myself off. She says - and this is the sentence that gets under my skin because I cannot fully answer it - that the dogs did not need a better spreadsheet, they needed someone to sit on the floor with them.

My argument is that a van is eleven extra collections a week, and that eleven months of me making animals more anxious was not a moral achievement just because it was uncomfortable for me. That there is a kind of vanity in insisting on doing the difficult, visible job badly when you could do the invisible one well.

I believe that. I also think she might be right that I found the exit slightly too gratefully, and that I have built a very tidy justification for something that was, in the moment, mostly relief.

We had the argument again at Christmas. She said, you never even tried with Bess. I said I did, twice, and she was more frightened when I left than when I arrived. She said, that is the job. I said, no, that is your job.

Nothing was settled. Nadia still goes on Saturdays. I still do their accounts on Sunday nights, and I have not been back to the kennels. What I challenged was the idea that caring converts into capability if you just want it enough. What I have not worked out is whether that conclusion is honest or convenient.

meta.topic: volunteering at an animal shelter and being bad at it
meta.prompt: Reflect on a time when you questioned or challenged a belief or idea. What prompted your thinking? What was the outcome?

text:
I started learning to code because my cousin Ines was seven and had had a bad year, and I thought I could make her a game about a frog.

That was the whole plan. Her parents had separated, she had moved schools twice, and when she came to us in the summer she mostly sat under the dining table with an iPad. She liked frogs, specifically, with a seven-year-old's total commitment. So I downloaded a Python tutorial and decided I would build her something in a fortnight, because I had assumed that programming was a matter of knowing the right words, and that once you knew them you typed and things happened.

The fortnight became four months. I want to be honest that most of that time I did not enjoy it. I found it humiliating in a way I had not been prepared for. I am the kind of student who is used to being competent quickly, and here was a thing that would refuse to run because of a colon. Not a wrong idea - a colon.

The frog game was, by October, a rectangle that could jump. I showed Ines on a video call and she said, where is the frog, and I said it is being a rectangle at the moment, and she said, oh.

Here is where I changed my mind, and it happened at about eleven at night in November over something small.

I was trying to make the frog fall back down after jumping, and I had written it so that every frame the frog moved down by three pixels. It looked wrong. It looked like the frog was being lowered on a string. I could see it was wrong and I could not say why. And then - I genuinely remember the physical feeling of this - I thought about my mechanics homework, and the fact that falling things do not have a constant speed, they have a constant acceleration. So instead of moving the frog down three, I made a number called velocity, and each frame I added a bit to the velocity, and then moved the frog down by the velocity.

It took two lines. And the frog fell like a real thing falls.

I sat there for a while. What had happened was not that I had learned a coding trick. What had happened was that a piece of physics I had been able to recite for two years - that gravity is an acceleration, not a speed - had for the first time been something I could see. I had written the sentence "a = 9.81" perhaps two hundred times. I had never once believed it in my body until a green rectangle fell correctly off a ledge on my laptop.

That reorganised what I thought I was doing. Until then I had understood code as instructions: a way of getting a machine to perform tasks. From that night I understood it as a way of building a small claim about how something works and then watching whether the claim behaves. If your model of falling is wrong, the frog looks wrong. The screen is not judging your typing. It is judging your understanding.

After that I stopped being humiliated by the errors, mostly, because I had a different relationship with them. An error meant my model was incomplete, which is interesting, rather than that I was slow, which is not.

Ines got her game at Christmas. It has a frog, sprites I drew badly in Piskel, lily pads that sink if you stand on them too long, and a bug where if you jump at the exact edge you can get inside the log. She found the bug in four minutes. She likes the bug more than the game, and she has shown it to her friends, and now she wants to know how to make her own one, which is how I ended up teaching a nine-year-old about velocity over FaceTime on Sundays.

meta.topic: learning to code to make a game for a younger cousin
meta.prompt: Discuss an accomplishment, event, or realization that sparked a period of personal growth and a new understanding of yourself or others.

text:
The harmonium sits on the floor of the back bedroom at my grandparents' flat in Southall, on a folded blanket because the legs of the case have gone, and the place where I feel most myself is sitting cross-legged behind it with my left hand on the bellows. My grandfather thinks this is a waste and we have never agreed about it.

It was his. It is a Monoj Kumar Sardar, bought in Delhi in 1971 and carried here in a crate, and three of the reeds are flat and the D above middle C sticks if the room is damp. He played it for forty years at the gurdwara and at home on Sunday mornings, and then his hands went - arthritis, both of them, the joints at the base of the fingers - and it went into the back bedroom in 2016 and stayed there.

I started playing it when I was thirteen because nobody else was going to. That is not a noble reason. It was sitting there and I was bored.

Here is the disagreement, and I want to set out his side properly, because he has a real argument and I get tired of people assuming a grandfather's position must be sentimental.

He says I am learning it wrong. Specifically, he says I am learning it as an instrument and not as an accompaniment. The harmonium in the tradition he learned it in is not a solo instrument; it exists under a voice. You play what the singer needs, you follow, you never lead, and the ornament belongs to the throat, not the keys. He says that what I do - sitting in that room working out the raag on the keyboard, playing it as a melody, no voice at all - is like learning to be a shadow with nobody standing in the light. He said that to me almost exactly, in Punjabi, and it is a better line than anything I could come up with.

My side is this. I do not sing. I cannot sing; I have tried and it is genuinely unpleasant to be in the room. So the choice he is describing is not available to me. It is not a choice between playing correctly and playing incorrectly. It is a choice between playing it wrong and it sitting under a blanket for another decade with three flat reeds, and I think an instrument that is played wrongly is more alive than an instrument that is preserved.

He does not accept this. He says a thing done wrong is not the same thing. He says I have taken a religious object and made it into a hobby.

I have started to think he might be partly right, which is annoying.

Because the reason that room is where I feel most myself is not devotional and I should not pretend it is. It is physical. It is the pump of the bellows with the left hand, which has to be continuous, which means your left arm is doing something rhythmic and slightly effortful the entire time and cannot stop, so there is no such thing as a pause. It is the smell - old wood and the particular dust of a room nobody vacuums. It is that the instrument is loud enough that I cannot hear my phone. I go in there on Sunday afternoons when we visit and I come out ninety minutes later and I have not thought about school once.

So he is right that I am not doing what he did. What I am doing is using his instrument for something he did not intend, which is to get out of my own head, and calling it inheritance because that is a more flattering word than escape.

We still argue. Two weeks ago I played him something and he listened all the way through and then said the left hand was uneven, which is true, and then said nothing else. My grandmother says that is approval. I do not think it is. I think he genuinely believes I am doing it wrong and has decided that I am going to do it anyway, and that being in the room while I do it is better than the alternative.

That is roughly where I have got to as well.

meta.topic: learning to play a grandfather's harmonium
meta.prompt: Describe a place where you feel most yourself, and why.

text:
The roof of our block is eleven flights up and you get to it through a fire door that is supposed to be alarmed and is not. There are two hives up there, a National and a smaller nuc box, on breeze blocks I carried up myself over three trips, and between April and September that is where I am most Saturday mornings before anyone else in the building is awake. It is where I feel most like myself. It is also where I did the worst thing I have ever done, which was not deliberate and which killed about thirty thousand animals.

I should explain the roof first. It is asphalt and it slopes slightly towards a drain, there is a satellite dish nobody has used since before I was born, and if you stand at the north end you can see the gasholder and, on a clear day, the hills past Dinnington. But the reason it matters is not the view. It is that when you open a hive, everything else stops. You cannot be distracted while your hands are inside a colony. You cannot check your phone. You cannot think about the chemistry mock, because there are between forty and sixty thousand insects in there and your entire attention is being asked for at once, and there is a specific quality to that attention that I have never found anywhere else. The sound changes when you have done something they dislike. It goes from a hum to something harder, and you feel it in your sternum before you consciously hear it. Standing in that sound, moving very slowly, being wholly in one place - that is the closest I get to being a person rather than a list of deadlines.

Now the thing I got wrong.

Varroa is a mite. It is about the size of a pinhead, it attaches to the bee and feeds on it, and it carries viruses; if you do not manage it, a colony that looks strong in August is dead by February. Every book says the same thing. Monitor, treat, monitor again. In my first full year I did a sugar roll count in August, got a low number, and decided I was fine.

The mistake was not skipping the treatment out of laziness. It is worse than that. I wanted the count to be low. I had told a boy at school that I kept bees, and I had told my aunt, and there was a version of myself I was enjoying being - the kid on the roof, the one who does something unusual - and a mite problem did not fit in it. So I did one sample, from one frame, at one moment, which any beekeeper will tell you is not a count, it is an anecdote. And I wrote a low number in my book and felt relieved and did not test again.

I opened them in March. There is a particular smell to a colony that has died out and I do not want to describe it. The cluster was the size of a fist. There were bees head-down in cells where they had crawled in looking for the last of the stores. There were deformed wings, which is the virus, which is the mite, which is the thing I had decided not to look for.

I cried on a roof at seven in the morning, which is a ridiculous image and was not funny at the time.

I keep bees differently now. I count from three frames. I count when I do not want to. I have a laminated card in the box with the dates on it because I have learned that I cannot trust the version of me that is holding a smoker and feeling good about himself. And I have stopped telling people about it at school, mostly, which I think is related.

What the roof gives me now is not the identity. It is the check. Eleven flights up, hands in a hive, being told the truth by a colony that has no interest in whether I am impressive. I am most myself there because it is the one place where wanting something to be true does not make the slightest difference to whether it is.

text:
For two summers I was a lifeguard at a pool that almost nobody used. Tuesday and Thursday mornings, half six to half nine, at the leisure centre where the early session had maybe four regulars and some weeks had one. So what I mostly did was sit in a high chair above eight lanes of undisturbed water and watch nothing happen.

Nobody teaches you that part. The qualification teaches you rescues. You spend a weekend hauling a rubber dummy off the bottom and learning how to get someone out with a suspected spinal injury, and you come away thinking the job is the emergency. It isn't. The job is the four hundred hours before the emergency, and there is no course for that, and I had to work it out on my own, badly, over two years.

What I got wrong is simple to state and took me a long time to see.

I thought watching was a thing you did with your eyes. So I kept them open and I kept them pointed at the water, and I thought that was the job being done. And because almost nothing ever happened, I had no way of knowing whether I was doing it well. There is no feedback. If you watch perfectly for three hours, the result is that nothing happens. If you watch terribly for three hours, the result is also, almost always, that nothing happens. Those two mornings look identical from the outside and, more dangerously, they feel identical from the inside.

So I drifted. I want to be honest about how far. I was not on my phone - that would have got me sacked and I knew it. But I was in my own head. I planned things. I had long arguments with people who were not there. I would come out of a stretch and genuinely not be able to tell you whether the man in lane three had been swimming or resting for the last four minutes, and I would tell myself that if something had happened I would have noticed, because I was looking.

That is the thing I still think about: I was looking at the water for three hours and seeing it for perhaps forty minutes of that, and I had no idea, because looking and seeing use the same muscles from where I was sitting.

What broke it was small. A woman, one of the regulars, got out of the pool one morning and stood at the shallow end holding the rail for a while, and I clocked it and assumed she was catching her breath. She was there maybe ninety seconds. Then she left. And afterwards - an hour afterwards, in the changing room corridor - I found out from the receptionist that she had felt faint and gone and sat in reception for twenty minutes before driving home.

Nothing happened. That is the point. Nothing happened and I still had not seen it. She was six metres from me in my direct line of sight and I had processed her as scenery.

After that I stopped trusting my eyes and started building a system, which is the actual thing I taught myself. I gave myself a route: near lane, far lane, deep end, shallow end, the doors, back to the near lane, and I did it as an actual circuit, and I made myself name what I saw silently. Blue cap, breaststroke, steady. If I could not name it I had not seen it. I also learned that ten minutes standing up is worth thirty sitting down, and that if I let myself get warm I was finished, so I would take the cover off the chair.

Any experienced guard would tell you the scan pattern in a sentence. But there wasn't an experienced guard there at half six, and so I invented a worse version of something that already exists, which I have since decided is what most self-teaching actually is.

The larger thing it showed me is about attention rather than swimming pools. I had assumed attention was a state - that you were either paying it or not, and that a conscientious person paid it. It isn't a state. It's a task, and it decays, and it decays invisibly, and the only defence is a structure you impose on yourself from outside because you cannot feel it going.

I still think about the woman on the rail. She was fine. She came back the following Tuesday. But I sat in a high chair looking directly at her and did not see a person in trouble, and I would have sworn on anything that I was watching.

text:
In Year Ten I won the regional science fair with a project that was wrong.

Not wrong in a small way. The conclusion was wrong, the method was wrong, and the reason it won is that the presentation was excellent and I was very confident, and I have never fully got over how easy that turned out to be.

The project was on the water quality of the Ryhope Beck, which runs behind our estate and comes out near the old sewage works. The idea was to sample at five points along its length and show pollution increasing downstream of the industrial units on Coleman Road, which everyone locally assumes is the source. I bought a kit and tested for nitrate, phosphate, pH and dissolved oxygen. I made a poster with a map on it. My results showed exactly what I expected: readings got worse as you went downstream, with a big jump after Coleman Road.

Here is what I did wrong, and I did not find it out until the following spring.

I sampled all five sites on the same afternoon, in order, starting upstream at about two and finishing downstream at about half four. It is in fact the single thing you must not do, because the beck is affected by the treatment works discharge cycle, and it was a hot day in June, and dissolved oxygen falls through the afternoon as the water warms. So my downstream sites were not just downstream. They were later, and hotter, and I had built a beautiful graph in which the x-axis said distance and actually meant time of day.

I also had one sample per site. One. No repeats. A single reading from a moving body of water, which is roughly as meaningful as one photograph of a road reported as the traffic.

Nobody caught it. Not the judges, not my teacher, not the man from the water company. The only thing anyone asked me was why I had chosen the topic, and I said something about growing up next to it and caring about my community, which was true, and which they liked a lot.

What found the error was a boy called Aidan in the year above, who was not being kind. He said, at lunch, months later, that my graph would look the same if the beck was completely clean, because I had measured a day rather than a river. I was furious for about two hours and then I went home and looked at my times and felt the floor go.

I redid it that spring, properly. Three sites, sampled at the same time of day on nine different days, three replicates each, temperature recorded alongside every reading. It took eleven weeks instead of one afternoon, and the results were much less impressive. There is a real signal after Coleman Road, smaller than my first graph claimed, and a much bigger one after heavy rain everywhere, which turns out to be combined sewer overflow.

The thing I still think about is not that I was wrong. It is that I was wrong and rewarded, and that the reward came from the parts of the work that had nothing to do with whether it was true - the map, the confidence, the answer everybody in the room already believed about the industrial units.

I do not really trust myself when a result comes out the way I hoped. When my chemistry practical works first time I get suspicious rather than pleased, which I think is the most useful thing that fair gave me.

The certificate is still on the wall at my nan's. I have not had the conversation with her about it.

text:
I stopped playing the piano in March, after eleven years, and my mother has not forgiven me, and I am not sure she is wrong.

I want to put her case first, properly, because when people hear this story they arrive already on my side and that annoys me. Her case is not that she paid for it, though she did, for eleven years, forty minutes a week with Mrs Petrov and then with Mr Ainsworth after Mrs Petrov's hip. Her case is not even that I was good, though I was - Grade 8 at fifteen, distinction, the Wigmore Hall thing with the county youth orchestra where I did not play a wrong note in the Poulenc and have never once been able to enjoy the recording.

Her case is that quitting is a decision made by a version of me that will not be here in ten years, on behalf of a version of me who will be, and who will want it back and will not be able to have it.

She has evidence for this. She played the violin until she was nineteen and stopped when she went to university, and she has said, more than once, in a completely flat voice, that it is the thing she regrets. She has a violin in the loft. She has not opened the case since we moved.

So when she says you will regret this she is not guessing. She is reporting.

My case is harder to say without sounding ungrateful. It is not that I hate the piano. I do not hate the piano. It is that I had stopped being able to tell the difference between playing and being seen to play. Somewhere around Grade 7 the instrument became a thing I was measured by, and after that every hour at the keyboard had a small auditor sitting in it. I would learn a piece and my first thought at the end of it was never that was beautiful, it was that's about eighty per cent.

And it was consuming everything. Two hours a day, which is not a boast, it is an accounting. Two hours a day is fourteen a week, is the reason I have never had a Saturday job, is the reason I stopped drawing at thirteen.

The argument itself was not one argument. It was about eight, over four months, in kitchens and cars. She said: you are throwing away eleven years. I said: I am not throwing them away, I have them, they are in my hands. She said: they will go. And this is the sentence I have not been able to answer, because she is factually right. It does go. I am worse now than I was in March. I sat down at my grandmother's in August and my left hand had already got stupid.

What I said back was that I would rather lose something I had than keep spending my life defending it. She said that was the kind of thing you say at seventeen. Which - again - is a fair point that I cannot disprove for about a decade.

We do not really talk about it now. She has stopped mentioning it, which is worse than the arguing. The piano is still in the front room and nobody has suggested selling it and I do not know what that means. Sometimes I play in the evenings when the house is empty, badly, sight-reading things I have no business attempting, and I like it more than I liked any of the exams, and I have not told her that because she would take it as proof.

Maybe it is proof. Maybe in fifteen years I will have a violin in a loft of my own and I will understand exactly what she was trying to save me from, and I will not be able to explain it to my own child either.

But I am seventeen now, and it is my two hours a day, and the person who has to spend them is me. That is the whole of my argument, and I know it is not enough, and I did it anyway.

text:
The tin is an old Amul milk powder tin, the blue one with the label mostly scraped off, and it holds two hundred safety pins, a spool of black thread, four spare blouse hooks, a roll of double-sided tape, and a pair of nail scissors. My mother gave it to me on the first morning of my cousin Meera's wedding and said, you are in charge of the back room. She meant the small storeroom behind the stage at the banquet hall, the one with the mop bucket and the stacked chairs and the tube light that buzzed. That is where I spent three days. That is, I think, where I am most myself.

I was sixteen and I had not asked for the job. My aunts had decided that because I was calm and had no other function at a wedding - too old to be cute, too young to be consulted - I would be the person who solved things. Within two hours it turned out this was an actual job. A pleat came loose. A garland split at the knot. A great-uncle's kurta button went missing somewhere between the car and the door. Someone's grandmother needed to sit down urgently in a room that was not full of noise. Each time, somebody would find me and I would go into the storeroom with the tin.

What I noticed, standing under that buzzing tube light with a pin between my teeth, was that I was not nervous. Out in the hall I was terrible. I did not know what to say to relatives who had last seen me at eight. I hovered near the food. But three feet inside the storeroom door, with a specific problem in front of me and a tin of things that might fix it, I was completely comfortable, and people spoke to me differently - quickly, plainly, telling me what was wrong instead of asking me how school was.

The best moment came on the second evening. Meera came in by herself, still in the heavy red, and sat on a stack of chairs and asked me to unpin a section of her dupatta that had been fastened too tight across her shoulder for four hours. She did not want her mother, who would have fussed. She wanted somebody who would just do it and not make it a conversation. I unpinned it, put the pins back in the tin, and she sat there for maybe ninety seconds in the quiet with her eyes shut, and then she went back out. Neither of us said anything about it. That silence felt like the highest compliment I have ever been paid.

I have since noticed that I look for that room everywhere. It is behind the counter at the canteen on sports day, the sound desk at the back of the auditorium, the corner of the lab where the glassware is washed. Any place slightly to the side of the event, where the work is concrete and the only test of success is whether the thing is now fixed.

I still have the tin. It sits above my desk and I have added to it - superglue, a screwdriver, spare shoelaces. When I picture myself at my best, I am not on a stage. I am three feet behind it, under a bad light, with the lid already off.

text:
My mother is a librarian, which is why the school asked me, and it is also why we are still not speaking about it properly a year later.

The school library had not been touched in fifteen years. Six thousand books, a Dewey system that had drifted so far from itself that the poetry sat in three separate places, and a card catalogue nobody had opened since before I was born. When Mr Adeyemi asked for volunteers to reorganise it over the summer I said yes before he finished the sentence, and I went home and told my mother, and she was delighted for about four minutes.

Then I told her my plan, which was to abandon Dewey entirely.

I had thought about it. Nobody in our school browses by number. I had watched people for a term: they come in wanting something like the last thing they read, or something a friend mentioned, then they wander, then they leave with nothing. Bookshops group by subject in ordinary words and people find things in bookshops constantly. So I proposed sections - Other Countries, People Who Actually Lived, How Things Work, Very Short Books - with a spreadsheet linking every title to its old number.

My mother said no. Not in an argument. She said it the way you tell someone something obvious. A classification system is not for the person browsing, she said. It is for the person who comes after you. You will leave school in two years and take the whole scheme with you in your head, and the next librarian will inherit six thousand books arranged according to the private taste of a sixteen-year-old.

I said that Dewey was also somebody's private taste, just an American man's from 1876, and that his taste had put every religion that was not Christianity into a single subdivision. She said that was true and beside the point. I said it was exactly the point. We went round like this at the kitchen table for most of an evening. It was the first time I had disagreed with her about the thing she has spent twenty-six years doing.

I did it my way. Eleven days, four volunteers, and by the end of August the library was resectioned, relabelled, the spreadsheet nine hundred rows long. Borrowing that autumn went up by a third. I am not going to pretend that number does not matter to me.

But last April our librarian left, and the woman who replaced her spent a fortnight unable to find anything. In June a Year Eight could not find a book on volcanoes, because I had shelved volcanoes under How Things Work and she had looked, reasonably, in Other Countries. My mother has never said I told you so. She asked in October how the library was going, and I said fine, and she nodded, and that was the whole exchange.

What I cannot resolve is that I still think I was right about the browsing and she was right about the inheritance, and I do not know how those two things are supposed to fit together. She believes a system should outlive the person who made it. I believe a system that nobody uses has already failed, whoever inherits it. We are both, I think, describing something true about what we are afraid of.

The spreadsheet is on the school server and also on a memory stick in my desk drawer. I check occasionally that it is still there.

text:
My brother Daniel is twenty and he fits industrial refrigeration units, mostly in supermarkets, mostly at night because that is when you can shut a chiller down. He is very good at it. He earns more than our mother did at his age and he owns a van. He did not go to university, and he did not go because he decided not to, and I have never been able to leave it alone.

We had the argument properly once, in the summer I turned sixteen, in the car park of a Tesco in Warrington at two in the morning while he waited for a compressor to come down to temperature. I had got a lift with him because I was interested in what he did, which was true, and because I wanted to make my case, which was also true and which he could see coming from about forty miles away.

My argument was the obvious one and I made it badly. That he had got four As. That his physics teacher had cried, actually cried, when he said he was not applying. That the trade was fine now but bodies do not stay fine, and that our uncle has a shoulder that does not go above his head any more. That he was closing a door at eighteen that gets heavier every year you leave it. I had prepared this. I think I even said the phrase "opportunity cost", in a car park, to my brother, at two in the morning.

He listened all the way through, which is worse than interrupting. Then he said: you keep telling me what I am giving up, and you have never once asked me what I am getting.

So I asked. And what he said was that he had spent thirteen years in rooms being told that the point of what he was doing now was what it would let him do later. Thirteen years of later. And that on his second week of the apprenticeship, a woman who ran a corner shop in Runcorn had shaken his hand because her freezers were working and she was not going to lose four thousand pounds of stock, and that nothing at school had ever felt like that, and he was not willing to be told that the feeling was a lesser thing than a degree by people who had never had it.

I did not have an answer. I still do not, exactly. But I also did not change my mind, and that is the part I find hard to write down honestly. I think I am right. I think there is a version of Daniel at thirty-five who wants to do something else and finds that the door has swollen shut, and I think loving someone includes saying so before it happens rather than after. I also know that every time I say it I am telling him that the life he is actually living is a provisional one, a holding position, and that must be an unbearable thing to hear from your younger brother.

So we have arrived at a settlement neither of us likes. I do not raise it. He knows I have not stopped thinking it. Occasionally he sends me a photograph of some enormous piece of pipework at three in the morning with no caption, and I send back a photograph of my chemistry notes, and that is the whole conversation, conducted entirely in exhibits.

I am applying to university this year to read engineering, which he thinks is funny, because half of what made me want it is watching him work. He drove me to an open day in the van. On the way back he asked whether they had said anything about refrigeration cycles and I said yes, actually, quite a lot, and he said good, and neither of us said anything else for a while.

text:
We lost the semi-final by a single ballot. Two-one. I found out standing in a corridor at a school in Sheffield that smelled like floor polish and cheap deodorant, holding a paper cup of squash, and my first thought was not about the loss at all. My first thought was: my dad is going to want to know which judge.

He did. He asked in the car before we got out of the car park.

Here is the thing about my father. He is not a pushy parent in the way that phrase usually means. He never made me do debating. He came to it because I did, and then he read about it obsessively, the way he does with everything, and by the time I was fifteen he could break down a first proposition case better than most of my teachers. He would sit at the back of rooms with a notebook. Afterwards, in the car, we would go through it line by line. I loved that. I want to be clear, because of where this is going, that I loved that.

The loss itself was not complicated. We were opposition, the motion was about mandatory voting, and about eight minutes in I realised our opponents had made a genuinely good point - that low turnout among the poorest voters is not a preference, it is a barrier, and compulsion removes the barrier. It was better than the argument I had prepared against it. And I did the thing you are trained to do. I did not engage with it. I reframed, I dodged, I attacked a weaker version of it that they had not said, and I did it smoothly enough that two judges bought it and one did not. The one who did not wrote on her ballot: *Opposition second speaker never actually answered the barrier point.* She was right.

I have that ballot. It is in a folder under my bed.

What I told my father in the car was that we lost. What I did not tell him, for about four months, was that I thought we deserved to.

The change did not happen in a moment, which I know is the wrong shape for this kind of essay. It happened over a season. I started, in practice rounds, doing something that our coach found irritating and my partner found actively dangerous: when the other side said something that was true, I said so. Out loud. Then I argued that it was not sufficient. That is a much harder speech to give. You are handing your opponent a sentence they can quote. You are also, and this took me a year to understand, the only person in the room who now looks like they are telling the truth.

My results got worse for a term and then better. Not the point, but I want to be honest that it worked out, because otherwise this is a story about virtue and it isn't.

The unresolved part is my dad.

He thinks I have talked myself into a handicap. He is not rude about it. He says things like, "You conceded the whole framework there," and, "You know they weren't going to give you credit for being fair." Last November, after a round I lost, he said that competitive debating is a game with rules and I had decided to play a different game and then be disappointed by the score. And I said - this came out worse than I meant it - that I did not want to get good at not answering questions, because I could already see what that turns into, and I would rather lose.

He went quiet. Then he said, "That's not what I taught you."

And that's it. That's where we are. We still go. He still sits at the back with the notebook, and the notes are still the best coaching I get, and I still read them twice. But there is a category of comment I now skip past, and he knows I skip past it, and neither of us has said so.

I do not think he is wrong about the game. He is right that the rules reward the thing I stopped doing. What I cannot make him see, or maybe what I cannot say properly, is that I was becoming very fast at a specific manoeuvre - hearing something true and instantly locating the angle that makes it disappear - and that I did not want to find out who I would be at thirty if I kept practising it four hours a week.

We had a round in Manchester in February. Motion about assisted dying. I conceded a point early, on purpose, in front of him. We won.

In the car he said the judges must have liked me. Which might be a compliment. I have decided to take it as one.

text:
For the first eleven weeks, the only person listening to Radio Fenn was my sister Orla, in her bedroom, forty feet from the studio, on purpose, so that the number would not be zero.

The station lives in what used to be a stock cupboard off the sixth-form corridor. I found it in Year Ten looking for a place to eat lunch away from people, and it had a broken projector and - this is the part I could not get over - a proper acoustic ceiling, because it had been a music practice room in the eighties. I asked Mr Halloran what would happen if I put a microphone in there. He said write it down and put it in my pigeonhole, which I have since learned is what teachers say to make a thing go away, and which did not work on me.

What I had was two hundred and forty pounds from a summer of shelf-stacking, a second-hand mixer off eBay with one dead channel, and a plan to stream it over the school's network at lunchtimes. The first broadcast was on a Tuesday in November. I talked for twenty-two minutes about nothing in particular and played four songs, and the listener count in the corner of the screen said one. It said one the next day too. It said one for most of a term.

I did it every weekday anyway. I want to be honest that this was not perseverance in any noble sense; it was that the cupboard was the first place in that school where I had felt entirely all right, and I would have gone in there and talked to nobody regardless of whether it was being broadcast.

It grew slowly and then not slowly. A teacher mentioned it. Two girls in Year Nine asked to do a Thursday slot about football. By the second year we had eleven presenters, a scheduling spreadsheet, and a Friday show where people submitted anonymous questions and we tried to answer them badly. The listener number is a few hundred now, which is not many, except that it is a few hundred people who chose it.

Orla and I do not agree about what any of this is.

She is twenty-two and she has known me longer than anyone, and her position, put plainly, is that the radio station is somewhere I go instead of being with people. She has said versions of this since the beginning. That I will talk for forty minutes into a microphone about my grandfather's allotment and then not manage four sentences at a family lunch. That the reason I love the cupboard is the reason she worries about it: nobody can interrupt me, nobody can look at me, and I have complete control over when it stops. She thinks I built a machine for being heard without being met.

The worst part of the argument, from my side, is that the first half of it is true. I do find broadcasting easier than talking. Of course I do. And she is not being unkind when she says it - she stayed in her bedroom listening to a dead-air stream for eleven weeks so that a boy she loves would not have a zero on his screen. That is not the behaviour of someone attacking me.

But I think she has the direction wrong, and I have never been able to say why in a way that lands. The station is not where I hide from people; it is the reason I know any of them. I have had a conversation with almost every person who has ever presented on it, because somebody has to teach them how to use the desk, and there is no way to teach somebody the desk without sitting nine inches away from them for an hour. Two of my closest friends arrived that way. When I imagine the version of me without the cupboard, he is not at a party. He is at the back of a common room, alone, and nobody knows he has anything to say.

We had it out properly in August, in her car, outside our nan's house. It ended with her saying "I just don't want you talking to a room," and me saying "It isn't a room," and both of us leaving it there.

She still listens most days. She sends me a message afterwards, usually one word. She has never missed a Friday.

text:
There is a stapled essay in the bottom drawer of my desk, eleven pages, on lined paper, with a comment in green ink at the end that I have read more times than I would like to admit. The comment says: This is competent. You are not a writer, and you should know that now rather than later.

I was fourteen. The essay was on Of Mice and Men and it was, I think, competent. That is not the part that stayed.

I did not throw it away. I put it in the drawer and did not look at it for about a year, and then I started looking at it fairly often, in a way that was not entirely healthy. When I wrote something I liked, I would take it out and read the green ink and feel a specific unpleasant thrill, half proof and half accusation.

I want to be fair to him. He was not being cruel, or did not think he was. He believed he was doing me a service by telling me early, and said as much when I asked him about it, once, standing at his desk after class with the pages in my hand and my voice not working properly. He said that a lot of teachers tell every student they can be anything, and that he thought this was dishonest, and that competent was not an insult. I have thought about that conversation for three years and I still cannot decide how much of it was principle and how much was a man having a bad Thursday.

What I know is what I did next, and it was not defiance. For about eight months I stopped writing anything that was not set work. I told myself I was being sensible. I was fourteen and an adult who read for a living had assessed me, and the reasonable response to that is to accept it. That period is the thing I would go back and change - not his comment, mine. The eight months of agreeing with him.

What ended it was small. Our school newsletter needed someone to write up a sports day and nobody volunteered, so I did it, and I made it funny on purpose, and a boy I did not know quoted a line of it back to me in the lunch queue two weeks later. But I noticed that I had spent forty minutes on four hundred words about the Year Eight relay and had enjoyed every one of them, and that this fact was not affected in any way by what was in the drawer.

I write now most days. Mostly things nobody sees. I have had two pieces in a regional youth magazine and one rejection that ran to a page and a half, which I have also kept, in the same drawer, because it took me seriously enough to be specific.

I keep the essay for a reason that has changed. At fifteen I kept it as evidence to be overturned. Now I keep it because it is the clearest example I own of how much weight I will hand to one confident adult if I am not paying attention. He was not lying and he was not right; he was one person, on one Thursday, reading eleven pages by a fourteen-year-old, and I let it decide something for the better part of a year.

I have not shown it to him. He still teaches there. Occasionally I think about walking in and putting the drawer's whole contents on his desk, and then I think that would be a story about him, and I would rather it stayed a story about me.

meta.topic: a teacher who told them they were not a writer

text:
The place is the bottom of the stairwell in our block, between the ground floor and the basement, where there is a window with a wide ledge and a radiator that comes on at six. It is not a nice place. It smells of the bins. But nobody has any reason to go down there, the light is on a timer you can slap back into life, and I have done most of my real thinking on that ledge since I was about fourteen.

What I do there is sit with a problem I cannot solve. Usually physics. For most of last year it was one specific problem.

It was from an old olympiad paper. A ball is dropped onto a fixed incline and bounces elastically, and you are asked where the second bounce lands. That is all. I got an answer in fifteen minutes and it was wrong, and I could not find the error, and I went back to it twenty times over four months.

I want to be honest about those four months. It was irritating. I would get an answer, check it against the back of the book, and be wrong by a factor I could not account for. Twice I gave up in a way that felt permanent.

The moment it turned was in February, on the ledge, and it was not a moment of solving anything. I stopped trying to get the answer and asked myself, out of frustration, why I was so certain the velocity after the bounce should be measured along the ground. The answer was that I had never chosen that. I had inherited it. Every problem I had ever done had horizontal and vertical axes, so I had drawn them on this one too without noticing it was a decision. Rotate the axes so one runs along the slope and the collision becomes trivial - one component flips, one carries on - and the whole thing falls out in four lines.

Four lines. Four months.

What changed my mind that night was not about physics. It was about where I had been looking. For four months I had been checking my working on the assumption that the error was inside the calculation. The error was in the frame I had set up before the calculation started, in a choice so automatic I could not see it as a choice. Since then I have found that most things I get badly wrong are like this. Not mistakes in the argument. Mistakes in the setup, made silently, in the first thirty seconds.

So: the stairwell. I am aware it is an odd answer to the question of where I feel most myself. My mother thinks I go down there to avoid my brother. But it is the only place I know where I am not performing competence at anybody. In a classroom, being stuck is a state to get out of quickly. On that ledge, being stuck is the entire activity, and I can sit inside it for an hour, not interrupted and not helped, which is the thing I actually want and the hardest to ask for.

I have that problem drawn on the back of a receipt, rotated axes and all, stuck inside my locker door. It is not there to remind me of the answer. It is there to remind me that I sat under a bad light next to the bins for four months, being wrong, and that this turned out to be the most useful place I have ever been.

meta.topic: the physics problem they could not stop thinking about
meta.prompt: Describe a place where you feel most yourself, and why.

text:
There is a spot on the wall above my desk where the paint has gone slightly grey, and it is my fault. For about two years now I have been standing in front of it with a mug of tea, not drinking the tea, and touching the wall with two fingers while I think. My mother has painted over it twice. It comes back.

The problem I am usually thinking about is not a hard one. That is the embarrassing part. In my second year of physics we were given a question about a ladder leaning against a frictionless wall, and we were told to find the angle at which it slips. I solved it. I got the mark. Then, walking home, I realised I did not understand why the wall being frictionless mattered so much when the wall was doing almost nothing anyway, and that I had produced a correct answer by a route I could not have defended if anyone had stopped me in the street and asked. I had matched the problem to a shape I recognised. The shape had been right. That is not the same as knowing.

So that evening I stood at the wall for the first time, and I have been doing some version of it ever since.

The habit is small enough to sound like nothing. Every night before I sleep, I take one thing I supposedly understand and try to say it out loud, to the wall, in ordinary words, with no equations and no jargon, until either I can or I discover that I cannot. That is it. Eight minutes, maybe ten. I do not write it down. I do not tell anyone I am doing it, mostly because "I explain physics to a wall" sounds like the beginning of a bad joke and my sister already has enough material.

What I found, very quickly, was how much of my knowledge was decoration. I could not explain, that first month, why a pushed object stops. I knew the answer - friction, of course, everybody knows friction - but when I tried to say what friction actually was, in words, I ran out after about eleven seconds and stood there holding a cold mug. Same with pressure. Same with why the moon does not fall down, which I had "known" since I was nine and could not defend at sixteen. Same, humiliatingly, with the ladder.

The ladder took me four months. Not four months of work; four months of eight-minute nights, most of which went nowhere. I would get halfway through and hit the same wall - not the painted one - where I could describe the forces but not say why they had to balance in that particular way, and then I would notice it was midnight and go to bed slightly annoyed. Then one night in February I was explaining something completely different, about a book falling off a shelf, and I heard myself say a sentence about how the floor pushes back exactly as hard as it needs to and not one newton more, because it is not deciding anything, it is just being squashed. And I stopped. Because that was the ladder. The whole thing had been sitting inside a sentence I already believed and had never bothered to actually listen to.

I want to be careful here, because I know how this story is supposed to go. I am meant to say that I felt a great light and became a physicist. What actually happened is that I stood in my room at half past eleven feeling extremely stupid for four months' worth of reasons, and then I went and made toast. The good feeling came later and it was quieter than triumph. It was something more like relief - the relief of a thing that had been slightly the wrong shape in my head finally sitting flat.

The habit has changed what I am like. I am slower now in arguments, which my friends find irritating. When someone says something confident about economics or about a person we both know, I have started noticing the difference between a claim I could explain and a claim I have simply heard often enough to repeat. Most of what I believe, it turns out, is in the second category, and I do not think that is a personal failing so much as how people work. But I do think there is a difference between not knowing something and not knowing that you do not know it, and the eight minutes are the only reliable method I have found for moving things from the second state to the first.

My physics teacher, Mr Aduba, once told the class that the purpose of a problem set is not the answers. I nodded along with everyone else. I did not understand what he meant for another year and a half, and I only understood it because I had been standing in front of a wall failing to explain a ladder.

I do not know yet what I will study, exactly. I know the shape of the thing I want to keep doing: taking something I am sure of, saying it plainly, and finding out. My mother says she will paint the wall again before I leave. I have told her not to bother. I would only put it back.

text:
For four years I sang in a church choir I did not believe in, and the thing I taught myself there was how to read music, which nobody ever sat down and explained to me.

I joined because my grandmother asked. She had sung in that choir since before my mother was born, and when her knees got bad she wanted somebody in the family holding the alto line. I said yes the way you say yes to a grandmother. I was thirteen and I had already quietly decided that I did not believe any of it, and I did not tell her that, and I still haven't.

Nobody in the choir taught anyone anything. That is not a complaint, it's just how it worked. The director handed out photocopied sheets on Thursday, played the alto line once on the piano, and then we sang. If you could not read the page you learned by ear, which most people did, and which I did for the first eight months. I would follow the woman beside me, half a beat behind, and hope.

The habit started because I was embarrassed. On the bus home from Thursday rehearsal, twenty minutes, I would put the sheet on my knees and try to work out which mark meant which sound. I had the melody in my head from rehearsal, so I had the answer key. All I had to do was match the shape on the paper to the shape in my memory. Up meant up. A filled-in note went past faster than a hollow one. Two lines and then a dot after a note meant it stretched.

Twenty minutes on a bus, once a week, for four years. That is the whole method. I never bought a book. I never looked anything up until much later, and when I finally did I found out I had gotten the names wrong for almost everything - I called the flat sign "the little b" for two years - but the system underneath was right, because I had built it out of things I could actually hear.

What learning it that way showed me is that I am much slower and much more stubborn than I thought I was. I did not have a breakthrough. There was no Thursday where it suddenly made sense. There was a Thursday about a year and a half in when the director put a new piece in front of us, something we had never heard, and I opened my mouth and the right note came out, and I remember being more suspicious than pleased. I thought it was luck. It happened again the next week.

I still sing there. I still don't believe it. My grandmother knows now - she asked me directly two winters ago and I did not lie to her, and she said that was fine and that I should keep coming, and I have. The disagreement is not settled and I do not think it will be.

But I can sight-read now, more or less, and I got it entirely off a bus seat with a photocopy on my knees, and I know exactly how long it took because I was there for every one of those twenty-minute pieces. It has made me distrust anyone who says a thing can be learned quickly. Mostly it has made me patient with the version of myself who is still bad at something, because that version is the one who does the actual work.

meta.topic: the church choir they sang in but did not believe in
meta.prompt: What is something you have taught yourself, and what did learning it without a teacher show you?

text:
The motorcycle was a 1978 Yamaha RD200 and it cost me eleven thousand rupees and every free hour of the summer I was sixteen, and at the end of it, it did not run.

I want to be precise about that, because there is a version of this story where it runs on the last day and everyone cheers, and I have caught myself telling that version to people who were not there. It did not run. It has never run. It is in my grandfather's shed right now with a tarp over it.

I bought it from a man in Sarita Vihar who was selling it because it had been sitting in his family's parking spot for nine years and his wife wanted the space. He was honest with me. He said it hadn't started since before his son was born. I heard that as a challenge, which was the first mistake, and I paid him in cash from my tutoring money, and my cousin and I pushed it four kilometres home because neither of us had thought about how you move a motorcycle that does not move.

Then I spent June, July, and half of August on it.

I learned a great deal. I learned to take a carburettor apart and put it back with the same number of parts. I learned that a two-stroke needs the crank seals to hold pressure or it will never idle right no matter what else you do, and I learned this the hard way, over about five weeks, after I had already replaced the plug and the points and the fuel line and the reed valves and the tank, which I lined with a kit that cost more than I told my mother it cost. I learned that YouTube videos of American men in clean garages are not made for a bike sold only in Asia in 1978.

Around the second week of August I hit the thing. Not hard. I had it on the stand and I had kicked it maybe two hundred times that afternoon and my leg was shaking, and it caught for a second and died, and I kicked the side of it with my heel and something plastic cracked. Then I sat on the floor of the shed and I was furious in a way that scared me a bit.

That was the day I changed my mind about what I was doing.

Because what I noticed, sitting there, was that I was not angry about the motorcycle. I was angry because I had told about nine people I was rebuilding a motorcycle, and August was ending, and I was going to have to tell those nine people that I had not. The bike was fine. The bike had been sitting for nine years and would sit for nine more and did not care. The whole summer had quietly stopped being about the machine somewhere around the third week and become about the announcement.

What I did next was I stopped, which sounds like giving up and I have gone back and forth on whether it was. I put the tarp on it. I did not touch it again that year. What I did instead, for the last two weeks of that summer, was write down everything I had actually learned about that engine - the sequence, the torque figures, which bolt on the left case is a different length and will bottom out and strip if you swap them - and it came to fourteen pages in a notebook.

I go and read that notebook sometimes. It is the only real thing I made that summer. I still want to finish the bike. I have not told anyone that I want to, which is different from last time, and I think that is the point.
