text:
The habit was that I wrote down what people said, exactly, in a small notebook, and it got me into more trouble than anything else I have done.

I started doing it in ninth grade for a boring reason. I joined the school paper and my first assignment was a piece about the new cafeteria contractor, and I interviewed the vice principal and then went home and wrote up what he had told me, and when it was published he said he had not said that. I did not have proof. He was probably not lying either - I think he genuinely remembered it differently - but the piece got pulled and I got a talking-to and my byline was replaced with the word Staff.

So I bought a notebook. The kind with the elastic band. And from then on, whenever anybody said anything to me for a story, I wrote it as they said it, in the moment, with the date at the top of the page. Not summary. The words.

For two years this was invisible. It looked like a tic. People teased me for it - my friend Ravi used to say things very slowly in a fake official voice so I could keep up. I filled four notebooks. Most of what is in them is nothing: what time the bus leaves for the debate meet, somebody's guess about the exam schedule, three pages about a broken water cooler.

Then in eleventh grade I wrote a piece about the school's counselling office. It was not an exposé. It was supposed to be a service piece about how to book an appointment. But in reporting it I found out that eleven students had been told there was a waiting list, and that there was no waiting list, and that the actual situation was that the counsellor's hours had been reduced to one afternoon a week in September without anyone announcing it. I put that in the piece, four sentences, near the end.

The article ran on a Thursday. On Friday I was in the principal's office with my faculty advisor and a man from the district whose role was never explained to me, and I was told that I had misrepresented the school, and that the counsellor had never said her hours were cut, and that I had invented the number eleven.

I had page seventy-three of notebook three. Date, time, her office, her words, including the sentence about the reduction and including her saying that she had asked twice about it. And I had the eleven students, each with a page.

It did not go the way it does in a film. Nobody apologised. What happened was that the room got quiet and the man from the district asked to see the notebook and I said he could look at the page and not the notebook, which I am still a little proud of, and after about ten minutes they told me I could go and that the matter was closed. The article stayed up. In January the counsellor's hours went back to three afternoons and no announcement was made about that either.

I got a reputation out of it that I am not sure I wanted. Teachers are careful around me now. One of them said, half joking, that talking to me is like being deposed.

But I have kept doing it, and I have thought a lot about why the habit worked, and I do not think it is because it protected me. It is that writing down exactly what someone says forces you to hear exactly what they said, which is different from what you expected them to say, and the gap between those two is where every real story I have ever found has been sitting.

I am on notebook seven. Most of it is still nothing.

text:
In eighth grade a boy named Tomas transferred into our school and he was deaf, and I learned sign language for him, and I have spent four years slowly understanding that I got the whole thing wrong.

I want to describe the wrongness accurately, because the story sounds good if you stop halfway. Here is the good-sounding half: I taught myself Indian Sign Language, badly at first, from videos and from a deaf woman's channel and from a photocopied dictionary I found at a library in Karol Bagh, an hour and a half of practice most nights for about eight months, until I could hold a real conversation. All of that is true. It is also the part that gets me a compliment when I tell it, which is why I no longer tell it that way.

The wrongness is this. I never asked him.

I decided, in the first week, that the reason Tomas ate lunch alone was that nobody could talk to him, and I decided that I would be the solution to this, and I began. I did not ask what he wanted. I did not ask whether he would rather I helped the class learn ten signs each than have one person learn four hundred. I did not ask whether he liked the interpreter he already had, or whether he was in fact lonely at all, or whether the thing he most needed was somebody to sit down without a project.

For eight months I practised at him. That is the phrase that arrived in my head at some point in tenth grade and has not left. Practised at him.

I found out what he actually thought in December of that first year, and not from him. His sister said it, in passing, at a school thing - she said, half laughing, that Tomas said I signed like a person reading a manual, and that he mostly went along with it because I was clearly having a very good time.

I was fourteen and I was humiliated for about a week, and then I did the thing I still think was correct, which was that I went to him and asked, four months late, what he wanted. It was an awkward conversation and my signing was not good enough for it and we ended up typing half of it on my phone.

What he wanted, it turned out, was for people to stop looking at his interpreter when they spoke to him. That was the main one. It was not a thing that required anyone to learn a language. It required people to move their eyes about fifteen degrees.

Tomas and I are still friends. My signing is much better now, and I use it, and I do not regret learning it. What I regret is the shape of the thinking - that I built a large private solution to a problem I had assumed the existence of, because assuming was faster and, if I am honest, because the solution was more flattering to me than asking would have been.

I still catch myself doing it. I caught myself doing it last month with my grandmother and her phone. I stopped, and asked, and the answer was not what I had built.

text:
The belief I challenged that summer was that understanding comes before doing, and the thing that dismantled it was a habit so small I did not know I had it until my grandfather pointed it out.

The motorcycle was a Bajaj Chetak, technically a scooter, which my grandfather bought new in 1989 and stopped riding in 2016 when his hip went. It sat under a sheet behind the house. I asked for it the summer I was sixteen because I wanted something to do that was not a screen, and he said yes on the condition that I did not sell it, which had not occurred to me and which I found slightly insulting at the time.

I approached it the way school had taught me to approach anything. I read first. I read a service manual PDF cover to cover before I touched a bolt - one hundred and forty pages, two evenings, and I took notes. I could have told you the ignition timing spec and the correct plug gap and the torque figure for the flywheel nut. I understood, in the way you understand a chapter.

Then I opened it up and I did not know what I was looking at. Nothing in the photographs was oriented the way the object was oriented. The manual said remove the flywheel and there was no way to remove the flywheel because it requires a puller, which the manual assumes you have, and which nobody in my house had ever heard of.

The habit started around the second week. When I got stuck, I would put my hands on the part and just move it. Turn it, wiggle it, follow the thing it was attached to with my fingers to where it went. Ten minutes at a time, no thinking, no phone. I did it because I was frustrated and it was something to do with my hands instead of giving up.

Almost every problem I solved that summer, I solved during those ten minutes.

Not because touching is magic. Because my hands would find the thing the manual had not mentioned - that this cable runs behind that bracket, that the cover will not come off until you loosen a bolt on the other side, that the reason the throttle stuck was a rubber grommet that had gone hard, which no page anywhere describes because it is not a fault, it is just what happens to rubber in Delhi after twenty-nine years.

My grandfather came out one afternoon in July and watched me for a while and said, you have started listening to it. I said I was just fiddling. He said that is what listening looks like.

So the belief. I had genuinely thought that competence was downstream of comprehension - that you read, you understand, and then you can do. What I actually found is that with a physical object the arrow goes the other way most of the time. You do, badly, with your hands, and the understanding assembles itself afterwards out of what your hands found out. The manual made sense to me in September in a way it had not in June, and nothing about the manual had changed.

The outcome, in the small sense, is that the Chetak runs. It runs poorly. It smokes and the horn does not work and it will not start below about eighteen degrees.

The larger outcome is that I have stopped waiting to understand things before beginning them, which has made me worse at some subjects and much better at others. In physics I now do the problem wrong first on purpose, quickly, before reading the section. My teacher thinks this is a strange method. It came off the back of a house in July with a grommet in my hand.

text:
My grandmother makes a dish called ghormeh sabzi about nine times a year, and she has never written it down, and she will not, and this is the only thing she and I have ever genuinely fought about.

I started trying to record it when I was fourteen. I stood at her elbow with a notebook. She would put a handful of dried fenugreek into her palm and I would say how much, and she would say this much, and hold out her palm, and I would write "1 palm (Maman's palm, smaller than mine)" and she would laugh at me. The kidney beans soak overnight, except when they don't. The limoo omani get pierced with a fork, four holes or five, and when I asked whether it mattered she said it depends on the lime.

I kept at it for two years. I have eleven versions in a green notebook. None of them work. I have made it seventeen times and it has been good four times and I could not tell you what was different.

The fight, when it came, was in her kitchen in March, over the herbs. I wanted her to weigh them. I had bought a scale. I said, if you don't write it down it dies with you, and I said it in that flat cruel way you can only use on somebody who will forgive you, and she put the scale in the drawer under the tea towels and said, "Then you will learn it the way I learned it."

She learned it standing next to her own mother in Shiraz for eleven years. She was not taught. She was present. She says the recipe is not information, that the amounts change with the herbs and the herbs change with the year, and that a written recipe would teach me to follow a number instead of the pot. I say that is a beautiful idea that will not survive her, and that half her sisters are gone and I cannot call them.

We have had this argument maybe six times. It has not moved. She is eighty-one.

What changed is not the argument. What changed is that I stopped bringing the notebook.

I go on Saturdays now. I do not write anything. I chop, badly at first, and she corrects my knife by moving my hand, and I have learned that the herbs go in when the onions are past golden and starting to catch, and that you know the sabzi is done frying when the kitchen stops smelling green and starts smelling dark, which is not a sentence I could have written down two years ago because I did not have the sense it describes. I know now that her palm holds about forty grams. I measured it once, when she was out of the room, which I am not proud of and which I did anyway.

I still think I am right. I think she is wrong about the notebook, and I think it is a kind of vanity, and I have not said that part out loud and I am not going to. She still thinks I am a person who wants a shortcut. Neither of us has conceded anything.

But I have made it three times now without her in the room and it has been right all three, and the last time my mother went quiet at the table, which is the only review that counts in our house. So something transferred. Not through the notebook. Through two hundred Saturdays and a hand on my hand.

The green notebook is still in my desk with its eleven wrong versions. I have not thrown it out. I do not expect to win, and I still go every week, because she is eighty-one and the arithmetic is not complicated.

text:
The article ran on page three of the November issue, under a headline I had argued for in a meeting: "Where Does the Activity Fee Actually Go?" I had spent six weeks on it. I had pulled the budget summaries the school posts every spring, made a spreadsheet, and found that the line item labeled "student programming" had shrunk by nineteen percent over four years while the fee itself had risen twice. I quoted two students who said they had never seen a dollar of it. I did not quote anyone from the administration, because the assistant principal did not answer my second email and I decided that silence was itself a kind of answer.

Three days later I was sitting across from her. She had a printout of my article with sections underlined in green pen, which somehow felt worse than red. She did not tell me I was wrong. She told me that the "student programming" line had been split into three lines in 2019, that two of those lines lived in a different section of the report, and that the total had gone up, not down. She slid a page across the desk. She was right. My nineteen percent was an artifact of a formatting change I had not thought to check.

What I remember most is not the embarrassment, though there was plenty of that. It is the thing I said next, which I am still not proud of. I said that the overall point still stood - that students did not know where the money went, and that the confusion in the report proved it. And she said, mildly, "That might be true. But that isn't what you wrote."

I went home and argued with her in my head for two days. I had a whole case. Journalism is adversarial. Institutions do not volunteer their failures. If I had waited for a comment I would have waited forever, and the fee would have gone up again in the meantime. I believed that the value of a story like mine was in the pressure it created, and that pressure was a blunt instrument by nature. Getting a number slightly wrong seemed like a rounding error against that.

The moment my mind actually changed was small and happened on a Tuesday. A sophomore I barely knew stopped me by the vending machines and said the article was great, that the school was stealing from us, and did I know if anyone was going to sue. He was genuinely angry. He had read my number and built something in his head on top of it, and my number was made of nothing. I had wanted to create pressure and I had. It was pointing in a direction I could no longer defend.

I asked for space in the December issue. Not a correction buried at the bottom - a full column, in my name, explaining the error, showing the two reports side by side, and then asking the question I should have asked in the first place: why is a public budget written so that a motivated seventeen-year-old with a spreadsheet gets it wrong? That question turned out to be a better story. The business office sent someone to talk to me for it. She was not hostile. She said the format was inherited from a state template nobody liked. The piece ended up longer and less exciting than the original and I think it was the first real thing I ever wrote.

I still believe institutions should be pushed. I have not become gentler about that. What I gave up was the idea that being right in general excuses being wrong in particular, that a good cause launders a bad fact. Now, when I finish a draft, I go back through and mark every sentence that is a number or a claim about someone else, and I make myself find where it came from. Most of the time it holds. The times it doesn't are the reason I do it.

text:
The scanner is called an RF gun and it weighs about six hundred grams, which does not sound like much until hour seven. It is bright yellow, with a rubber bumper and a pistol grip worn smooth at the trigger, and every one at the Brantley Road distribution centre has a number stencilled on the handle. Mine was 47. It was not mine - you sign one out at the start of shift and back in at the end - but for eleven months I took 47 whenever it was on the rack, because its trigger had a slightly shorter travel than the others and by August I could feel the difference.

I worked Thursday and Friday nights, ten until six, from the week I turned sixteen. My mother's hours had been cut and we had a plan about it that we did not discuss much. The warehouse is a hundred and ninety thousand square feet of racking under lights that never change, and there is no window anywhere in the picking area, so time inside it is measured entirely by the gun. It tells you where to go. Aisle, bay, level, quantity. You go, you scan, you take, you scan again, and it gives you the next one. It also tells you how fast you are doing it. There is a number in the corner of the screen that is your rate against target, and it updates constantly, and I would like to say I ignored it but I did not ignore it once in eleven months.

What the gun taught me, more than anything, is what it feels like to be measured by something that cannot see you. On a bad night the number goes red and there is no argument to make. It does not know that bay 14 in aisle J has a light out and you have to read the labels by phone torch. It does not know that the tote you just filled with forty-eight litres of fabric softener is heavier than the one the person ahead of you got. It is not unfair, exactly. It is just indifferent, which I found was a different and stranger thing.

I got fast. By spring I was running about a hundred and ten percent of target most nights, and I understood by then that this was not a virtue, it was a set of small tricks: hold the gun in your left hand so your right is free, walk the aisle in the direction that makes the next pick shorter, learn which SKUs come in cases you can split with a thumb. Nobody teaches you this. There is a training video about lifting. The actual job is transmitted between people at four in the morning, in fragments, near the vending machines.

The people are the part the gun does not record. Dariusz, who had been a structural engineer in Gdańsk and did the maths on his rate in his head faster than the screen did. Marie, who was sixty-one and slower than everyone and who nobody ever once complained about, because she was the only person who noticed when someone was having a bad week. A boy from my year named Callum who I had barely spoken to in five years of school and who became, on the night shift, someone I would tell things to. School has a hundred ways to sort people. A warehouse has one, and it is the number, and because the number is so obviously stupid, everyone quietly agrees to judge each other by something else instead.

I handed 47 back in for the last time in September, before sixth form got serious. The rack was in the same place, the lights were the same, the girl signing it out after me looked about my age and did not look up.

I am going to study economics, and I know how that sentence sounds after this one. But I want to be the kind of person who, when a system produces a number, asks what the number cannot see. I held one of those numbers in my hand for eleven months. It was yellow, it weighed six hundred grams, and it never once knew that the light in J14 was out.

text:
I carry a bobbin case in my pencil box. It is smaller than a bottle cap, nickel-coloured, with a little steel arm on one side and a screw the size of a grain of rice on the other. It came out of a Singer that my mother has had since before I was born, and it is the first thing I ever fixed. Nobody taught me how.

The machine started skipping and eating the thread in the winter of ninth standard. The mechanic in Sadar Bazaar takes three hundred rupees and does not explain anything; he turns the machine towards himself, does something for four minutes, and turns it back. I asked him once what had been wrong and he said the machine was old. That answer annoyed me for weeks, which is probably the real beginning of this.

So I opened it myself. I watched videos where the man's hands were in the way of the part he was naming, and I read a scanned manual in English I half understood, and mostly I took things out and put them back and wrote in a notebook what happened. For eleven days that machine did not sew. My mother was patient in a way I did not deserve.

The bobbin case is where I finally understood something. All the trouble was in that screw. It sets how hard the case grips the thread coming off the bobbin, and the whole stitch is a negotiation between that grip and the tension from above. Too loose and loops come up under the cloth. Too tight and the top thread gets pulled down and the seam puckers. There is a test where you hold the case by its thread and let it hang, and give it a small jerk, and it should slip down about an inch and stop. Nobody can tell you what an inch feels like in your fingers. You have to be wrong about it maybe forty times.

That is the first thing learning it alone showed me. There is a large gap between knowing the name of a part and knowing the part, and a teacher can only carry you across the first half of it. The second thing is that I learned to work backwards from the symptom. A tailor does not say the timing is off; he says it is making a knot on the underside, or the needle is breaking on thick cloth, and you have to translate that. With no one to ask, the only way to be sure was to change one thing at a time, which is a slow, boring discipline I did not have before. The third thing is less comfortable. I broke a needle plate on a neighbour's machine by forcing a screw, and I had to go tell her, and pay for it out of my tuition money. Learning without a teacher means the mistakes belong to you completely, and so do the repairs after them.

Since then I have worked most Sundays at Iqbal chacha's tailoring shop in our lane, not sewing, just servicing. Cleaning lint out of the feed dogs, oiling, setting hook timing on the two industrial machines, arguing with him about whether a wobbling handwheel matters. He pays me in samosas and in letting me take apart anything a customer has abandoned. I still keep the old bobbin case, even though the machine it belongs to has a new one now. When I am stuck on something that is not a machine, I have started asking the same question I asked that screw, which is: what exactly is this holding, and how tightly.

text:
The most important object I own is a cracked twenty-litre bucket that used to hold wall putty. It is white going grey, there are four holes drilled in the bottom with a heated nail, and a split runs down one side which my father closed with a strip of cycle tube and copper wire. It sits in the north-west corner of a balcony that is four feet by nine. For six years it has grown chillies.

The seeds came from my grandmother, in a plastic film canister that smelled of her cupboard. She grew sannam chillies in Guntur district on ground that belonged to her, and when my father took a job in Ghaziabad and we became people with a flat instead of land, she gave him the canister at the railway station as though it were money. He put it on a shelf and forgot it. I was eleven, and I found it, and I planted eight seeds in the putty bucket because it was the biggest container in the house. Two came up.

Almost everything I know now, I learned because that balcony is a bad place to grow anything. It faces north-west, so it gets direct sun only from about half past two until sunset, and in the monsoon it gets sheets of water off the roof of the flat above. I started dragging the bucket, first by hand and later on a wooden board with castor wheels my uncle welded, so it followed the light along the railing. I learned that market soil goes to concrete in a pot, and started mixing it with cocopeat and the compost from a second bucket where our vegetable peels go. I learned that chilli flowers on a balcony often fall off because there is no wind and no bee, and that you can shake the plant yourself, or touch each flower with a cotton bud, which I did for one whole February like a fool and which worked.

The year I was fourteen I lost everything. Thrips, which are so small that for three weeks I thought the leaves were curling from heat. I sprayed a neem solution I mixed too strong and burned what the insects had left. The bucket stood empty from March to July with a dead stem in it, and I did not throw the stem away, which my mother thought was strange. I had run out of the canister seeds by then, all except a pinch, and I was afraid of using them badly.

What got me back was that our neighbour in 301 asked for green chillies one evening because the shop had shut. I had none, and I minded that more than I expected. There are fourteen containers on our balcony now, and eleven of them are chillies: the Guntur ones from the canister, a bird's eye variety a friend's mother sent from Kerala, and a bhut jolokia that has produced exactly nine pods in two years and is the most arrogant plant I have met. I keep seeds in labelled envelopes and give them to whoever asks. Six flats in our building grow something now, mostly badly, and there is a WhatsApp group where people send photographs of yellow leaves and I say the same four things about drainage.

I am careful about what I claim for this. I have not solved anything. Eleven pots do not feed a family, and my grandmother, who died two winters ago, would have laughed at the amount of trouble I go to for a harvest she would call a handful. But I think this is the part of me that explains the rest. It is where I learned to look at a problem for three weeks before I understood it, and to accept that a thing can be entirely my fault and still be fixable. It is also, honestly, where I kept hold of a place I have only visited nine times.

The bucket is still in the corner. The copper wire has gone green and I have not replaced it, because the repair is now older than most of my memories of the plant that first grew there. Whatever I study, wherever I go, I am fairly sure I will start by finding out which direction the window faces.

text:
The shelter listed Biscuit as a two-year-old shepherd mix, house-trained, good with children. Two of those three turned out to be guesses. He came home in the back of my mother's car in March, shaking hard enough that the seat belt buckle rattled against the door, and for four days he lived under the dining table and would not eat unless the kitchen was empty. I decided, almost immediately, that I would be the one who fixed him.

I had a system. I had watched maybe forty hours of training videos by then, and I wore a canvas pouch of freeze-dried liver on my belt like a tool. Sit, stay, come, place. Three sessions a day, ten minutes each, exactly as the videos prescribed. I logged them in a notebook: date, duration, treats used, success rate. For a while the numbers moved. He learned sit in a week and his name in two. I remember telling my sister that people who complained about rescue dogs were simply not consistent.

Then we hit the thing that would not move. Biscuit could not be left alone. Not for an hour, not for ten minutes. He would scream, which is the only accurate word, and chew the doorframe until his gums bled, and once he went through a window screen and was found four streets away by a man walking to work. I treated this like every other item on my list. I built a schedule of departures: thirty seconds, then a minute, then two. I bought a camera and counted the barks. When the graph refused to bend, I ran the sessions longer, because longer had always worked before.

It took a vet to tell me what I had actually been doing. She used the word threshold and explained that every time I pushed past the point where he had already begun to panic, I was not teaching him that I come back. I was teaching him that panic is the ordinary condition of an afternoon. Eight months of careful, well-documented work had made him measurably worse, and my notebook was the record of it. You can find the exact page where the percentages stop and I started writing only the dates.

What I did next is less impressive than I wish it were. I stopped training him. We put him on medication, which I had resisted because it felt like conceding that effort was not the answer. My mother took over the departures at a pace so slow it embarrassed me, thirty seconds for three weeks before we tried forty. Biscuit is six now. He can be left for about three hours. That is not a triumph, only a life. He sleeps by the radiator and still cannot ride in a car.

I think about the notebook more than I expected to. Not because I was lazy or cruel, since I was neither, but because I was certain, and the certainty was the whole problem. I had confused working hard at something with being right about it, and I had built an entire apparatus of measurement that could only tell me how faithfully I was repeating the mistake. It never occurred to me to ask whether the thing I was measuring was the thing that mattered. I try to check that now, in labs and in arguments and with people, and I am honest enough to say I am usually not fast enough about it.

text:
My father coached me from when I was six until I was twelve, and last year I took the under-11s at the same club, on the same pitch, with the same cones out of the same shed. We went two wins, one draw, thirteen losses. I have the sheet. I did not throw it away.

The disagreement started in November and we have not finished it.

My rule was that everyone played half the match. I did not announce it as a philosophy. I just wrote the sheet that way every Saturday, and when we were losing by two at halftime I still took Rahul off and put Freddie on, because Freddie had come to every training session in the rain and had never once complained about not playing.

My father watched from behind the goal, the way he does, hands in his coat. After the Ashwell game in January - we lost six-one and Freddie was on for the last twenty of it - he said in the car that I was being unfair to the good players in the name of being fair to the others, and that at eleven, children can tell the difference between being included and being managed, and that Freddie knew perfectly well he was on because of a rule and not because of anything he had done.

I said that was exactly backwards. I said Freddie showed up in the rain and that was something he had done.

We have had that conversation, in some version, maybe nine times. It always ends the same way, which is politely. He says I am kind. He does not mean it entirely as a compliment. I say he only remembers the winning teams. He does not deny it.

What I did next was smaller than winning an argument. I stopped defending the half-match rule in the abstract and started asking the boys. Not "do you want to play more", because every eleven-year-old says yes. I asked what the worst part of a Saturday was. Four of them said the same thing, and it was not the losing and it was not the bench. It was standing in the line for the first ten minutes of training not knowing what we were doing. So I rewrote training instead. Everything starts inside ninety seconds now, small-sided, no line.

We still lost. We lost the next four. But the sessions filled up, and by March I had nineteen boys at a Tuesday in February, which the club had not had in years, and the man who runs the juniors asked me what I was doing differently.

I do not think I have proved my father wrong. I think it is possible he is right about the matches and I am right about the Tuesdays, and that we are having two arguments that only sound like one. He has come to more training this season. He stands at the far side. Last week he moved a drill I had set up badly and I let him, and neither of us said anything about it, and I have decided that not saying anything is not the same as agreeing.

text:
The ice storm took the lines down on a Thursday and the power did not come back until the following Wednesday night. I was fourteen. What I remember is that I loved it, and that loving it is the part I got wrong.

For me it was a holiday. School closed. We cooked on the camp stove in the garage with the door cracked, and my father showed me how to bleed the water heater so the pipes would not split, and at night we played cards by a lantern and my mother told a story about her cousin in Ohio that I had never heard and have never heard since. I thought: this is what a family is when you take the screens out. I actually said something like that out loud, on maybe the third night, in the pleased voice of a boy who has recently discovered an idea. My father agreed with me. My grandmother, who lived with us then, did not say anything.

She was eighty-one and on oxygen. Her concentrator ran on electricity. What I did not know at the time, because nobody told me and because I did not ask, was that my parents had spent Friday morning calling around for a generator, and Saturday driving to my aunt's in Millbrook with two cylinders of backup oxygen in the trunk that were rated for about thirty-six hours, and Sunday deciding whether to move her to the hospital, which would have meant a bed she might not have gotten back. I found this out two years later, at a Thanksgiving, when my aunt mentioned it the way you mention weather.

I had been playing cards. I had been having the best week of that winter.

What I still turn over is not that I failed to help. There was nothing a fourteen-year-old could have done about a generator. It is that I built a whole small philosophy out of that week - about simplicity, about how we do not really need all of this - and I built it standing on a floor that other people were holding up. The candlelight was charming because it was temporary and because somebody else was tracking the hours of oxygen left. Every romantic idea I had about going without depended on the fact that I was not the one keeping anybody alive.

I think about it now whenever I hear the word resilient. People use it about neighborhoods after storms, and they mean it kindly, and sometimes it is true. But I have learned to ask who is doing the work that the word is covering for. When our school ran a canned-food drive after the floods last year, I was on the committee, and I pushed us to ask the shelter what they actually needed instead of guessing. They said batteries and extension cords and, oddly, phone chargers. Not romantic. Not simple.

My grandmother died in 2022, of something unrelated. She never brought that week up with me. I do not know if she was frightened. I have decided not to ask my mother, which may itself be a thing I am getting wrong. But I no longer trust an experience of hardship that felt good to the person having it.

text:
The filing cabinet was beige, three drawers, and it sat against the wall behind my desk at the internship for the entire six weeks. Someone had put a strip of masking tape across the top drawer and written SERVICE TICKETS 1998 - 2004 on it in marker. There was a dent in the bottom drawer at about shin height, the kind of dent a person makes with a foot when a drawer sticks. That cabinet is the only thing from that summer I could draw from memory.

I want to be honest about what the internship was. I was told to come in at nine. I was given a desk, a login that did not work for the first four days, and a supervisor who was genuinely busy and genuinely apologetic and who, when I asked for work, would say he'd get me something and then not. I sat there. I read the company website twice. By the end of the first week I had done about ninety minutes of actual assigned tasks, and most of that was moving chairs for a meeting.

The cabinet was the thing I looked at. Around day eight I opened it, mostly out of boredom, and found that it was full - genuinely full, jammed - with carbon-copy service tickets, handwritten, going back to the year before I was born. Customer name, address, what broke, what the technician did, how long it took. Nobody had touched them in a long time. There was dust on the top edge of the folders in a way that dust does not get in three years.

I asked if I could do something with them. My supervisor said sure, in the tone of someone agreeing to a thing he did not expect to be asked about again.

So I taught myself a spreadsheet. Not a spreadsheet the way I had used one in school, where you type numbers in boxes. I mean I had to figure out how to turn six thousand handwritten pieces of paper into something a person could ask a question of. I typed tickets in for two days before I realized my columns were wrong, and that I had been entering "burner assembly" and "burner assy" and "brnr assembly" as three different things, and that everything I had done was going to be useless unless I fixed it. I started over. I learned what a dropdown list is because I needed to stop myself from typing the same thing three ways. I learned pivot tables from a video, badly, and then from another video, less badly. I learned that a date typed as text does not sort, which took me an embarrassing afternoon.

By the last week I had about eleven hundred tickets in and I could show a chart of which part failed most often in which month. I showed my supervisor. He was interested for maybe four minutes, which is a real four minutes and more than I expected, and he asked me to email it to him. I do not know if he opened it.

What learning it without a teacher showed me is smaller than what I would like to claim. It is this: nobody was going to tell me my columns were wrong. In every class I have ever taken, being wrong is a thing that gets caught for you, usually within a week, usually in red. In front of that cabinet the only person who could catch it was me, and I caught it late, and starting over cost me two days I could not get back. I did not enjoy that. I am not sure I would have chosen it.

But I have noticed since that I check my own work differently now. I look for the version of the mistake I cannot see, the one where everything is running fine and the categories are quietly wrong. That is what the cabinet taught me, and it was not trying to teach me anything.

text:
The bracket is still in my desk drawer. It is a piece of 3mm aluminium about the size of a playing card, with four holes drilled in it and one corner filed down where it used to catch on the servo horn. I keep it because it is the smallest object I own that proves I was wrong about something important.

For most of two years I believed that our robotics team's problem was a lack of ambition. We were a small school with a small budget, and every design meeting ended with someone saying we should keep it simple. I hated that phrase. Simple felt like a word people used when they had already decided to lose. So when I became build lead in Year 12, I pushed for a four-bar lifting arm with a rotating gripper, which meant more joints, more moving parts, and more brackets like this one holding it all together. Priya, who had been on the team longer than me, said we were building something we wouldn't have time to test. I told her testing was what the last week was for.

The bracket was the piece I made myself, on a Tuesday, in the workshop after everyone had gone home. I cut it, drilled it, filed the corner, and bolted it into the arm. It held the second joint. It worked in the workshop. It worked in the corridor outside the workshop, which we used as a practice field because it was the only space long enough. It worked eleven times in a row the night before we drove to Coventry.

On stage, in the second match, the arm rose about forty centimetres and then stopped. The bracket had not broken. That is the part I did not expect. It had bent - a soft, almost polite curve, maybe five degrees - because the competition floor had a lip at the edge of the field that our corridor did not have, and the extra jolt of going over it put a load on the joint at an angle I had never modelled. Five degrees was enough to bind the servo. We scored eleven points across three matches. Teams with two-motor scoop designs, the kind of thing I would have called unambitious, scored sixty.

What I had actually believed, I realised on the drive home, was not that complexity was good. I had believed that being cautious was a character flaw, and that the people around me who wanted fewer parts wanted less of everything, including less of themselves. That was an insult I had been carrying quietly for two years, and it was wrong. Priya wasn't unambitious. She had simply understood something I hadn't: that every part you add is another thing that must be true for the whole to work, and you only have so many hours to make things true.

I did not stop wanting to build difficult machines. What changed is that I now ask a different question first. Not "can this work" but "how many ways can this fail, and have I seen the floor it will fail on." This year we built a two-joint arm instead of four. It is less impressive on paper. It went eight matches without stopping.

I kept the bracket because it did not fail dramatically. It bent five degrees. Most of the things I get wrong will look like that: not a break, just a small quiet deviation from what I assumed, somewhere I never thought to check. The bracket sits in the drawer to remind me to go and look.

text:
My mother thinks that summer was the worst thing that happened to me, and I have never been able to convince her otherwise. We have had this argument, in different forms, maybe forty times. It always ends the same way, with her saying "you were fifteen" as though that settles it, and me saying "I know" as though that settles it too.

The shelf was in the Fairmount branch, second floor, the section between the window and the water fountain. Call numbers 813 through 813.54, American fiction, which meant it ran from a water-stained Willa Cather to four copies of the same John Updike nobody had checked out since 2009. Seventy-one books. I counted them the first week of June because I wanted to know what I was agreeing to.

I did not choose that shelf for any reason worth defending. My friend Priya had gone to Ahmedabad for the summer, the pool cost eleven dollars, and my father had just moved into the apartment on Delancey with the balcony that faced a parking structure. The library was air conditioned and free and nobody there asked me how I was doing. I sat in the same orange chair every morning at ten. I read the way you eat when you are not hungry but the food is in front of you.

Here is where my mother and I disagree. She says I hid. She says a fifteen-year-old who reads seventy-one novels in eleven weeks is not curious, he is barricaded, and that if she had understood at the time what she was watching she would have driven me to the pool herself and paid the eleven dollars. She says this with real grief in her voice, which is the part I cannot argue with, because I think she is grieving something she did not do.

And I say: but I liked it.

That is my whole case, and I know how thin it sounds. I liked it. Not every book. I abandoned three, which felt like a betrayal of the project until I decided that abandoning was allowed if I could say why. I liked the strange accident of order - reading a 1922 novel about a farm on Monday and a 1978 novel about a divorce on Tuesday, and finding, without looking for it, that both of them had a scene where somebody stands in a doorway and does not come in. Nobody assigned me that. No teacher had built a unit around doorways. I found it because I was going alphabetically through a shelf like a person walking a fence line, and the pattern surfaced on its own.

That is the thing I have tried to explain to her and failed. When you read everything in a category, including the bad ones, including the four Updikes, you stop reading for the good parts and start reading for the shape of the whole. You notice what a decade was afraid of. You notice which sentences were fashionable. I did not have the vocabulary for any of this at fifteen. I only had the feeling that the books were talking to each other over my head, and that if I stayed in the chair long enough I would catch the thread of it.

I still go back to that shelf. It has been reordered twice; the Cather is gone. I am applying to study literature, and I have practiced saying that out loud to my mother in a way that does not sound like an accusation, because it isn't one. She was right that I was sad. She has always been right about that. What she has never accepted is that the sadness and the reading were not the same thing wearing one coat. One of them ended in September. The other one is why I am writing this.

We are still not agreed. Last month she said, "You would have been a person who read anyway." Maybe. I cannot run the summer again without the divorce in it. But I know what I was doing in that chair, and it was not hiding. It was the first work I ever chose.

text:
The podcast was called Second Shift and it ran for four episodes. My cousin Elias and I recorded it in his mother's laundry room on a borrowed microphone, on a folded quilt to kill the echo, and the premise was that we would interview people in our town about the job they had before the one they have now. Episode one was a woman who had been a court stenographer and now runs the bakery on Delmar. Episode two was a man who repaired pinball machines and now sells insurance. Three was my own grandfather, who left a shipyard in 1979. Four was a substitute teacher who had spent eleven years as a long-haul driver, and it is the best thing either of us has made.

Then it stopped. Not with a decision. We recorded a fifth in November, and I never edited it, and Elias asked about it in December and I said soon, and he asked in January and I said soon, and in February he stopped asking. The file is still on my laptop. It is forty-one minutes long and it is fine.

I want to describe the failure accurately, because for a long time I described it wrong. For most of a year I said we ran out of time, which is the version that lets me off. What actually happened is that Elias and I disagreed about what the show was, and neither of us ever said so out loud, and the disagreement ate it.

Elias thought we were making a document. He wanted to talk to anybody who had a before, and he did not care whether the episode was good, because the point was that the interview existed and would exist after the person didn't. He said this once, sort of, about my grandfather - that he was glad we had his voice on a hard drive. I thought we were making a show. I wanted the fourth episode standard every time. I wanted the pacing right and the cold open sharp and I wanted people who were not related to us to listen to it, and forty-seven people did, and I checked that number more than I have admitted to anyone.

So when the fifth interview was fine and not good, I did not edit it, and I told myself it was a scheduling problem. Elias would have released it that week. He would have said that a fine conversation with a man who used to install church organs is worth more on the internet than in a folder. And he would have been right about that, and I would still not have released it, and the fact that I can hold both of those at once is exactly why I never brought it up.

What I did next was not noble. I let it die and I let him think I was busy. That went on for months. The thing that broke it was our grandmother's birthday in July, where the whole family was in one backyard, and my aunt asked if the podcast was still going, and Elias said "ask him," and it was not cruel, it was just tired, and I heard it.

I drove over the next week and we sat in the laundry room, which still had the quilt in it. I told him the truth, which is that I had killed it on purpose because I did not think episode five was good enough and I had not wanted to say that to him about an interview he had set up. He said he already knew. He said the part he minded was not the standard, it was the eight months of soon.

We did not resolve the disagreement. That is the honest ending. He still thinks I care too much whether a thing is good, and that this makes me slow and a little bit of a coward, and he says so cheerfully. I still think a document nobody finishes listening to is not a document, and that his version would have produced forty episodes nobody remembers. We have argued about it since, in a way that is now enjoyable, which is different from resolved.

What changed is procedural. We restarted in September under a rule we both agreed to: he publishes, I edit, and I get one veto per season and have to use it in writing within four days. I have used it once. I have released three episodes since that I would not have released before, and one of them, about a man who used to tune pianos for a funeral home, is better than anything from the first run, and I would have buried it.

I do not think I was right and then wrong. I think I was right about the standard and wrong about what I owed the person holding the other end of it, and the second thing was the one that cost us a year.

text:
I learned to swim at sixteen, in the shallow end of the municipal pool on Ferndale Road, on Tuesday mornings at seven, in a class that was otherwise entirely adults. There was a retired postman named Colin, two women in their forties who came together and talked the whole time, and me. The instructor was twenty-three and called all of us "folks."

My mother does not know I did it until it was finished, and that is the disagreement.

She cannot swim either. Neither can her mother. This is not an accident of our family, it is a fact about where she grew up, where the river took two boys from her school in one summer and the response of every adult in that town was to teach the children to fear water rather than to enter it. She taught me the same thing and she taught it well. Until I was fifteen I genuinely believed I had a body that did not float, that some people are made denser, that this was physics and not fear.

What changed was stupid and small. My cousin's wedding was at a hotel with a pool and I sat in a plastic chair in jeans for four hours while everyone I am related to under the age of thirty was in the water. Nobody said anything to me about it. That was worse. I went home and looked up adult beginner classes on my phone that night, and the first one I found was Ferndale, and it cost forty-two pounds for eight weeks, and I paid for it out of the money I make at the garden centre.

The first three weeks I did not put my face in. Week four I did, for about a second, and came up making a sound I did not know I could make. Week six I swam the width. It took me eleven strokes and I was not breathing correctly and Colin clapped, which was mortifying, and it remains one of the four or five best things that has ever happened to me. I can now swim about two hundred metres badly. I go on Sundays.

I told my mother in August. I had expected - I don't know what I expected. Pride, maybe, or the version of relief where someone says they always wanted you to. What I got was quiet for a long moment and then, "Who did you go with?"

Nobody. That was the wrong answer. She was not angry that I had learned. She was frightened that I had been in water for eight weeks and she had not known, that if something had happened she would have found out from a phone call. And underneath that, which she has said out loud twice since, is her belief that the sensible response to a dangerous thing is distance, and that what I have done is not competence, it is a slightly better-informed way of drowning. She thinks confidence in water is the thing that kills people. She is not entirely wrong; the boys from her school could both swim.

We have not resolved it. She has not come to the pool. I have stopped asking, because asking makes it a test she has to fail, and I have started just telling her when I go and when I am back, which she has never requested and which she has also never told me to stop doing.

What I actually learned, apart from the swimming, is that I had been treating her fear as an error in her that I could correct with evidence. Every time I brought a fact - the depth of the shallow end, the lifeguard, the number of strokes - I was arguing with the wrong thing. Her fear is not a belief about water. It is a memory of two funerals. You cannot out-argue a funeral.

So the disagreement stands, and I have gotten more comfortable with it standing. I go on Sundays. I text her when I am out. She reads it and does not reply, and then at dinner she asks how far I got.

text:
Three mornings a week for the last three years I have left the house at ten past six and walked twenty minutes to a flooded gravel pit on the edge of town that the council calls a nature reserve and everybody else calls the pits. I am back by half seven. I do not tell many people about it, partly because it sounds like an affectation and partly because for two of those three years I was doing it for a reason that did not work out.

The reason was a bittern.

There had been one at the pits in the winter of 2021, before I started. Somebody photographed it in the reeds at the north end and it went on the county bird group's site, and there were about forty records over six weeks and then it left. A bittern is a heron that has decided to be invisible: streaked brown, motionless, standing in reeds pretending to be reeds. Most people who watch birds in this country go years without seeing one. Some never do.

I decided I was going to see one at my pits. That was the project. That was, in a real sense, why the habit started at all - I had a target and the target justified the alarm at half five.

I did not see one. Not in the first winter, not in the second, not in the third. I stood at the north end in fog and in rain and in a cold that made my hands stop working, and I looked at reeds. I got very good at looking at reeds. There was a morning in January two years ago when I convinced myself for a full ninety seconds that a dead branch at the edge of the reedbed was a bittern, and the feeling when it resolved back into a branch is one I can still summon exactly.

So: I failed. Three years, roughly four hundred and fifty mornings, one specific goal, not achieved.

What I did next is that I kept going, and I would like to be honest about why, because the honest answer is not perseverance. I kept going because by then the habit had detached itself from the reason. I had stopped needing the bittern about halfway through the second winter and had not noticed. The alarm went off and I went, in the way that you go to a place where your life happens.

And the thing that had grown underneath the failed project turned out to be worth much more than the project. I have three years of notes on that pit now - sixty-odd pages, undated at first because I was careless and then rigorously dated because I taught myself better. I know that the gadwall arrive in the second week of October within about four days every year. I know which of the three willows on the west bank the kingfisher uses and that it changed from the middle one to the far one after a branch came down in 2023. I know that the water level drops about forty centimetres between May and August and that when it does, a mud shelf appears at the south end and waders stop there - I have logged green sandpiper eleven times on that shelf and never anywhere else on the site.

Last spring I sent the notes to the county recorder, mostly because a man I met on the path told me I should. He wrote back and asked if I would take on the pits as a formal recording site, which means I am now the person whose numbers go into the county report. I am seventeen and I am nobody, and I got that because I turned up four hundred and fifty times to fail at seeing one bird.

I still look at the north end every time. I would still like to see a bittern.

But what I actually learned is that I am bad at judging in advance which part of a thing is the valuable part. I chose the bittern because it was rare and hard and would have made a good story. The good story was the gadwall arriving in the second week of October, every year, unremarkably, in front of a boy who happened to be standing there.

text:
The canvas bag is olive green and says HERALD-EXAMINER on the side in letters that have gone the color of weak tea. My brother Danny carried it for three years before I did. There is a stain near the bottom seam shaped like Delaware that neither of us has ever identified. When he handed it over the summer before eighth grade, he gave me the rules of the route as if they were laws of physics: the Petrosyans get theirs on the porch, 214 gets it in the mailbox, and you never bother the man at 331. Danny said the man at 331 was mean. He said it flatly, the way you'd say a street was one-way.

So for two years I threw the paper from the sidewalk at 331, into the general vicinity of the yard, and then I pedaled hard. I believed the man was mean because Danny believed it, and Danny believed it because a kid named Aaron told him, and Aaron got it from whoever came before him. The route had been handed down for a decade, and the belief came with it, folded into the bag like the stain.

The winter I turned fifteen it snowed badly enough that the paper landed in a drift and vanished. I got off my bike to dig for it. While I was on my knees in his yard, the man came out. He was maybe eighty, in a bathrobe over a sweater, and he was holding a snow shovel, which for one second I read as a weapon. He handed it to me. He said the drift went deeper than it looked and I should scoop, not paw. Then he went inside and came back with the paper he had already found, and a cup of instant coffee that I did not want and drank anyway.

His name was Mr. Kolar. He had lived there fifty-one years. He was not mean. He was deaf in his left ear and slow to the door, and at some point a kid on a bike had knocked, gotten no answer, decided he was ignoring them, and passed that story down the line like the bag.

What bothers me still is how little it took to keep believing it. I never tested the claim. I had passed his house six hundred times and never once knocked twice. The belief was cheap to hold and would have been cheap to check, and I held it because checking would have meant contradicting my brother, who was seventeen and knew things.

I finished the route in June and gave the bag to a kid named Marcus down the block. I told him the Petrosyans want it on the porch and 214 wants the mailbox. Then I told him Mr. Kolar is deaf in one ear, so knock twice, and hand it to him if you can. I don't know if Marcus does it. But the thing I passed down was true, and I had gone and found out.

meta.topic: delivering newspapers on a route inherited from an older sibling

text:
I started writing the first line for them. That's it. That's the whole thing.

Let me back up. Tuesdays and Thursdays, room 114, the math lab, which is a converted storage room with one window that doesn't open and a poster of a cat hanging from a branch. I've been there since sophomore year. Mostly Algebra I kids, mostly sophomores and juniors who took it, failed it, and are taking it again, which is a specific kind of tired that I didn't understand until I'd been doing this a while.

The first semester I was terrible at it. Not at math. At the other part. A kid named Ruben would sit down with a worksheet on factoring and just look at it, and I would explain factoring, clearly, correctly, using the same words Mrs. Achebe used, and he would nod, and then he'd go home and do nothing. Every time. I thought he wasn't listening.

He was listening fine. The problem was that when I left the table he had a blank page and no idea what a person is supposed to physically do first. Not conceptually. Physically. Where does the pencil go.

So one Thursday, out of frustration honestly, I took his pencil and wrote x² + 7x + 12 and then underneath it I wrote a set of empty parentheses. ( )( ). Nothing else. And I said, okay, go. And he did.

That became the thing. Every kid, every session, I write the first line and then I stop and I don't help until they ask. Just the first line. The problem restated, or the equation copied over with a box drawn around what you're solving for, or two empty parentheses, or on word problems, just the words "let x =" and then a blank.

It sounds small because it is small. It took me about four seconds per problem. But something happens when the page isn't blank anymore. Ruben passed with a C+. He is now in Algebra II and he texts me sometimes to complain about it, which I consider a win.

I've watched this work on maybe forty kids now. Not all of them. There was a girl last year, Priya, who genuinely did not know her multiplication tables and no amount of first lines was going to fix that, and we spent six weeks on times tables and both of us hated it and she still got a D. So it's not magic. I want to be straight about that.

But the pattern holds more than it doesn't. Almost nobody in that room was failing because they couldn't do math. They were failing because starting is expensive and they'd been paying that cost alone, forty problems a night, and had quit paying it. My job turned out not to be explaining. It was going first.

Here's the part that changed how I think about myself. I always assumed I was good at math and that's why I could help. That's not it. I'm good at math because for eight years my dad sat at the kitchen table and did the first line of my homework with me and I never once noticed he was doing it. He'd say "okay, what are they even asking" and write it down. I thought that was just talking. I found this out last spring, when I described the math lab to him and he laughed and said where do you think you got that.

I don't know what I'm going to study. I know I'm going to keep sitting down next to people and writing the first line.

text:
There is a wall calendar in our kitchen that nobody has taken down. It is from four years ago. The months are printed in my first language, and under each date there are small squares where my mother used to write what needed doing, in that language, in her handwriting, which slants.

That was the year we stopped speaking it at home.

I want to be careful here, because I do not fully know why it happened, and I have never been able to point to a day. There was no decision. Nobody sat anyone down. My brother was starting school and struggling, and my parents were told, by somebody, that it would help if he heard more English at home. I think that was the start of it. But I am reconstructing. What I remember is that at some point in that year the language stopped being the one the house was made of and became the one that came out when someone was tired, or angry, or on the phone to my grandmother.

The calendar stopped being written on in about March. After that the squares are empty. The months keep going, printed, in a language that was still on the wall but not really in the room.

I am supposed to be describing a place where I feel most myself. I have thought about this for a long time and the honest answer is that I do not have one, and that the reason I do not have one has something to do with that calendar. Which is a difficult thing to write in an essay that is meant to end well.

In English I am fluent and I am funny and I am, I think, slightly a different person - quicker, more sarcastic, more likely to say something to fill a silence. In my first language I am about eleven years old. My vocabulary stopped growing the year the calendar stopped. I can talk about food and weather and family. I cannot talk about what I want to do with my life, or about how I feel about anything complicated, because I never learned those words as an adult would need them and I did not know, at eleven, that I was going to need them.

So there is no room where all of me is available. There are two rooms and I am partial in both.

The place I come closest is the kitchen, with the calendar in it, when my mother is cooking and my grandmother is on speakerphone. In that specific arrangement the language comes back for maybe forty minutes. It is not good. I make mistakes and my grandmother corrects them and my mother laughs at both of us. But it is the only situation where the two halves of the house are in the same air at the same time, and I am not translating, I am just in it.

I have thought about whether I should be angry about this, and I have decided that I am not, or not exactly. My parents did what they were told would help my brother, and my brother is fine now, and he does not speak the language at all, which is a separate fact I do not know what to do with. He is thirteen. He calls my grandmother and says hello and then hands the phone over. She is very kind about it.

What I feel is more like the thing you feel when you notice a door in a house that has been painted over. Not grief. Just the awareness of a shape.

I have started trying to fix it, in a small and inconsistent way. I have an app, which is not much use. Better is that I have started calling my grandmother myself on Sunday evenings, without my mother in the room, so there is nobody to fall back to. Those calls are slow and a bit awkward and I run out of things I can say in about twenty minutes. But they are getting longer. Last month I described my chemistry teacher to her, which took a very long time and involved a lot of pointing at nothing, and she understood, and she said something back about a teacher she had, and I understood most of it.

I do not have a conclusion about this. The calendar is still on the wall. Nobody has taken it down and nobody has said why, and I think if I asked, my mother would just take it down, so I have not asked.

If I am most myself anywhere, it is on the phone on a Sunday, badly, in eleven-year-old sentences, getting slightly better.

meta.topic: the year they stopped speaking their first language at home
meta.prompt: Describe a place where you feel most yourself, and why.

text:
My grandfather has a brass measuring cup, about the size of a fist, with a lip on one side and a dent near the base where it was dropped a long time before I was born. It sat on a shelf in his room in Coimbatore and it sits on a shelf in our flat in Leicester now, and for most of my life it was just an object I had to move when I dusted.

He grew up in a village called Perumbakkam that is not there anymore. It was cleared in the seventies for a reservoir project, and the people were relocated to a town nine kilometres away with better roads and a school and no history. He was fourteen. He has told me about it perhaps two hundred times, and until I was fifteen I heard almost none of it, because he tells stories in a loop and I had decided, somewhere around age eleven, that the loop meant nothing new was coming.

When I was sixteen I decided to fix this. I was going to record him. I had a plan and a phone and a list of questions, and I was going to build an oral history - that is genuinely the phrase I used, to myself, in my own head - a proper document of a place that no longer existed, so it would not be lost.

It did not work, and the way it did not work is what I want to write about.

The first session lasted forty minutes and I got almost nothing. I asked him what the village looked like. He described the temple. I asked how many houses. He said, many. I asked what his father did and he told me a story about a bullock that had already been told at three weddings. I pushed him with the questions I had prepared, the good ones, the ones about how it felt to leave, and he answered them in about eleven words each and then asked if I wanted tea.

I tried again a month later and it was worse, because by then he knew what I was doing and he performed. He gave me the version he gives to guests. He got dates wrong that I knew he knew. Halfway through he said, in Tamil, "you are writing a report," and it was not a compliment.

I gave up for nearly a year. I told myself he was old and it was too late, which was a comfortable thing to believe and also unfair to a man who does the crossword faster than I do.

What I did next was accidental. Last August, cooking, my mother needed a measure for rice and could not find the cup we use, and my grandfather went and got the brass one off the shelf and said, without anyone asking, that this was the padi his mother had used and that in Perumbakkam a bride's family sent one to the new house, and that theirs had been left behind in the move and this one was bought in the town afterwards to replace it, and that it was the wrong size, slightly, and his mother complained about it for eleven years.

That was more than I got in eighty minutes of interviews. He talked for an hour. I did not record it. I have thought about that a lot and I have decided I am not sorry.

What I was wrong about was the form. I had assumed that a life comes out when you ask for it, in order, at a table. It doesn't. It comes out sideways, attached to objects, when someone needs a cup for rice. My questions were a container of the wrong shape, and every time I held it up he could see it and adjusted himself to fit.

So now I do not interview him. I cook with him. I ask about the thing in his hand. I have filled a notebook in fourteen months, badly, out of order, undated, and it contains more of Perumbakkam than my recordings ever would have.

The cup is still the wrong size. It holds about three-quarters of what it should.

meta.topic: a grandfather's stories about a village that no longer exists
meta.prompt: Describe a time you were not successful. What did you do next?

text:
I started birdwatching for a stupid reason, which is that I wanted a thing. I was fourteen, everyone around me seemed to have an identifiable interest, and I did not, and there was a pair of binoculars in the hall cupboard that had belonged to my late uncle. So I got up early one Saturday and went to the scrubby bit of ground behind the retail park where there is a pond, and I taught myself birds, alone, out of a secondhand Collins guide with somebody else's pencil marks in it.

For about two years I did this before school. Out at six, back by half seven, three or four mornings a week. And for about two years I was, I now realise, doing it wrong in a way that I was completely satisfied with at the time.

What I was doing was collecting. I had a list. I ticked things off. When I saw a bird, the question I asked was "what is it," and once I had an answer I stopped looking, because the transaction was complete. Reed bunting. Tick. I got to eighty-three species by the end of the first year and I was proud of that number the way you are proud of a high score. My knowledge was entirely a knowledge of names and of the four or five diagnostic features you need to attach a name to a shape. Wing bar. Eye stripe. Whether the tail is forked.

The morning it changed was in February of Year 11, and it was not dramatic. There was a heron at the pond, which was not a new bird, I had ticked heron in the first month. I had nothing to do because it was too cold and too early for anything else, so I just watched it, out of boredom, for about twenty-five minutes.

In twenty-five minutes it did not catch anything. It moved four times, each time a few steps, each time slower than I would have believed a living thing could move. Once it stopped mid-stride with a foot lifted and held it there for what I counted as fifty-one seconds. And at some point in there I understood that I had seen herons perhaps forty times and had never once seen a heron do anything, because I had always stopped watching at the moment of identification.

That was the turn. Not "I saw a rare bird." The opposite. I saw an extremely common bird properly for the first time and realised my whole method had been designed to prevent exactly that.

What teaching myself showed me, in the end, is that when there is nobody checking your work, you will unconsciously optimise for whatever you can measure. Nobody told me to keep a list. But a list gives you a number, and a number gives you the feeling of getting better, and so I built two years of practice around the one part of the activity that produced a score. A teacher would have asked me a question I never asked myself: what is this for? An expert would have said, on day three, forget the list, sit down and watch one bird for an hour. Self-teaching is enormously good at building competence and enormously bad at telling you whether the competence is pointed anywhere.

I still go out before school, though now it is two mornings a week because of coursework, and I still have the list, but it has not moved much. I have a second notebook now that is just behaviour - a sparrowhawk that hunts the same hedge on the same side every time, gulls that follow the bin lorry down Farrow Road on Thursdays and not Wednesdays, the fact that our local blackbirds start singing about eleven minutes earlier under the streetlight on the corner than they do fifty metres away in the dark.

None of that is in the Collins guide. That is the point of it.

meta.prompt: What is something you have taught yourself, and what did learning it without a teacher show you?

text:
There is a cardboard box in my garage with the words THANK YOU EASTSIDE! written on it in green marker, in my handwriting, in letters that get smaller toward the right because I ran out of room. The exclamation mark is doing a lot of work. I made forty of those boxes over a weekend in October, cutting the tops off and lettering each one at the kitchen table while my sister complained about the smell of the marker. Thirty-nine of them came back with something in them. Most came back with less than a third.

I had promised four thousand items. I had said the number out loud, at a school assembly, into a microphone, with a slide behind me. We collected eleven hundred and sixty-two.

The food drive was mine in the way that a thing is yours when nobody stops you. Our town's pantry had put out a notice in September that their shelves were the emptiest they'd been in six years, and I read it and thought: this is arithmetic. Twelve hundred students. Four items each. Four thousand eight hundred. I rounded down to four thousand because I wanted to sound reasonable. I built a spreadsheet. I assigned boxes to homerooms. I designed a leaderboard. I genuinely believed the hard part was logistics.

The hard part was not logistics. The hard part was that a fourteen-year-old has to remember on a Tuesday morning, while also remembering a gym kit and a permission slip, to have asked their parent on Monday night to buy an extra can of something, and then to carry that can on a bus. I had built a system that assumed everyone's home life was a small warehouse with a willing quartermaster. About a fifth of our school qualifies for free lunch. I did not think about that when I made the leaderboard. I put the leaderboard up in the main corridor. Homeroom 9C, whose catchment is mostly the estate behind the rail line, was last for three weeks in letters two inches high.

That is the thing I actually carry. Not the number I missed. The leaderboard.

I took it down in the fourth week, after a teacher named Ms. Adeyemi asked me, without any particular edge in her voice, what I thought a kid in 9C felt walking past it. I said I hadn't thought about it. She said, that's the honest answer, and left it there, which was worse than being told off.

What I did next is the part I would want anyone to know about me. I did not abandon the drive and I did not pretend it had gone well. I rewrote it. We stopped counting by homeroom and started counting as one school total against one bar drawn on butcher paper. We added a thing where you could donate an hour of sorting instead of an item, and about seventy people did, including six from 9C. We set up a table where the pantry itself could tell us what it actually needed, which turned out to be nothing like what people give - not beans, which they drown in, but cooking oil, nappies, tinned fish, shampoo. I had spent a month collecting things that were easy to give rather than things that were needed. Nobody had asked me to check. I hadn't checked.

The second drive, in March, collected two thousand nine hundred, and about six hundred of those were on the pantry's actual list. Still short of four thousand. I stopped promising numbers.

I keep the one box that came back empty. Somebody had written under my green letters, in pencil, sorry, in small handwriting, no name. I do not know who it was and I have decided not to try to find out. It sits in the garage with the flaps folded in.

I want to study public policy, and the reason is not that I am good at organising things. It is that I now know exactly how it feels to build something well-intentioned that quietly humiliates the people it was meant to help, and to not notice for a month, and to have to be told. That is not a talent. It is closer to a scar. But I would rather apply somewhere with it than without it, because it is the only reason I now ask, before anything else: who does this make feel worse, and have I bothered to look?
