text:
The calculator I tutor with is a TI-84 my cousin left behind when she went to college, and the battery cover has been held on with a strip of blue painter's tape for so long that the tape has gone gray and I've stopped noticing it's there. Half the buttons have lost their printed labels from being pressed so many times - the 2 and the equals sign are basically smooth plastic now, no numbers left on them at all, so you have to know where they are by memory. I've used this thing almost every school day for two years, in a spare classroom off the cafeteria where I tutor algebra during lunch to kids who are failing it.

I started tutoring because a friend was about to fail ninth grade math and asked me to help her study for a retake, not because I had some plan about contributing to anything. I sat with her at a picnic table for maybe forty minutes with this calculator between us, walking through factoring, and she passed the retake by six points. Word got around the way it does in a school that size. By the next semester I had a standing lunch slot and a list of names on a sign-up sheet taped to the classroom door, and the calculator went with me every single day because most of the kids I work with don't own one, or their families can't afford the eighty dollars a graphing calculator costs, which nobody tells you is basically required equipment for algebra in most classrooms here.

There's a girl, Jasmine, who I tutored for most of last year. She'd failed the same unit test twice and had decided, out loud, in front of me, that she was "just not a math person," which is a sentence I've heard from almost every kid I've worked with, always delivered like a fact about themselves rather than a gap in what they'd been taught. She was suspicious of me the first few sessions, answered in single words, clearly there because a teacher had told her to be. What actually opened things up wasn't anything I explained. It was that I'd hand her the calculator to check her own work, and she'd hand it back, and I'd use it, and we kept passing it back and forth across the table for weeks before she said much of anything real to me. There's something about sharing one physical object between two people, taking turns with it, that does work a conversation alone doesn't.

By March she was correcting my arithmetic before I finished the problem on the board. She still has the same handwriting she started with, cramped and slanting hard to the right, but she stopped erasing every wrong attempt like it was evidence against her, started leaving the crossed-out work visible, which I think is its own kind of progress nobody grades.

What I'd bring to a campus isn't really about being good at math, though I am decent at it. It's this specific willingness to sit across a table from someone who has decided they're bad at a subject and just keep showing up, keep handing over the calculator, keep not being impatient with the sixth wrong attempt at the same kind of problem. That's not a skill anyone taught me in a classroom. I think I learned it from watching how many kids just needed one person to not give up on them before they gave up on themselves, and from a battery cover held together with tape that I've never bothered to actually fix, because somehow it still works exactly the way it needs to.

meta.topic: tutoring maths to students who were failing it
meta.prompt: What would you contribute to our campus that would not be here if you were not?

text:
The Eastside Community Pool opens at 5:45 in the morning, and for a little over a year now I've been there most weekdays before it opens, sitting on the bench outside with my goggles already around my neck, waiting for the lifeguard to unlock the gate. I didn't learn to swim as a kid. My family didn't have easy access to a pool where we lived before we moved here, and by the time I was old enough to really want to learn, I was already sixteen and embarrassed about it in the specific way you get embarrassed about things you feel like you should have outgrown having to learn.

I started with adult beginner lessons two summers ago mostly to stop being embarrassed. What I didn't expect was how completely the mechanics of swimming would take over my attention once I had a basic handle on staying afloat. There's something about counting strokes per length, feeling for the exact moment your hand should catch the water instead of slapping it, timing a breath to the rotation of your hip rather than gasping for it, that I can only describe as absorbing. I'll get in the water at quarter to six planning to do forty minutes, and the next thing I know the lifeguard is blowing the whistle for lap swim to end and the pool is filling up with people doing water aerobics.

It became a habit almost without my noticing it turn into one. First it was three mornings a week, then it was every weekday, then it was weekday mornings plus Saturday, until at some point it stopped being a thing I was doing to fix a gap in my abilities and became just what my mornings are. I keep a small waterproof notebook by the pool deck now, mostly just numbers - lengths swum, approximate pace, which drill I worked on that day - not because anyone asked me to track it but because I like having a record of a version of engagement with something that has nothing to do with school or grades or anyone else's evaluation of me.

What captivates me about it, if I try to name it, is that swimming well is a problem of tiny corrections compounding. You don't fix your stroke in one session. You notice, on a Tuesday, that your elbow is dropping too early on the recovery, and you spend three weeks trying to feel the difference between a high elbow and a low one, and then one morning it clicks and you're a half-second faster without doing anything consciously different, and then there's a new tiny thing to notice. It's the most patient kind of problem-solving I've ever done, and it's the only place in my life where I genuinely don't check the clock, where forty minutes disappears the way people say time does when they're doing something they love, except I've never quite believed that phrase until this pool made it true for me specifically.

I go to the same coach for technique corrections sometimes, a retired competitive swimmer named Hollis who volunteers a few mornings a month, and he told me once that most people who learn to swim as teenagers or adults end up more attentive to the details than people who learned as toddlers, because we actually have to think about what our bodies are doing instead of it being automatic from the start. I don't know if that's true for everyone. It's true for me. I think about water more than I think about almost anything I actually study, and I still don't fully understand why, except that it asks me to pay a kind of attention I didn't know I was capable of until I was standing outside a locked pool gate at quarter to six, waiting.

meta.topic: learning to swim at sixteen
meta.prompt: Describe a topic, idea, or concept you find so engaging that it makes you lose all track of time. Why does it captivate you? What or who do you turn to when you want to learn more?

text:
I told Mrs. Okafor I was quitting piano on a Thursday in October, eleven years and two months after my first lesson with her, standing in her front hallway with my shoes still on because I didn't plan on staying long enough to need to take them off. I'd just come off a regional competition where I'd frozen halfway through the second movement of a Chopin piece I'd played probably four hundred times in practice, gone completely blank in front of six judges and a room of parents, and walked offstage feeling like eleven years of Tuesday afternoons had just proven themselves worthless in about ninety seconds.

I expected her to argue with me. She'd invested more time in me than any teacher I'd ever had, had rearranged her own schedule around competition seasons, had driven me to two out-of-state events herself when my parents couldn't take the days off work. I had a whole defense prepared in my head for the conversation I thought was coming.

She didn't argue. She just nodded, said okay, asked if I wanted to come in anyway for one more lesson since I was already there, since it was already paid for that month. I said fine, mostly out of guilt about the money.

That last lesson wasn't a lesson. She didn't have me touch the Chopin, didn't bring up technique or competitions or anything I'd been working toward for the past year. She went to her shelf and pulled out a piece of sheet music I'd never seen, a Satie piece, one of the Gymnopédies, and put it on the stand and said she wasn't assigning it to me, that I didn't have to learn it, that she just wanted me to hear it once before I stopped coming, because she thought I'd like it and she'd never had a reason to show it to me before. Everything we'd worked on for eleven years had been in service of something - a recital, a jury, a competition. This had no purpose attached to it at all. She played it through once herself, slow and unhurried in a way I'd genuinely never heard her play anything, and then she just closed the book and said that was it, that was the lesson, and thank you for eleven years, and she meant it, I could tell she meant it.

I went home still fairly sure I was done. But I kept thinking about the fact that she hadn't tried to keep me, hadn't made one argument for why I should stay, and instead had used her very last chance with me to give me something with absolutely no strings on it, just because she thought it was beautiful and thought I might too. That felt like a strange kind of gift, the kind where someone gives up their own interest in the outcome entirely in order to give you something real. I sat at our piano at home a few days later, found a recording of the Satie piece, and taught myself the first page just from listening and picking it out, badly, no sheet music of my own yet.

I never went back to lessons with her, not formally. But I started playing again within about three weeks, on my own terms, pieces I picked because I wanted to hear what they sounded like under my own hands, no recital deadline attached to any of it. I'm more grateful to Mrs. Okafor for that last lesson than for any of the technique she built into my hands over eleven years, because she gave me the one thing that made it possible to come back to the instrument at all: proof that it could exist without anyone judging what I did with it. I don't think she knew, when she pulled that Satie off the shelf, that she was handing me a reason to keep going instead of a goodbye. I don't think I knew it either, not for a while.

meta.topic: quitting piano after eleven years
meta.prompt: Reflect on something that someone has done for you that has made you happy or thankful in a surprising way. How has this gratitude affected or motivated you?

text:
My cousin Priya asked me to be in charge of her wedding day the way you'd ask someone who has never actually run anything before, which is to say she trusted me with far more than I understood I was agreeing to. I was sixteen. She was getting married in June, and because both of our mothers were consumed with a hundred other things that morning, I became the person responsible for making sure my grandmother's jewelry - a set that had come down through three generations, a necklace and earrings that had been worn by Priya's great-grandmother at her own wedding in Amritsar - got from our house to the venue safely, along with about six other small logistical tasks that all landed on me at once because I was the oldest cousin around and everyone assumed, correctly in most cases, that I could handle it.

I put the jewelry box in a cloth bag and carried it around with me all morning while I also tried to coordinate which car the photographer needed to ride in, whether my uncle had picked up the extra folding chairs, and where the priest's assistant was supposed to park. At some point, in the middle of moving between three different conversations at once, I set the bag down in the back seat of my uncle Rajan's car while I helped carry something else, and he left. He was running to pick up ice and extra chairs from a store fifteen minutes away, had no idea what was sitting behind him, and his phone, I found out afterward, had died sometime that morning without him noticing.

For almost two hours, nobody could reach him. My aunt discovered the jewelry was missing around ten, when she went to get Priya ready, and the next ninety minutes are still, honestly, some of the worst of my life so far - my mother's face when I admitted I'd set the bag down and walked away from it, my aunt calling every relative's number she had for Rajan, Priya herself, still in her robe, asking quietly what was going on while trying not to let it show in front of the makeup artist. I remember standing in the driveway convinced I had ruined the single day my cousin had been planning for over a year, over jewelry that wasn't even replaceable, that had a history in our family longer than any of us had been alive.

Rajan came back a little after eleven, jewelry untouched in the back seat exactly where I'd left it, utterly unaware anything had happened. The relief in that driveway was enormous and short-lived, because underneath it I still had to sit with the fact that nothing bad happening didn't mean I hadn't done something genuinely careless. Priya got married on time. The necklace is in photographs from that day that our family will keep for decades. And I still think, more than I'd like to admit, about how easily that outcome could have gone the other way, and how the difference between a story we laugh about now and a family heirloom lost forever came down to nothing I actually did - just luck, just a fifteen-minute errand that happened to end where it started.

What I took from it wasn't really about jewelry. It was about what it means to be handed real responsibility, the kind with consequences that don't undo themselves, and to learn in one morning that being trusted and being careful are not the same thing, that I'd assumed I was the second because people kept treating me like I was. I think what I'd bring to a campus is exactly that lesson, still raw enough that I don't get to forget it: I no longer set important things down and walk away, not literally and not in the larger sense either. I check twice now, on things that matter and things that don't seem to yet. Nobody has to ask me to.

meta.topic: a cousin's wedding they were made responsible for
meta.prompt: What would you contribute to our campus that would not be here if you were not?

text:
My grandmother used to grow chillies in Guwahati, on a strip of land behind the house she left when she moved here to live with us, and she talks about that garden more than she talks about almost anything else from her old life. Two years ago, for her seventy-fourth birthday, I decided I was going to grow her a full crop of chillies on our apartment balcony as a surprise, ready by the time she came back from a month visiting my uncle. I had never grown anything in my life. I figured how hard could it actually be, and that confidence is basically the whole story of what went wrong.

I bought six pots, some Kashmiri chilli seeds and some bird's eye seeds I found online because I wanted variety, and I started them in March, giving myself what I thought was plenty of time. I watered them every single day without fail, which I now know was the first real mistake, because chilli plants apparently prefer to dry out somewhat between waterings, and what I was doing was slowly drowning the roots while feeling proud of my consistency. I also used regular potting soil from the hardware store instead of anything with proper drainage, so the water had nowhere to go, and by May the leaves on four of the six plants had started curling and yellowing in a way I assumed, at the time, meant they needed more water, so I gave them more.

By the time my grandmother came home, two plants were dead outright and the other four were struggling, pale and stunted, with maybe a dozen small green chillies between all of them combined, nothing like the abundant, almost aggressive growth she'd described from her own garden. I hadn't told her about the project beforehand, so the surprise I revealed on the balcony that first evening was six sad pots that I had to explain were supposed to be a birthday gift, three months in the making, that had mostly failed.

She didn't laugh at me, though I think a part of me expected her to. She walked along the pots, picked up a handful of the soil, let it fall through her fingers, and said, quietly, that I'd drowned them, the way you'd say it about a fact rather than a failing. Then she asked why I hadn't asked her for help in the first place, since she'd grown these exact plants for probably fifty years before I was even born. I didn't have a good answer. I think I wanted it to be entirely mine, some kind of gift that didn't need her input to work, which is a strange thing to want when the whole point of the gift was to remind her of something she already knew everything about.

We replanted that same week, together this time, in terracotta pots with drainage holes she picked out herself, watering on a schedule she set based on how the soil actually felt rather than a fixed daily habit. The second attempt worked. We had chillies by August, not a huge crop, but real ones, and she used a handful of them in a curry that I thought tasted almost exactly like what she'd described from Guwahati, though I have no real way of knowing that for certain.

I still think about the six dead pots more than I think about the ones that survived. Not because the eventual chillies didn't matter, but because the failure taught me something the success never could have: that wanting to give someone a piece of their own life back requires actually asking them how it worked, not assuming I could reconstruct it out of confidence and an internet search. I got that wrong first. I don't think I'll get it wrong that particular way again.

meta.topic: growing chillies on a balcony
meta.prompt: The lessons we take from obstacles we encounter can be fundamental to later success. Recount a time when you faced a challenge, setback, or failure. How did it affect you, and what did you learn from the experience?

text:
The radio station I started sophomore year broadcasts to exactly one place: the cafeteria speakers, during the twenty-eight minutes of lunch, on a system left over from some previous administration that nobody had used in years. I found the equipment in a closet off the AV room while looking for extension cords for something else entirely, asked a teacher if I could use it, and got a yes mostly because nobody thought it would go anywhere.

For the first six weeks, close to nobody listened. I know this because I could watch the cafeteria while I talked, and people kept eating and talking exactly as they had before I started, like the speakers were just producing background noise indistinguishable from the hum of the ice machine. I'd planned playlists, prepared little segments about music or school events, and most days I was talking into a microphone that fed a room where I was pretty sure I was the only one paying attention to what came out of it.

I kept doing it anyway. Every single school day, I'd get to the cafeteria fifteen minutes before lunch started to set up, and I'd run the full twenty-eight minutes whether three people looked up or nobody did. I didn't have a plan for how this was supposed to turn a corner. I just decided that if I stopped the first time it felt pointless, it would always feel pointless, and the only way to find out if it could become something else was to keep showing up on the days it clearly wasn't working.

Somewhere around week nine, a kid I didn't know came up afterward and asked if I could play a specific song the next day, for his friend's birthday. I did. The day after that, someone else asked for something. Neither of these felt like much on their own, but they were the first evidence that the room had actually been listening the whole time, quietly, without me knowing it. By the spring, I had a rotating cast of about eight people asking for shoutouts or songs most weeks, and the cafeteria had gotten noticeably quieter during the mornings I gave school announcements, which I hadn't expected at all.

Nothing about the routine itself changed much between week one and week twenty. I still showed up fifteen minutes early, still ran the same twenty-eight minutes, still talked into a microphone in a cafeteria that mostly ignored me for the first two months. What changed was that I stopped needing daily proof that it mattered in order to keep doing it, and I think that's the actual obstacle I was up against, more than the silence itself - the temptation to quit something the moment it stops giving you evidence that it's working.

I still run the station most days, now with two other students helping. It's not big. It's a cafeteria at lunch, not an actual broadcast reaching anyone outside a hundred-foot radius. But I think the six weeks nobody was listening taught me something I wouldn't have learned if it had worked immediately, which is that most things worth building don't announce the moment they start working. You just keep showing up until, one day, someone asks for a song.

meta.topic: starting a school radio station nobody listened to at first
meta.prompt: The lessons we take from obstacles we encounter can be fundamental to later success. Recount a time when you faced a challenge, setback, or failure. How did it affect you, and what did you learn from the experience?

text:
Our robot's arm dropped off. Not metaphorically - the actual servo-mounted arm, the one we'd spent four months getting to grip and lift a foam block, detached at the shoulder joint and clattered onto the stage floor in front of maybe two hundred people, forty seconds into our qualifying match at the regional competition, and I remember the specific sound it made, a flat plastic clack that the microphones definitely picked up, because someone on another team laughed, not meanly, just startled, and I heard that laugh and felt my whole face go hot.

I was the one who'd mounted that arm the night before. Late, rushed, everyone else had gone to find food and I'd said I'd finish it, and I used two screws where the design called for four because we were out of the right length and I told myself it would hold for one competition, I'd fix it properly after. It didn't hold. We scored eleven points that round out of a possible sixty-something. We didn't advance.

Here's the part I actually want to talk about, though, because the arm falling off isn't really the story.

My teammate Priya didn't say anything to me about it in the moment. We packed up the robot, drove home in near silence, and I assumed - genuinely assumed - that she was furious, because I would have been, and I spent the whole ride composing the apology I was going to give her once we got out of the car.

I never got to give it, because she got there first, and what she said wasn't what I expected. She said thank you.

I actually laughed, out loud, thinking she was being sarcastic. She wasn't. She said thank you for staying late and finishing the mount instead of leaving it half-built, because half-built was worse than badly-built, half-built meant the whole thing wouldn't have even made it onto the stage, and she said she knew I'd been tired and could have just gone home like everyone else and let the team show up with an incomplete robot to forfeit the round entirely. She said the arm falling off in front of everyone was humiliating, sure, but it was a specific, fixable kind of humiliating, the kind you learn from, versus the shapeless humiliating of not showing up ready at all.

I did not think of it that way. I still don't fully think of it that way, if I'm being honest, because some nights I still replay that clack sound and feel my ears go hot all over again, still angry at fifteen-year-old me for the two screws instead of four. But her thank-you rearranged something in how I hold the memory. I had built the whole event, in my head, as a story about my failure. She was telling me it was also, somehow, a story about my effort, and that those were allowed to sit in the same place at the same time without cancelling each other out.

I think about this a lot more than the actual competition, honestly. I think about how easy it would have been for her to just be angry, and how much more useful it was that she wasn't, and how I still don't fully understand why she chose gratitude over blame when blame was clearly sitting right there, available, deserved even. I've asked her since. She just shrugs and says something like, you did the work, the work just wasn't finished, that's different from not doing it.

I've tried to carry that distinction into other things since - the difference between an effort that fails and an effort that never happens - but I'm not sure I've earned the right to say I've mastered it. Mostly what I've carried is smaller and stranger than a lesson. It's just the memory of being thanked for something I was braced to be blamed for, and not knowing, even now, exactly what to do with that.

meta.topic: building a robot for a regional competition that failed on stage
meta.prompt: Reflect on something that someone has done for you that has made you happy or thankful in a surprising way. How has this gratitude affected or motivated you?

text:
Mr. Halvorsen kept the wheel exactly as it was, and I could not understand why. It wobbled on the downstroke, a visible little limp in the metal that threw off every pot I tried to center, and I told him, more than once, that the community center should just replace it. He ran the ceramics studio out of the back room of a converted garage two nights a week, mostly for retirees and a handful of us from the high school who needed something to do that wasn't a screen, and he had opinions about almost everything, delivered in the same unhurried voice whether he was talking about glaze chemistry or the wobble.

"That wheel taught me more than any straight one ever did," he said, the third time I brought it up. I didn't believe him. I thought he was being sentimental about a piece of equipment the way old people get sentimental about things that have simply outlasted their usefulness, and I said so, maybe not in those words but close enough that he raised an eyebrow at me over his glasses.

I respected him. That's the part that made it hard. He'd been throwing pots since before I was born, and when he touched a lump of clay it did what he wanted almost instantly, like the clay recognized something in his hands that it didn't recognize in mine. So when he wouldn't budge on the wheel, it needled me in a way that arguing with someone I didn't respect never would have. I spent three weeks convinced he was simply stubborn, attached to an old machine the way some people are attached to old cars that run badly.

I brought it up a fourth time in October, holding up a bowl that had gone lopsided again, blaming the wheel outright. He didn't argue with me that time. He just handed me a scrap of clay and told me to close my eyes and center it on the wobbly wheel while he watched. I did, badly at first, the clay slapping unevenly under my palms, but somewhere in the second minute my hands started making small corrections without me deciding to make them, adjusting pressure a half-second before the wobble arrived rather than after. I opened my eyes. The cone was crooked but centered, which shouldn't have been possible, and he was smiling the way he did when he already knew what was going to happen.

"A straight wheel lets you get lazy," he said. "This one won't let you."

I still think he might have half-invented that explanation on the spot, a good line assembled to fit a situation he liked the shape of. But it worked, and it kept working for the rest of the semester, and by December I could center clay on a straight wheel faster and steadier than kids who'd been throwing for two years, because the wobbly one had trained my hands to correct constantly instead of relying on the machine to hold still for me. I had wanted the studio to fix the equipment. He had wanted me to fix myself, and he was right, and I was so sure of myself that I nearly missed it.

What bothers me now isn't that I lost the argument. It's how sure I was while I was losing it, how the wobble seemed like such an obvious flaw that I never once asked what it might be teaching me instead of what it was ruining. I catch myself doing that still, in physics lab mostly, deciding a piece of equipment is broken before I've considered that the difficulty might be the point. I think about that wheel more than I think about most of the pots I actually finished that year, because the pots got thrown away eventually, chipped or cracked in the kiln, but the correction in my hands never left.

meta.topic: learning to make pottery on a wheel that wobbled
meta.prompt: Tell us about a time you disagreed with someone whose opinion you respected.

text:
My finger landed on the wrong key again, and Dadu didn't stop pumping the bellows, just kept the drone going underneath my mistake like it hadn't happened. "Again," he said, not unkindly, and I pressed the same key, wrong again, and felt my face go hot in the small front room where the harmonium lived under a yellowing cloth when nobody was playing it.

I had asked to learn only because my mother mentioned, offhand, that nobody in the family could play it anymore once Dadu was gone, and something about that sentence had lodged in me. The harmonium itself was older than my mother, wood gone dark at the corners where three generations of hands had rested, keys slightly yellowed, one of the reeds sticking so you had to strike it a little harder than the others to get it to sound. Dadu had learned it from his own father in a village I had visited exactly twice, and he played it every evening after his tea, songs I didn't know the names of, words in a language I understood maybe a third of.

For the first two months I hated the lessons. I was fourteen and used to being good at things quickly, or at least competent, and here I was fumbling through scales that Dadu's hands moved through without looking, his eyes half closed, his foot tapping a rhythm I couldn't feel yet. He never raised his voice. He also never told me I was doing well when I wasn't, which somehow felt worse than if he had yelled. I kept coming back anyway, some mixture of stubbornness and guilt, and I told myself I was doing it for my mother, or for some vague idea of heritage I couldn't have explained if you'd asked me directly.

Then one Sunday in March he asked me to accompany him instead of playing alone, just the drone, just holding a single note steady while he sang over it, and I realized halfway through that I wasn't thinking about my fingers anymore. I was listening to where his voice was going and trying to feel it a half-second before it arrived, the way you learn to anticipate a wave instead of getting knocked down by it. My note held. It wasn't much, one sustained pitch under an old song about a river, but something in me reorganized itself in that half hour, from a kid doing a chore out of guilt into someone actually inside the music, even at the most minor possible position within it.

I go to his house every Sunday now, not because my mother suggested it once and I felt bad, but because I've started to understand what the room sounds like when I'm not in it. My aunts and uncles drift in during our practice, half-listening while they cook or argue about something on the news, and my youngest cousin has started asking to sit next to me on the bench, watching my hands instead of Dadu's, which feels like a kind of inheritance I didn't expect to receive this early. Nobody assigned me a role in that room. I found one, in the space between a note I could barely hold and a song I couldn't yet sing, and I keep going back to hold it a little longer each time.

meta.topic: learning to play a grandfather's harmonium
meta.prompt: Describe a community you belong to and your place within it.

text:
I decided, in the fall of eighth grade, that I was going to stop speaking Tagalog at home. Nobody told me to. My parents never once asked me to, and my grandmother, who lived with us and spoke almost no English at all, certainly never asked me to. I decided it on my own, in the particular quiet way that thirteen-year-olds decide things that will matter more than they understand, sitting in the back of a classroom where a boy had mimicked my mother's accent at pickup the week before, not cruelly exactly, just carelessly, the way kids repeat things without weighing them.

I told myself it was about efficiency. English was faster for me by then, more natural, and switching between languages mid-sentence felt like static I didn't want to deal with anymore. That was the story I gave myself, anyway. The truer story is that I had started to associate the sound of my first language with being marked as different, and I wanted, badly, to stop being marked.

So I answered my mother in English when she spoke to me in Tagalog. I answered my grandmother the same way, even though her English vocabulary topped out at maybe two hundred words, even though I watched her face do something small and confused every time, a kind of recalibrating, before she'd either repeat herself in broken English or just let the thread drop. I told myself she understood more than she let on. I told myself this went on for almost a year, and it worked, in the sense that my accent flattened out and nobody at school commented on my house sounding foreign anymore.

What it also did was slowly wall my grandmother out of my daily life. Our conversations shrank to logistics - food, homework, whether I'd locked the door - because anything with nuance required a language I had decided I was too good, or too embarrassed, to keep using. She had stories about growing up during a typhoon that flooded her town for two weeks, about my grandfather courting her with letters he couldn't really write and had a neighbor draft for him. I know these stories now only in fragments, secondhand, because I spent a year making sure I wouldn't have to sit through them in the language they actually lived in.

I started speaking Tagalog again the following summer, clumsily, after I noticed how much my grandmother's face changed when I managed a full sentence, like a door had opened that she'd stopped expecting to open. It came back faster than I thought it would, muscle memory more than knowledge, but a year is a long time to withhold yourself from someone who has less time left than you do. I think about that gap more than almost anything else from those years, the version of myself who thought fitting in was worth that particular cost and didn't fully register what he was paying.

What I would bring to a campus is not some neat resolution to that story, because I don't think there is one. It's the specific attentiveness of someone who has watched a language nearly slip away and knows exactly how ordinary and how quiet that kind of loss can be - no dramatic scene, just a year of small refusals adding up. I notice, now, when someone's grandparent is sitting at the edge of a gathering not quite following the English around them, and I go sit next to them and ask what language they'd rather use. I bring the particular discomfort of having gotten something wrong that can't be fully undone, only kept from happening again, and the habit that discomfort built in me of not letting anyone go quiet at the edges of a room if I can help it.

meta.topic: the year they stopped speaking their first language at home
meta.prompt: What would you contribute to our campus that would not be here if you were not?

text:
The Cedarbrook pool closed to the public at the end of June, some dispute between the HOA and the management company that never got fully explained to me, and I kept my job anyway, guarding a rectangle of blue water that nobody swam in for eight weeks straight. My mother thought this was absurd. She said so almost every night at dinner, some version of why are you still going, what exactly are you protecting, and I never had a good answer except that I liked it there, which she considered evidence that something was wrong with me rather than an actual argument.

I want to say I convinced her eventually. I didn't. That's not really what this is about.

I sat in the chair from nine to five, sunscreen sweating off by noon, whistle around my neck for emergencies that were never going to happen, and I watched the water do the small things water does when nobody's disturbing it - the way light broke up on the surface in the early afternoon, the way a stray leaf would drift the exact same slow arc across the deep end every single day because of some current in the filtration system nobody had bothered to fix. I brought books. I did math homework I actually understood for once because there was nothing pulling my attention away from it. My mother called this wasting a summer. I called it the first time in my life I'd had eight hours a day with genuinely nothing demanding anything of me, and I didn't know how to explain that this felt less like waste and more like the only rest I'd gotten in years of overscheduled Saturdays.

She'd ask what I was even guarding against, and I'd say emergencies don't announce themselves in advance, which is true and also not really the point I was trying to make. The point, if I'm honest, was harder to say out loud. I liked being useful in a way that didn't require producing anything. I liked that my job that summer was simply to notice, to keep my eyes moving across a surface even when the surface never changed, and something about that felt like it was teaching me a kind of attention I couldn't get anywhere else - not in a packed classroom, not in the club meetings I ran, not in the tutoring I did on weekends. She heard "sitting by an empty pool" and pictured a summer thrown away. I heard the same words and felt like I'd found a version of stillness I hadn't known I needed.

We never resolved it. She still brings it up sometimes, usually when she's annoyed about something else entirely, a shorthand for a summer she thinks I squandered. I still don't think I can make her see it the way I saw it, sitting up in that chair with the whistle doing nothing, watching a leaf circle the deep end for the eleven hundredth time. I respect her too much to just let the disagreement go quiet and pretend I've come around to her side, and she respects me too much, I think, to pretend she's come around to mine. We just live with it sitting between us, mostly unspoken, the way you live with a lot of things about people you love that you can't fully explain to them and they can't fully explain away.

I don't know if that pool changed anything about who I am in a way I could put on a resume. I know I think about that unbothered water more than I think about most of what I actually accomplished that year, and I know my mother still doesn't understand why, and I've mostly stopped trying to make her.

meta.topic: working as a lifeguard at an empty pool
meta.prompt: Tell us about a time you disagreed with someone whose opinion you respected.

text:
The leash is red nylon, six feet, bought for four dollars at a rescue thrift sale, and about eight inches from the clip there's a lump where I repaired it myself with a fisherman's knot after Otis chewed clean through it in April. I didn't replace the leash. I could have - we have three others in the closet - but I use the mended one on purpose, most days, because I like being reminded that something can break almost all the way through and still hold weight.

Otis is a cattle-dog mix we pulled from a county shelter fourteen months ago, found tied to a guardrail off Route 9 with no collar and a look in his eyes that the shelter worker described to us, honestly, as "a project." We were told this. We adopted him anyway. He is smart in a way that makes training him harder, not easier, because he learns exactly how far he can push a boundary before anyone notices, and he came to us with a level of fear around strangers that six months of consistent work only partly wore down. He is, by any normal measure, a difficult dog. I love him more than almost anything I've ever loved.

My mother did not want to keep him. Not from the start, exactly - she agreed to the adoption, she signed the paperwork - but by month three, after he'd bitten through two leashes, destroyed a couch cushion, and nipped a delivery driver hard enough to break skin, she started saying the word "shelter" out loud, at dinner, like it was a reasonable next sentence in an ordinary conversation. I understood her fear. I did not agree with her conclusion. We had this argument, in different forms, for months.

The worst version of it happened in June, after Otis got loose in the yard and lunged at our neighbor's son, a seven-year-old named Miles who wasn't hurt, not physically, but who cried, while his mother stood on our porch with her arms crossed and my mom apologized on Otis's behalf like he owed somebody something. That night my mom told me, flatly, that we were done, that loving a dog doesn't override the fact that other people's kids have to be able to walk past our yard. I told her she was giving up on him the second things got genuinely hard - a cruel thing to say to a woman who has never once given up on me, and I knew it while I was saying it.

We didn't return him. I want to be honest about why: it wasn't because I won the argument. It was because I begged, and because my dad sided with me by staying quiet in a way that counted as a vote, and because my mom, in the end, could not make herself do it. But she has never agreed that keeping him was right. She still flinches when the doorbell rings. She still keeps the yard gate double-latched in a way she didn't used to, and every time Otis growls at something ordinary - the mail carrier, a bike, a shadow - her face does a specific thing, like she's watching the thing she predicted come true all over again.

We have not resolved this. Otis is better now, genuinely - he hasn't bitten anyone in eight months, he walks fine on that mended red leash, he sleeps against my door most nights. But my mother and I have simply stopped discussing whether keeping him was the right call, which is not the same as agreeing that it was. I love her. She is one of the most careful, protective people I know, and that instinct is exactly what made her want to give him back. I still think I was right. I don't think she's wrong to have wanted otherwise.

The knot in that leash holds. It's not invisible - you can feel the lump if you run your hand down the nylon, and I'm sure it's weaker there than the rest of the line. But it has held for fourteen months, through every walk, every lunge, every moment I was sure it would finally give. I think that's most of what I know about my mother and me right now. Not fixed. Still holding.

Some nights I catch her watching him sleep by my door, and her face isn't afraid then, it's something else, something closer to reluctant. I've never asked her what that look means, because I think some disagreements are better left as they are - not settled, just carried, the way you carry a leash you've already decided not to throw away.

meta.topic: training a rescue dog that could not be trained
meta.prompt: Write about an object that is important to you.

text:
My grandmother thinks I'm wasting my time learning sign language, and she's told me so more than once, in the specific patient tone she uses when she believes she's protecting me from something I haven't lived long enough to see coming.

There's a boy in my chemistry class, Tomas, who is deaf, and who came to our school this year with an interpreter who isn't always available for every class period, every lunch, every hallway conversation that makes up most of what school actually is. I started learning ASL in September mostly because I was tired of watching him sit alone during the gaps where the interpreter wasn't scheduled, tired of a friendliness between us that had to route entirely through a laptop screen and typed sentences that lose almost everything a real conversation carries.

It was hard in a way I hadn't expected, not intellectually - I'm decent at picking up patterns - but physically, in my hands, which apparently have never been asked to carry meaning before and resisted the assignment for weeks. I practiced constantly, videos at night, a app on my phone during lunch, badly signed sentences at Tomas that he'd patiently correct without ever making me feel small for getting it wrong.

My grandmother, who raised me for large stretches of my childhood while my parents worked, found out about all this around November, and her reaction surprised me. She didn't think it was sweet. She thought it was a distraction from what she calls "the real work" - my grades, my college applications, the handful of things she believes actually determine whether a life goes well or badly. She grew up believing effort should be spent where it counts on paper, and to her, hours spent learning a language for one classmate, a language I might never use again after this year, counts as effort spent somewhere it shouldn't be.

We've argued about this more than once, always circling back to the same unresolved place. I tell her it matters because Tomas matters, because friendship shouldn't require a translator every single time, because some things are worth doing even if they don't show up as a line on a transcript. She tells me she loves that I think that way and she also thinks I'm being naive about how the world actually rewards people, that colleges won't ask who I signed hello to in a hallway, that I'll regret hours I could have spent on the SAT prep she keeps buying me instead.

Neither of us has moved the other, not really, not after months of this same conversation resurfacing at different dinners. I don't think she's wrong that the world runs on transcripts and test scores more than it runs on kindness people don't put on a resume. I don't think I'm wrong that spending my afternoons that way has changed something in me I can feel but can't fully explain to her - a patience, maybe, or a willingness to sit in not-understanding long enough to eventually understand.

Tomas signed something to me a few weeks ago, slow enough that I actually caught the whole sentence without asking him to repeat it, something small about a joke from class, and I laughed before I'd even consciously translated it in my head, my hands had gotten there faster than my thinking had. I went home and told my grandmother about it, hoping the story might finally land differently. She smiled, and said that's wonderful, mija, and then asked, in the same breath, how the practice test had gone that week.

I don't think we'll ever fully agree on this. I've mostly stopped trying to make her agree. I just keep signing anyway, and she keeps buying practice books, and somehow we still sit at the same table every night without either of us conceding an inch.

text:
I promised the food bank two thousand pounds of canned goods. I told them that number in an email in September, three weeks before our drive even started, because I wanted a number that would sound ambitious on the posters, and two thousand felt round and achievable and impressive all at once. We collected six hundred and forty.

I was the one who chose the number, and I was the one who chose almost everything else about that drive, because I'd run the club for two years by then and had a specific way I liked things done, and I think if I'm honest that specific way of liking things done is a large part of why we came up six hundred pounds short of what I'd promised a food bank that was counting on us for their November distribution.

I turned down help. That's the plain version of it. Two members of the club, a sophomore named Deja and a junior named Miles, suggested early on that we split the outreach across all four grade levels instead of running it centrally through the club's usual channels, get homeroom teachers involved, put bins in the gym instead of just outside the cafeteria. I said no, or something politer than no that still meant no, because I had a system that had worked at a smaller scale the year before and I didn't want to manage the complexity of a bigger one. I wanted to control the thing I'd be accountable for. I told myself this was responsible. It was actually just fear wearing the costume of competence.

The bins outside the cafeteria filled slowly. I checked them most mornings and watched the fill line creep instead of climb, and I kept telling myself there was still time, we'd get a surge in the final week, that's how drives work. There wasn't a surge. There was a slow, honest trickle that added up to six hundred and forty pounds by the deadline, and a food bank coordinator named Mr. Osei who had planned part of a distribution around a number I'd given him with total, unearned confidence.

I had to call him. That phone call is the part I actually think about, more than the shortfall itself. I explained the number, apologized, offered to extend the drive another two weeks, and he was kind about it in a way that somehow made it worse - he said this happens, organizations overpromise all the time, they'd adjust the distribution, don't worry. I hung up feeling like I'd been let off a hook I thought I deserved to stay on longer.

What I got wrong wasn't the estimate. Estimates are allowed to be wrong; that's what estimates are. What I got wrong was mistaking my own comfort for the right process, deciding a smaller, more controllable drive was better than a bigger, messier one just because the messier one scared me. Deja and Miles's idea would have worked. I know that now with a kind of certainty that doesn't do anyone any good in hindsight. Homeroom bins, more hands, more visibility, exactly the kind of reach a drive that size actually needed, and I said no to it because I liked being the person who ran things a certain way more than I liked the idea of the drive actually succeeding on its own terms.

I still run the club. I did things differently the next year - bins in every homeroom, a planning committee instead of just me, a number I built from the ground up instead of picked because it sounded good on a poster. We hit eighteen hundred pounds, still short of what I'd once promised but honest, this time, about how we got there.

I don't think about the eighteen hundred much. I think about the six hundred and forty, and Mr. Osei's voice being gentler than I deserved, and the version of that fall where I said yes to Deja in September instead of learning the same lesson the slow, expensive way. I don't know that I've fully forgiven myself for choosing control over the actual mission. I'm not sure that's the kind of thing you're supposed to fully forgive yourself for. I think you're just supposed to notice it, every time you feel that same instinct rising again, and choose differently.

meta.topic: organising a food drive that collected far less than promised
meta.prompt: The lessons we take from obstacles we encounter can be fundamental to later success. Recount a time when you faced a challenge, setback, or failure. How did it affect you, and what did you learn from the experience?

text:
The route was my brother Danny's before it was mine. Forty-one houses along Birch and Somerset, delivered before 6:30 every morning, seven days a week, for the Ridgefield Courier, a paper that most of my customers still pay for by check mailed to the office because half of them don't trust anything you can't hold. Danny did it for four years and handed it to me the summer before he left for college, walking me the route once, pointing out which porches wanted the paper tucked behind the screen door and which ones wanted it thrown, underhand, onto the second step exactly.

House twenty-six is Mrs. Ostrowski's. She's eighty-something, lives alone, and Danny told me on that first walk-through that she reads the whole paper every morning with her coffee before anyone else in the family is awake, obituaries first, then the crossword, then everything else. He said take care of her specifically. I said I would.

For almost two years I did. Then, in October, my parents told my sister and me they were separating, on a Tuesday night, and I will not pretend the next week was normal for me in any way. I stopped sleeping right. I stopped doing a lot of things right. And for four mornings in a row, I did not deliver Mrs. Ostrowski's paper. I delivered everyone else's - I was on autopilot enough to finish the route, I just kept skipping house twenty-six without registering that I was doing it, walking right past like my body knew the way better than my head did that week.

I found out on the fifth day, when she called the paper's office, not to complain, just to ask if the delivery had stopped for some reason, and the office called my mom, and my mom told me in a tone I still feel bad about. I went to Mrs. Ostrowski's door that afternoon to apologize in person. I had a whole explanation ready about my parents, figuring I'd need it to excuse myself.

She didn't let me get through it. She just said she'd figured something was going on, that a route boy doesn't miss four days for no reason, and she wasn't upset, she'd just been worried about me specifically, not the paper. Then she handed me a tin of shortbread and a five-dollar bill folded in half, and said it was for hot chocolate on cold mornings, and to come knock if I ever needed to sit down for a minute on my route, any morning, rain or not.

I did not expect that. I'd built up, in my head, some version of this conversation where I got yelled at or reported or at minimum made to feel like the screwup I was pretty sure I'd been. Instead an eighty-something-year-old woman I'd failed for four straight mornings was worried about me and gave me shortbread.

I think about those four missed mornings more than I think about almost anything else from that fall, and not in a way that's fully resolved, honestly - I still feel the specific shame of walking past a door I knew mattered. But Mrs. Ostrowski's kindness did something to how I carry that memory. It didn't erase the mistake. It just turned the mistake into something I owed a debt for, rather than something I was only ashamed of, and a debt is a thing you can actually act on. I have not missed a morning since, at her house or anyone else's, and some mornings I still knock, just to sit for a minute, the way she told me I could.

meta.topic: delivering newspapers on a route inherited from an older sibling
meta.prompt: Reflect on something that someone has done for you that has made you happy or thankful in a surprising way. How has this gratitude affected or motivated you?

text:
Every evening at six, for as long as I can remember, my grandfather pulled his harmonium out from behind the couch and played for twenty minutes before dinner. Same time, almost every day, rain or heat or the one time the power went out and he played anyway by the light of his phone propped against the bellows. I used to sit cross-legged next to him doing homework, half listening, until the year I turned eleven and he handed me the bellows side and said, without much ceremony, that my hands were finally big enough to pump and press keys at the same time.

He never used sheet music. He taught the way he'd been taught, by ear, humming a line and waiting for me to find it on the keys, correcting me with a tap on my wrist when I landed a half-step off. The harmonium itself is older than my mother - a boxy wooden thing with a crack along the side that he glued back together twice, and a middle C-sharp reed that buzzes slightly no matter how many times it's been serviced, so that every song we play carries this one small imperfection in exactly the same place. I know that buzz better than I know most things about myself.

When his hands started shaking too much to manage the stops reliably, I didn't decide to keep the six o'clock habit going. It just kept going, the way habits do when nobody announces they're ending. I started playing while he sang, then playing the melody while he hummed along under his breath, then eventually playing alone in the next room while he listened from his chair, correcting me by voice instead of by touch. Twenty minutes a day, for seven years now, on an instrument most people my age have never heard of, let alone heard played.

I don't know how to explain what this means for a campus that doesn't already have anyone doing it, except to say that I've watched a two-hundred-year-old kind of music survive inside one small daily habit, passed hand to hand instead of downloaded or streamed, and I think that's a specific, useful thing to bring somewhere new. I'd bring the actual harmonium, cracked side and buzzing reed and all. I'd play in a common room some evening the way my grandfather played in our living room, not performing exactly, just doing the thing at six o'clock because that's when it happens, and I'd teach anyone curious enough to sit down next to me the way he taught me, by ear, correcting a half-step at a time. Whatever community forms around that, badly played at first and slowly less so, wouldn't exist there without me carrying it in.

meta.topic: learning to play a grandfather's harmonium
meta.prompt: What would you contribute to our campus that would not be here if you were not?

text:
Every Tuesday and Thursday for eleven years, at 4:30 in the afternoon, I sat down at the same piano bench in the same small studio above a dry cleaner's and played scales for the first ten minutes before my teacher, Ms. Feld, would let me touch anything that sounded like actual music. C major, then G, then D, around the circle, both hands, metronome ticking at a speed she'd slowly ratchet up over the years until my fingers moved faster than I consciously thought about them moving. I did this so many times that I could probably still do it half-asleep, and for a long time I assumed that ritual - the walk up the narrow stairs, the smell of dry-cleaning chemicals mixed with the studio's old carpet, the ten minutes of scales - was just the boring part I had to get through to reach the real thing.

I quit in March of this year. I told Ms. Feld first, before my parents, which she pointed out was unusual, and I said I didn't know why I did it that way either.

The community I want to talk about isn't the one you'd expect - not a youth orchestra, not a competition circuit, though I did those too. It's smaller and stranger than that. It's the studio itself, the rotating cast of maybe six or seven other students who shared that same narrow staircase over the years, whose lesson slots bordered mine, whom I saw for ninety seconds at a time twice a week for over a decade, in passing, one of us leaving as the other arrived. I knew almost nothing about most of them beyond a first name and whatever piece was currently propped on their stand. And yet I knew, with total certainty, when Owen finally nailed the Chopin nocturne he'd been stuck on for months, because I heard it through the door on my way in and stopped on the landing to listen to the whole thing before Ms. Feld noticed I was late.

That's the part I didn't understand until I stopped going. The scales weren't the boring ten minutes before the real thing. They were the real thing, or at least they were doing something the real thing couldn't - they were the ten minutes where nothing was being judged, where Ms. Feld would half-listen while making tea, where my hands got to just move without anyone, including me, deciding whether it was good.

I quit for reasons that had nothing to do with the music itself and everything to do with time - junior year, and something had to give, and piano was the thing that didn't show up on a transcript the way calculus did. I made the decision in about four days, which felt fast at the time and feels faster now. What I didn't account for was how much of my week had been organized around that Tuesday-Thursday walk up the stairs, how much of my sense of my own competence - the specific, private feeling of a passage finally sitting right under my fingers after weeks of it not sitting right - had nowhere to go once the bench was gone.

I still see Owen sometimes, at school, where he mostly plays baseball and I don't think anyone there knows he can play Chopin. We don't really talk about piano. We don't need to, exactly - there's a strange shorthand between people who shared a staircase for years without sharing much else, a nod that means something like I heard you get that right once and I don't think either of us has forgotten it.

I don't know if I'll go back to it in college. Ms. Feld told me, at my last lesson, that eleven years of scales doesn't disappear from your hands even if you stop practicing them, that they're in there somewhere, waiting. I didn't believe her completely. But I noticed, packing up my sheet music for the last time, that my hands found the closing chord of my last piece without me really looking at the page, the way you find a light switch in a room you've lived in long enough not to need to see it.

meta.topic: quitting piano after eleven years
meta.prompt: Describe a community you belong to and your place within it.

text:
The dough splits along the same seam for the third time, right at the pleat where I've pinched it closed, and a thin thread of khoya filling leaks out into the oil and turns instantly, furiously black. I fish the ruined gujiya out with a slotted spoon before it can scorch the rest of the batch and set it on a paper towel next to its two failed siblings, and I stand there in my grandmother's kitchen, which is now just my kitchen, holding a spoon and trying not to cry about fried dough.

My phone is propped against the flour tin, open to a recipe some woman in Ohio posted with exact measurements, two hundred and forty grams of maida, one hundred grams of ghee, a photograph of dumplings so uniform they look machine-stamped. I have made this recipe twice this week and both times it has come out wrong, not badly wrong, just wrong in a way I can taste but can't name, missing the specific density Dadi's always had, the way hers gave slightly under your teeth before the crunch. She never once, in eleven years of watching her make these before every Holi, wrote down a single measurement. She'd tell me a fistful of this, enough of that to feel right, and I used to think that was carelessness, honestly. I used to think, standing at her elbow at nine years old, that a woman who loved her family as much as she clearly did would have taken twenty minutes at some point to write the recipe down so that this exact moment, three years after she died, would not be happening to me.

I call my mother in from the living room to taste the black one's replacement, and she chews for a second too long before she says it's close, not it, but close, and something in her face when she says it makes me understand she isn't grading my cooking. She's remembering. She tells me, while I start pleating a new one, that Dadi learned this from her own mother in a kitchen in Meerut with no written recipe either, that she used to complain about the exact same thing I'm complaining about now, a fistful of this, enough of that, and that somewhere along the way she stopped complaining and started measuring with her hands instead of her eyes, the way you learn a language by living inside it instead of by memorizing a dictionary.

I had wanted, this whole week, to solve my grandmother like a problem, to reverse-engineer her into two hundred and forty grams of maida so that nothing about her would ever be at risk of disappearing again. I am realizing, with my hands full of dough that will not behave exactly like the Ohio woman's dough, that this was never going to work, and that maybe it was never supposed to. My mother takes the spoon from me and shows me, not tells me, how much khoya to use, pinching it between two fingers, and it is more than the recipe says and somehow obviously correct the second I see it in her hand.

By the fifth batch the pleats hold. They're not identical to Dadi's, a little thicker on one side, filling slightly off-center, and when my mother bites into one she doesn't say it's exactly right, she just goes quiet in the particular way she goes quiet when something has actually worked, and keeps eating standing up at the counter instead of sitting down, the way you do when you're not thinking about whether it's good, you're just eating it.

meta.topic: a family recipe nobody wrote down
meta.prompt: The lessons we take from obstacles we encounter can be fundamental to later success. Recount a time when you faced a challenge, setback, or failure. How did it affect you, and what did you learn from the experience?

text:
There's a stopwatch in my backpack, the cheap plastic kind you'd get free with a magazine subscription, and it doesn't even work anymore - the display went dead sometime last spring - but I still carry it to every tournament, and I still take it out of my bag before every round and set it on the table next to my flow pad, dead screen and all.

It was Sam's before it was mine. My debate partner handed it to me in a parking lot the fall of junior year, a few weeks after I'd lost a semifinal round at States that I should have won, in a match where the judge's ballot used the word "aggressive" three separate times, not as a compliment. I'd argued the whole round the way I argued every round back then - fast, loud, cutting in the second I heard an opening I could exploit, treating silence like wasted time. The other team's first speaker just let me finish. Every time. And she beat me doing it.

Sam's fix wasn't a pep talk. It was the stopwatch. He said I needed to physically time my pauses in practice because I genuinely could not feel the difference between two seconds of silence and half a second, that my sense of pacing had been trained wrong for three years running and no amount of me just deciding to be different was going to undo that on its own.

So we made it a routine. Every Tuesday practice round, before we started, Sam would click the stopwatch and hand it to whoever was judging that day, and the rule was simple: after my opponent finished speaking, I had to let two full seconds pass, visible on that little plastic screen, before I opened my mouth. It sounds small. It felt, the first few weeks, like holding my breath underwater - physically uncomfortable in a way I hadn't expected silence to be. I'd sit there counting in my head, one, two, watching the numbers change, fighting the exact same reflex every single time.

I did this every Tuesday for months. Not because it was fun - it wasn't, particularly, it felt like practicing patience is supposed to feel, which is to say tedious and slightly humiliating - but because it was the one thing standing between the debater I'd been and the one I was trying to become. The stopwatch broke in February, right in the middle of a practice round, the screen just going dark mid-count, and by then it didn't matter. I'd counted to two so many times that my body did it without the numbers anymore.

I won a round at a tournament in March against a team ranked well above us, and afterward the judge said something about my composure, my willingness to let silence sit in the room instead of filling it, and I remember standing there thinking about a dead stopwatch sitting uselessly in my backpack, still doing its job somehow, months after it stopped being able to tell time.

I don't need it anymore, not really. I could leave it home and nothing about my next round would change. But I still take it out before every match and set it next to my flow pad, dead screen up, and I couldn't tell you exactly why except that it feels less like superstition and more like keeping the receipt for a debt I paid off slowly, one uncomfortable Tuesday at a time, and some habits you keep going through even after they've stopped being necessary, because the going-through is what taught you something in the first place, and you're not entirely sure who you'd be without it.

meta.topic: a debate tournament loss that changed how they argue
meta.prompt: Write about an object that is important to you.

text:
The leash hangs on a hook by my desk, red nylon gone pink from the wash, the clip slightly bent from a car door. It belonged to a dog named Duke, and I am, by any honest measure, one of the worst volunteers the Millbrook Animal Shelter has ever had, which is exactly why I have it.

I signed up sophomore year for service hours and turned out to be bad at nearly all of it. I let a beagle mix slip his collar in the parking lot and had to chase him past four cars while a staff member watched, unimpressed. I mixed up two cats' medication schedules. I was scared of the bigger dogs in a way I tried to hide and clearly didn't hide well, since Priya, who ran the volunteer desk, started quietly assigning me to laundry instead of walks, which I also folded wrong.

By November I'd decided to quit. I sat in the little office off the kennel hallway, waiting to tell Priya I wasn't coming back, rehearsing something about how I wasn't cut out for it, which was true. While I waited, a volunteer walked past with Duke, a fourteen-year-old shepherd mix missing a back leg, slow and gray around the muzzle, the kind of dog nobody photographs well. Nobody wanted to walk him. He took twenty minutes to cover what a healthy dog covered in five, and most people had other dogs to get to.

Priya was on the phone, so I ended up outside holding his leash by default, the only volunteer standing around with nothing better to do. We went maybe forty feet before he stopped, sat down on the pavement, and leaned his whole weight against my leg, breathing hard, not going anywhere for a while. I didn't know what to do except sit down next to him on the curb, so I did, and we stayed there for the better part of ten minutes while I told him, out loud, like an idiot, that I was planning to quit that day.

I didn't quit. I asked Priya, when she got off the phone, if I could keep walking Duke specifically, and she said, a little surprised, that nobody had ever requested him before. I walked him three times a week for the next eight months, twenty slow minutes at a time, until he was adopted by a retired couple who'd specifically asked for an older dog nobody else wanted.

I still can't hold a leash steady around a dog that pulls. I'm still, by most measures, mediocre at the job. But Duke's leash sits on my hook now, and some days it's the only proof I need that being bad at something in general isn't the same as being wrong for it entirely.

text:
The tuning fork is cold against my palm even in August, when the sanctuary's air conditioning fights the heat outside and mostly loses, and I strike it against my knee the way Mrs. Castellano taught me freshman year, then press the stem to my front teeth so the hum runs straight into my skull instead of getting lost in the room's noise. A440. The other altos are still filing into the loft with their folders, and I'm off to the side doing this small private ritual that has nothing to do with God and everything to do with the fact that I can feel a pitch in my jaw before I properly hear it in my ears, which is a thing I have never stopped finding strange.

I should say plainly that I don't believe any of what we sing. I joined because the choir was short two altos the fall of freshman year and Mrs. Castellano cornered me after a school assembly where I'd been humming along without realizing it, and by the time I understood what the words in the hymnal were actually asking me to believe, I was already too far in to quit gracefully, and also, if I'm honest, I didn't want to. Nobody in the loft has ever asked me to pray and mean it. They've only ever asked me to listen, and listening turned out to be the part I couldn't stop doing.

Here is what happens, on the good nights, maybe one rehearsal in four: all four parts lock into a chord, really lock, not just correct but tuned to each other instead of to a piano, and a fifth note appears that nobody is singing. It sits low, underneath the sopranos, a hum with no mouth behind it, and the first time I heard it I turned around convinced someone in the back had joined in on a note that wasn't written. Nobody had. It's called a combination tone, or sometimes a Tartini tone, and it happens when two frequencies are close enough to a clean ratio that the difference between them becomes audible on its own, a note built entirely out of math, summoned by four teenagers holding their pitch steady enough not to wobble it away.

I have chased that sound in a way I've never chased anything assigned to me in a classroom. I hold the tuning fork after rehearsal, once everyone else is stacking chairs and talking about the parking lot, and I test intervals against it, a fifth, a fourth, a major third, trying to feel where the ratio goes clean and the ghost note threatens to show up. I emailed Mr. Osei, my physics teacher, over winter break with a question about beat frequencies that turned into a forty-minute conversation the first day back, and he loaned me a battered library book on the physics of just intonation that I have renewed six times and probably owe him an apology for. I've watched more acoustics lectures on my phone at 1 a.m. than I'd ever admit to a teacher directly, chasing the same handful of seconds, the four-part chord resolving into a fifth part that isn't there.

Nobody in the loft is thinking about ratios when it happens. They're thinking about the hymn, about their grandmother in the third pew, about getting the soprano entrance right. I'm standing there with a tuning fork in my blazer pocket, mouthing words I don't believe, waiting for four voices to accidentally build a note out of nothing, and for those few seconds I could not tell you what time it is or how long I've been standing there or whether the sermon that follows will be forty minutes or ninety. I only notice again once the chord breaks apart and the ghost note goes with it, and I'm back to being a girl in a loft on a Sunday, tuning fork already cooling in my hand, already thinking about the next hymn on the page.

text:
The object is a carburetor, specifically the left one off a 1978 Honda CB550, and if you'd told me two summers ago that I'd be able to identify a part like that on sight, disassembled, sitting in a coffee can of gasoline on my uncle's workbench, I would have laughed at you, because at the start of that summer I could not have told you what a carburetor even did.

My uncle Ray had the bike in pieces in his garage for what he claimed was "temporary," though judging by the layer of dust on the gas tank when I first saw it, temporary had been going on for roughly four years. It had belonged to my grandfather, who died before I was old enough to really remember him beyond a few photographs and the smell of a specific brand of pipe tobacco that apparently still lingers, according to my mother, in one corner of Ray's garage. Nobody had asked me to fix it. I offered, mostly because I was seventeen and bored and my uncle looked tired of feeling guilty about a bike he couldn't bring himself to sell and hadn't touched in years.

We started with the engine, because Ray said an engine that won't run makes everything else pointless, and for the first three weeks I mostly held flashlights and handed him wrenches of the wrong size until I learned to tell a nine-sixteenths from a half-inch by feel instead of by squinting at the little numbers stamped into the metal. But it was the carburetors - there were two, one for each cylinder - that actually taught me something, because they were small enough that Ray eventually just handed me one and said, essentially, good luck, ask before you force anything.

I took it apart on a card table in the driveway with a manual open beside me, laying every screw and gasket out on a towel in the exact order I removed them, because Ray told me on day one that a mechanic who doesn't lay parts out in order is a mechanic who's about to have a very bad afternoon. The float, the needle valve, the tiny brass jets with holes so small I had to hold them up to the sun to see if they were actually clogged or just looked clogged. I soaked it in gas, scrubbed the varnish out of channels smaller than a pencil lead with a guitar string because that's what Ray used, apparently that's a real technique, and put it back together twice because the first time I put the float in upside down and it flooded.

When the engine finally turned over - not that carburetor alone, obviously, months of other work besides - it didn't roar to life like in a movie. It coughed, caught, died, coughed again, and then, on the fourth try, settled into an idle that shook the whole garage floor, and Ray let out a sound I'd never heard him make before, something between a laugh and something else.

I keep that carburetor now, not on the bike - it's back where it belongs, doing its actual job - but a spare one Ray gave me afterward, cleaned and reassembled, sitting on my desk at home. I turn it over sometimes when I'm trying to think through something unrelated, homework, an argument with a friend, whatever. There's something in the specific, patient logic of it that I find calming: every tiny passage exists for a reason, every part only works because every other part is exactly where it should be, and if something's wrong, the fix is almost never mysterious, it's almost always just dirt in a channel that needs clearing.

My grandfather rode that bike for eleven years before his knees gave out and it went into the garage. I never knew him well enough to miss him the way my mother does, but I think I understand something about him now that I didn't before, something I only got access to through the specific stupid patience of cleaning out a jet with a guitar string in a hot driveway. Ray still doesn't ride it much. Neither do I, honestly - I'm not licensed yet. But some nights he starts it up in the driveway just to hear it idle, and I go outside and stand there with him, and neither of us says anything, because I don't think there's anything that needs saying.
