text:
I am not a natural with animals, which is an inconvenient thing to discover only after signing up for eight months of Saturday mornings at Fairview Animal Shelter. My leash technique is bad. I get tangled in it. Cats sense something in me that makes them go rigid and refuse to be held, and the first time I tried to clean a kennel I left the gate unlatched and a beagle named Pepper trotted calmly past three volunteers and out into the parking lot before anyone noticed. I cried in the supply closet that day, certain I would be quietly uninvited from ever coming back.

I wasn't. The woman who runs the shelter's volunteer program, Marisol, found me among the mop buckets, handed me a paper towel, and said, "You're on Saturday intake with me from now on." I assumed this was a demotion, a way of keeping the girl who loses dogs away from the dogs. It took me weeks to understand it was the opposite. Intake is where the newest, most frightened animals come in, and Marisol wanted someone there every single week, not because I was good at it, but because I kept showing up.

So I did. Every Saturday for the rest of that year, I sat on the concrete floor of the intake room with whatever animal had just arrived, usually terrified, sometimes matted or limping or too thin, and I did nothing more skillful than stay still and let them get used to a person being nearby. I was still bad at the parts that required competence. I still couldn't read a dog's body language the way the other volunteers could, still got told, gently, to step back from a growling shepherd I'd misjudged as merely shy. But I was there every week, on the same patch of floor, and somewhere in that repetition I stopped thinking of it as something I was failing at and started thinking of it as something I was simply doing.

What surprises me now, looking back, is how much Marisol's decision to keep me shaped what I understand about being useful. She never once told me I was good at the work. She corrected me constantly, without softening it, in a way that made it clear she took me seriously enough to bother. What she gave me instead of praise was persistence in me - she kept scheduling me, kept trusting the floor to someone who had let a beagle escape, kept treating my presence as worth something even when my skill wasn't. I didn't understand until much later that this was a form of generosity, maybe a rarer one than encouragement: the decision to keep counting on someone who hasn't proven they deserve it yet.

I think about this most on the mornings when I don't want to go, when I have a test Monday and my hands are still not steady with a leash. I go anyway, because someone once decided that showing up mattered more than doing it well, and treated me accordingly for long enough that I started to believe it myself. I am, I should say, still not particularly good at this. Just last month a cat bit me hard enough to draw blood and I still don't trust myself around anything larger than a beagle. But I have sat on that concrete floor almost every Saturday for two years now, and the animals that come through intake terrified usually leave the room a little less so, and I've come to understand that Marisol's stubborn faith in my ordinary, repeated presence is the closest thing to a gift I've been given that I didn't ask for and didn't expect to need.

text:
I still have issue fourteen. Not a photo of it, not some PDF somebody archived - the actual paper, newsprint gone soft at the folds, a coffee ring on the front page that isn't mine because I never got to finish my coffee that morning. It lives in the bottom drawer of my desk, under a calculator I broke sophomore year and still haven't thrown out for no good reason.

Here's what happened. Junior year I found out the district had quietly cut our school's counselor position from full-time to two days a week, right around the same month they approved forty thousand dollars for new turf on the football field. Nobody announced the counselor cut. I only knew because a friend went to make an appointment and got told the office was closed until Thursday. I wrote it up for the paper using numbers from a budget document a front-office secretary let slip after I'd asked one too many annoying questions in one too many visits. We ran it on a Tuesday.

Admin was not thrilled. That undersells it, honestly - the principal called our advisor, Mr. Danziger, into his office and wanted to know exactly who'd handed a seventeen-year-old district financial records. I was sure, walking past that office and seeing the door shut, that he'd give my name up. Why wouldn't he? He had a job. I had a byline and a stapler.

He didn't. I found out weeks later, from another student who'd overheard part of it through a wall that is apparently not as soundproof as the district thinks, that Mr. Danziger told the principal flatly that a paper doesn't function if sources aren't protected, and that if someone needed to be disciplined it should be him, not a kid doing exactly what journalism is supposed to do. He never told me this himself. He just kept running the paper the same way he always had, like nothing had happened, like he hadn't put his own job on a table for a story about counseling hours.

I found out the whole thing had almost gotten him formally reprimanded when I overheard my own mom on the phone with his wife - small town, everyone's moms know each other - and by then it was old news to everybody but me. I never even got to thank him properly. I tried once, after class, and he just said, "That's the job," and started erasing the whiteboard like the conversation was already finished.

That newspaper sat in the recycling bin outside the front office for exactly one afternoon before I fished it back out, cover a little damp, and I don't totally know why I kept it instead of just archiving the file like everyone else does now. I think I wanted something I could actually hold that proved a person had decided, on a random Tuesday, that protecting a seventeen-year-old was worth more to him than staying comfortable.

text:
The judge's paper said "aggressive" three times in the same paragraph, and not as a compliment, and I was still holding it in the hallway outside the round room when my partner Sam came out and asked how bad it was.

We'd lost in the semifinal of States to a team we'd beaten twice that season. I had gone into the round the same way I went into every round - fast, loaded, interrupting cross-ex the second I heard an opening, treating every exchange like a wall I needed to be first to climb over. It had worked all year. It worked right up until it didn't, against a pair from a school two hours north whose first speaker, a quiet sophomore, just kept letting me finish, nodding, and then dismantling exactly what I'd said with about a third of the words I'd used to say it.

The judge's ballot didn't say I was wrong on the substance. It said something worse, in a way - it said the judge had stopped being able to tell what I actually believed underneath all the speed and interruption, that somewhere around my third rebuttal I'd become a wall of noise instead of an argument, and that the other team's stillness had read, in the room, as confidence, while my volume had started to read as something closer to panic.

I didn't believe it at first. I told Sam the judge just liked their style better, some judges do, it's subjective, we'd get a different panel next time and win easily. I said all this in the parking lot afterward, fast, the same way I'd argued the whole round, and Sam let me finish - actually let me finish, didn't interrupt, which I noticed even in the state I was in - and then said, quietly, that maybe I should read the ballot again when I wasn't still angry.

I read it again that night. Then again a week later. It said the same thing both times, which is usually how you know a criticism is actually true and not just a bad mood on someone's part.

What changed wasn't sudden, and it didn't happen in that hallway, even though that's the moment I keep coming back to when I try to locate it. It happened slowly, over the following month, in practice rounds where I made myself do something that felt almost physically uncomfortable - stop talking. Let my opponent finish a sentence I already knew, in the first four words, that I disagreed with. Wait a full two seconds before responding instead of cutting in on the last syllable of their point. Sam started timing my pauses in practice, actually holding a stopwatch, because I genuinely could not tell the difference between two seconds and half a second without external proof.

The sophomore from that semifinal round beat me again later that season, at a different tournament, in a round I lost on a much narrower margin, arguing much more carefully than I had before. I remember shaking her hand afterward and asking, somewhat pathetically, how she'd learned to do that - the stillness, the letting people finish. She said her old coach used to tell her that the person who's actually right doesn't need to talk over anyone to prove it, that speed is what you use when you're not sure your argument survives someone else finishing their sentence.

I've thought about that sentence more than almost anything anyone's said to me in four years of doing this. I don't think I've fully become the debater she already was that day. I still catch myself starting to cut someone off, some reflex from three years of training myself the opposite way, and I have to physically stop my own mouth mid-syllable. But I keep the ballot from that semifinal in the folder with my other tournament papers, the good ones and the bad ones together, and it's the one I go back to first when I'm packing for a new round, before any of the ones that say I won.

text:
Every Sunday morning since I was seven, my job has been to climb the narrow steps to our rooftop before the sun gets too high and turn the pickle jars. There are usually six or seven of them lined up against the water tank, glass jars with mango or lime or green chili packed in mustard oil and salt, covered with cloth instead of lids so the sun can reach them, and my job is simple: tilt each one, let the oil run over the fruit, set it back down facing the light. My grandfather taught me this before he taught me almost anything else, and for years I thought of it as a chore, something between watering a plant and doing dishes, a five-minute task I did half asleep in my pajamas before anyone else was awake.

Nobody in my family has ever written down how much salt goes into those jars, or how many days of sun a batch needs before it's ready, or how you're supposed to know, just by looking, that the mustard seeds have finally started working instead of just sitting there inert. My grandfather knows by smell. He knows a jar is close by the particular sourness that rises off it when you lift the cloth, a smell I couldn't identify for years except to say it was the smell of Sunday.

What I didn't expect was to become genuinely obsessed with why any of it works. Somewhere around freshman year, turning the same jars I'd turned a thousand times before, I started actually wondering what salt does to a mango at the cellular level, why the oil rises the way it does, why some batches turn out sharp and clean and others turn cloudy and have to be thrown away. I started reading about osmosis and lacto-fermentation on nights I was supposedly doing homework, watching videos from food scientists explaining brine concentration and water activity, and bringing questions to my chemistry teacher that had nothing to do with the syllabus and that she answered anyway, clearly delighted someone wanted to talk about salt gradients before first period.

I started keeping a small notebook by the jars, which my grandfather found funny and never discouraged, writing down dates and weather and how each batch smelled on day four, day eight, day fourteen, trying to find the pattern underneath what he does purely by instinct. He still can't tell me the salt percentage. He can just tell me, correctly, every single time, whether a jar needs three more days of sun or is already gone bad.

I still climb those stairs every Sunday, even now that he moves more slowly and mostly watches from a chair instead of standing over my shoulder. It is still, on paper, a five-minute task. But somewhere inside those five minutes is the reason I want to study food chemistry, the reason an entire Saturday can disappear while I read about fermentation kinetics, the reason I know exactly what a jar of achaar sounds like when you shake it right. It started as something I did without thinking. It didn't stay that way.

text:
Every other Saturday at 7 a.m., I stand in Fox Run in hip waders two sizes too big, next to a retired chemistry teacher, a dairy farmer, and a man named Gene who has tested this creek's dissolved oxygen levels every month for eleven years and keeps every result in a green three-ring binder he will not let anyone photograph. That's the Fox Run Watershed Alliance. There are nine of us. I am the only one under fifty, and for the first four months I mostly held things and wrote down numbers other people called out to me.

I earned my place slowly. I learned titration in Gene's garage because the county extension office training happened on a school day. I built a spreadsheet that finally let the group compare five years of nitrate readings against rainfall data, which nobody had bothered to do before because nobody else there uses spreadsheets for fun. By spring, Gene handed me the clipboard without being asked, which in that group is close to a promotion. My place in that community is the person who turns other people's careful, patient fieldwork into numbers that actually mean something, and I take that seriously.

My science fair project used our own data, plus new samples I collected downstream of Riverside Poultry, the plant where my dad has worked for twenty-two years. The nitrate levels there are consistently the highest on the whole creek, high enough that I couldn't honestly leave it out of the project even though I knew exactly what that would mean at my own dinner table.

My dad is proud of that job. It put both my sister and me through braces and is the reason we have health insurance, and he has never once complained about the hours. When I told him what my numbers showed, he didn't yell. He just got quiet in a way that felt worse, and asked if I really had to name the plant specifically, or if I could say "an agricultural facility" instead, something vague and deniable. I said no. I said the whole point of the Alliance's work is that the data means nothing if you round off the parts that are inconvenient.

We have not resolved this. He came to my presentation, stood in the back, and told me afterward that he was proud of me and also that he wished I hadn't used the plant's actual name, both in the same sentence, like he hadn't noticed the contradiction or didn't know what to do with it. I don't think he's wrong to worry - people at his job have asked him about it, and he doesn't love explaining his daughter's science project to his coworkers. I don't think I'm wrong either. I love him, and I still turned in the project exactly as the numbers told me to.

Being part of the Alliance taught me that a community isn't only people who agree with each other. Gene once told me the creek doesn't care what any of us want it to say. I think about that a lot now, mostly at dinner, where my dad and I have quietly agreed not to bring it up again, which is not at all the same thing as agreeing.

text:
Bay fourteen had a jammed conveyor and I told Danny I could handle it myself, which was the wrong call, and I knew it was the wrong call about four seconds after I said it, but by then it was already out of my mouth and Danny had already walked off toward bay nine to deal with something else.

I worked night shifts at a distribution warehouse the summer between junior and senior year, ten p.m. to six a.m., mostly scanning and loading pallets alongside a crew of adults who'd been doing it for years and treated me, correctly, as the least experienced person on the floor. Danny was my shift lead, a guy in his forties who moved through the warehouse like he had a map of it memorized in his knees, and he had a rule about jammed equipment that he repeated probably every single shift: two people, always, no exceptions, because a conveyor jam under load can release fast and you do not want to be the only person standing there when it does.

I broke the rule because I was tired and it was three in the morning and asking for help felt, in that specific sleep-deprived state, like admitting I couldn't keep up, and I very badly wanted to keep up. So I climbed up to clear the jam alone. The belt released while my arm was still in the gap, not violently, nothing dramatic enough for an ambulance, but hard enough to leave a bruise that ran the length of my forearm and hard enough that I understood, immediately and completely, exactly why the rule existed.

Danny found me holding my arm at the water fountain a few minutes later. He didn't yell. That was somehow worse than yelling would have been. He just looked at the bruise starting to come up under my skin and asked, very evenly, whether I thought the rule was for people who didn't know what they were doing, or for everyone.

I didn't have a good answer. I still don't have a great one, honestly, months later, except that I think some part of me believed the rule applied to other people - to the actually inexperienced, to whoever the rule-makers had in mind when they wrote it - and not to me, because I'd been doing the job for six weeks by then and had started to feel like I understood it well enough to bend its edges a little. That's a specific kind of arrogance that I don't think you can be talked out of. You mostly just have to hurt yourself a small, correctable amount and let the lesson land the hard way.

The warehouse crew, I should say, is its own kind of community, one I didn't expect to find anything meaningful in when I took the job just for the paycheck. Nobody there knew me from school or church or any of the usual places people know each other. We knew each other from twelve hundred identical pallets a night and the specific rhythm of a shift that starts when everyone else's day is ending. There's a trust that builds in a place like that, quiet and mostly unspoken, built out of things like watching someone's back near a conveyor, or covering someone's break without being asked, or Danny walking the floor at 2 a.m. checking that everyone's where they're supposed to be like some tired, unglamorous shepherd.

I broke that trust a little, that night, not just the rule itself but the actual premise the rule is built on - that we look out for each other because none of us can fully look out for ourselves in a place with that much moving machinery. Danny didn't write me up. He didn't tell my parents. He just made me work the next three jams with him standing right there, not saying much, watching.

I think about that bruise sometimes, long faded now, when I'm tempted to skip a step somewhere else in my life because I'm tired and it feels efficient and nobody's watching. I don't think Danny ever fully forgot it either, not in a way he held against me, just in a way that changed how closely he watched me for the rest of that summer, and I understood why, and I never once resented him for it.

text:
I got the internship at Bell Voss Engineering through my uncle, who knows one of the partners, and I spent the first two weeks of it doing almost nothing. I mean that almost literally. I organized a supply closet once. I watched three CAD tutorials I could've watched at home for free. Mostly I sat at a desk that used to belong to someone named Carl - his nameplate was still in the drawer - refreshing my email and waiting for a task that never came.

My supervisor was a structural engineer named Priya Anand, maybe thirty-five, sharp, calm, the kind of person who says exactly as much as she means to and not one word more. I liked her immediately. I respected her professionally in a way I didn't respect most adults yet, honestly, because she was clearly good at her actual job, not just good at managing a teenager. So when I finally worked up the nerve, at the start of week three, to ask her directly why I wasn't being given anything real to do, I expected either an apology or a fix. I got neither. She told me, pretty evenly, that sometimes the job is waiting - that a firm mid-project doesn't always have a clean task to hand a seventeen-year-old, and that patience was part of what she was actually testing.

I did not like that answer. At all. It felt like a nice way of saying deal with it, and I was seventeen and annoyed and fairly sure I knew better, so I did something I still think about more than almost anything else from that summer: I emailed one of the partners directly, a man I'd met exactly once, and asked - politely, I thought, though rereading it later I'm not sure "polite" is the word - whether there might be more substantive project work available, since my current assignment wasn't using my skills.

He forwarded it to Priya. Of course he did. Why wouldn't he.

She came to my desk that afternoon, and she wasn't angry, which somehow made it so much worse. She just asked why I hadn't come to her again first if I still had concerns after our conversation, and I didn't have a real answer, because the honest one - that I didn't trust her answer, that I thought going over her head would get results faster than waiting on her - wasn't something I was proud enough of to say out loud. She told me, still calm, still not raising her voice at all, that she'd now have to explain to a partner why her intern had gone around her in week three, and that this wasn't actually about me.

Nothing dramatic happened after that. I wasn't fired. I wasn't even really punished, not officially. But something in how she talked to me shifted, just slightly, for the rest of the summer - more formal, a little more distant - and I don't blame her one bit.

Here's the part I keep turning over. About two weeks later, real work did show up, a drainage assessment for a site near the highway, and it turned out the reason nothing had come earlier wasn't some test of my patience at all - the project had genuinely been stuck in permitting, for reasons that had nothing to do with me and that she couldn't have explained without breaking client confidentiality. She'd been telling me the truth the whole time. I just hadn't been willing to sit inside an answer I didn't like long enough to find that out.

I think about that email a lot. Not because it ended my internship or ruined anything permanent - it didn't - but because it's the clearest example I have of a specific kind of mistake: mistaking my own impatience for good judgment, and being willing to undercut someone I actually respected rather than just sit with not knowing for two more weeks.

text:
The binoculars are a hand-me-down from my grandfather, a chunky pair of Bushnells with a strap that's been re-stitched twice, and for two years now they have lived by my back door, next to my shoes, so I can grab them without thinking. Every school day that isn't raining, I leave the house at 6:20, walk the four minutes to the drainage creek behind Lindale Elementary, and stand there until 6:55 watching whatever shows up. I started doing this alone. Then I met Mr. Ferris.

Mr. Ferris is seventy-four and has been birding that same creek for over thirty years, since before the elementary school existed, when the land behind it was still an actual field. He noticed me out there in October of freshman year, said nothing for about a week, and then one morning just started talking to me like we'd already been mid-conversation for years - telling me the difference between a downy and a hairy woodpecker, how to tell a Cooper's hawk from a sharp-shinned by the way it flies, not just the way it looks. I started bringing a notebook because I didn't want to keep asking him the same things twice.

For a year and a half, Mr. Ferris was the only birding authority I had, and I trusted him completely. So when I disagreed with him, in April of this year, it actually mattered to me in a way that a disagreement with a teacher or a classmate wouldn't have.

What happened was this. I saw a warbler in the willows on the east bank, small, yellow-and-black, with a wing pattern I didn't recognize, and I was almost sure - ninety percent sure - that it was a Golden-winged Warbler, a bird that is genuinely rare in our county, maybe one or two confirmed sightings a decade. I wanted to log it on the county list, the shared spreadsheet real birders use, the kind of thing that gets checked by a review committee. Mr. Ferris looked at my photo, which was blurry because my hands were shaking, and said no. Not "I'm not sure." No. He said it was almost certainly a Blue-winged Warbler, which looks similar at a distance and is far more common, and that submitting an unclear photo as a rare bird does real harm to the data other researchers rely on.

I argued with him. I said ninety percent was still ninety percent. He said the county list isn't built on ninety percent, it's built on documentation, and that every birder who's ever submitted a maybe-sighting because they wanted it to be true has made the record worse for everyone who comes after them. I remember feeling something close to betrayed, like he was choosing a rule over what I had actually seen with my own eyes.

I didn't submit it. Not because he convinced me that morning - I walked to school still annoyed - but because I kept turning it over, and by third period I understood that his caution wasn't about doubting me specifically. It was about a discipline he had spent thirty years building, one blurry photo at a time, and I was asking him to let me skip the part where you earn certainty.

I still have the photo. It's probably a Blue-winged Warbler. I'll never fully know, and that used to bother me more than it does now. What I kept from that argument is the binoculars themselves. They weren't good enough to have settled it, and neither was I, and every morning I stand at the creek with them I'm reminded that wanting something to be rare doesn't make it rare. Mr. Ferris still meets me there some mornings. We haven't seen a Golden-winged Warbler since, but I check every willow on that east bank like we might.

meta.topic: birdwatching alone before school

text:
I still have the microphone. It's sitting on a shelf in my room next to some books and a plant that's half-dead. I spent forty dollars on it after I decided to start a podcast, convinced that good equipment was the thing that was going to make my ideas matter. Looking back, that was the most optimistic I've ever been about anything.

The podcast was called "Half-Asleep Philosophy" because I thought the name was clever. The concept was that I would just talk about philosophical problems while sitting in my dark room late at night, the way you do when you can't sleep and your brain won't stop thinking about things like whether free will actually exists or if time is real. I recorded the intro probably fifteen times trying to get the right tone - casual but smart, conversational but intellectual. By take twelve I'd basically recorded the same thing four times and decided it was good enough.

The first episode was about Schrodinger's cat. I explained the paradox, talked about what it means for quantum states, rambled for about forty minutes about how this had changed the way I thought about uncertainty in my own life. I uploaded it to every podcast platform I could find and then I waited. I sent the link to my friends. My mom listened to it and said it was interesting but maybe a little hard to follow. One of my friends actually sent me a note saying she liked it, which felt like validation enough to keep going.

Episodes two and three came out every other week. They were about the ship of Theseus and then about whether AI could ever really be conscious. I spent hours researching before each recording. I rewrote scripts and then basically threw them out and just talked anyway. The audio quality was fine but not great. There were background noises - my fan, the ambient traffic from outside, that one time my mom knocked on my door. But I was getting maybe thirty downloads per episode, which didn't seem like nothing.

By the time I sat down to record episode four, something had shifted. I realized I was doing this performance of being the kind of person who has good ideas about philosophy, rather than actually exploring ideas. I was trying to sound smart instead of thinking clearly. The microphone in front of me looked less like a tool and more like a barrier.

I recorded episode four anyway. It was about determinism and it was the worst one. I was distracted the whole time. My thoughts were scattered. I published it and then I stopped. I told myself I was just taking a break, but I never went back.

Looking at that microphone now, I don't feel like I failed exactly. I made something that nobody asked me to make, for no money, with basically no audience, and I did it anyway. But I also learned that I was doing it for the wrong reasons. I was chasing the idea of being a podcaster instead of actually caring about the exploration. I wanted the credibility without the substance.

I still think about those philosophical problems sometimes. I still stay up late overthinking things. But now when I do, I'm not trying to package it into something. I'm just thinking. And I think that's actually fine.

meta.topic: starting a podcast that ran for four episodes

text:
My parents put me in the church choir when I was eight. I was good at singing. I had a clear voice that the choir director liked. And for a while, that was enough to make me feel like I belonged there, even though I didn't believe any of it.

I was never really a believer. I went to church because my family went to church, and that seemed like a normal thing to do, and I didn't know how to say no to it. The songs were pretty though. There was something about standing with the other singers and letting the harmonies just lift you up. I liked that part. But the actual believing part - the God part - I couldn't make myself do it. I tried. I really did try. I'd sit in the pews and I'd listen to the sermons and I'd wait for the moment when it would click for me the way it clicked for other people. It never did.

So I faked it. I was in choir for five years. Five years of showing up every Sunday and singing about faith I didn't have with conviction I didn't feel. I got really good at faking it. I could make my voice soar during the uplifting parts. I could make it break emotionally during the sad parts. I knew the theology well enough to talk about it if someone asked me a question. My own parents didn't really know that I was a complete imposter standing in that robes.

The weird part is that I don't think anyone else knew either. The choir director thought I was pious. The other kids thought I was devout. My parents thought they'd raised a daughter with faith. And maybe some part of me was actually faithful, like my voice believed even if my brain didn't. Maybe singing faith is a kind of faith, even if it's not the kind that comes with certainty.

But here's the thing that I still think about: I quit the choir not because I realized I didn't believe, but because I got tired of pretending. I was thirteen and I had this moment of actual anger, not at God or at religion, but at myself for accepting a role that felt dishonest. I walked into rehearsal one day and I just said I was done. The director looked shocked. My parents were disappointed. The other kids probably thought it was weird.

I wish I could say I quit for some noble reason. That I had a crisis of conscience or an epiphany about authenticity. But honestly I just couldn't do it anymore. I couldn't keep producing this exact amount of emotion on command. I couldn't keep being the girl who had faith when I didn't. It felt like lying, not to them, but to myself.

I'm still not religious. I've thought about it a lot since then. Maybe I would have found faith if I'd stuck with it. Maybe belief grows from repetition and I just gave up too early. Or maybe I would have stayed a fraud forever, and getting out was the only honest thing I did there.

I don't think there's a right answer. I just think about that thirteen-year-old version of me walking out of choir practice and deciding that some performances aren't worth maintaining. And I'm glad she did that, even though I can't entirely explain why.

text:
Ms. Chen wrote on my eighth grade essay: "You have good instincts but you're not a natural writer. Focus on your strengths elsewhere." I was thirteen. I remember reading those words and feeling like something had been officially diagnosed. Not a writer. Got it. I'd wanted to be one but apparently that want didn't matter. Instinct and talent matter. I didn't have talent.

I showed my parents and my mom immediately said she disagreed. She said teachers don't know everything. She said I wrote interesting things all the time. She said one critical feedback from one teacher didn't mean anything. It felt like she was being nice to me the way you're nice to someone who's trying their best but not actually succeeding. I appreciated it but I didn't believe it.

What followed was a three-year period where I basically stopped trying to be a writer. I took my mom's advice to focus on my strengths - math, science, debate. I was good at those things. Why bang my head against something I wasn't naturally good at? I wrote for school when I had to but it was purely functional. No creativity. No risk-taking. Just getting through the assignment.

Freshman year I took an English class with Mr. Patterson and we had to write something personal. A memoir piece, maybe two pages. I treated it like homework. Got a B. He wrote a comment about it being competent but wondering if I was afraid to take risks. That's when I actually got angry at him. Not because I was afraid to take risks but because I already knew I wasn't a writer. Why was he pointing out all the ways I was failing at something I'd already given up on?

He asked me to come see him after class and I was so defensive, so ready to explain that I knew I wasn't good at this and that was fine. He said that actually, he thought there was something there. That the hesitation in my writing was a choice I was making, not a limitation I had. He said I wrote like someone who was afraid of saying the wrong thing, which he thought was probably true about me in general but that I could write past it if I wanted to.

That conversation changed something. Or it didn't change something and just pointed out that something could change. I can't tell the difference anymore.

I started writing more after that. Taking more risks. Turning in things that weren't perfect. Things that were raw. Things that might be bad but were at least honest. Most of them were not good. But Mr. Patterson was right - the bad writing was better than the competent writing. There was something in it.

By senior year I was actually writing. Not like a professional writer or anything dramatic like that. But I was thinking like one. Taking feedback differently. Revising. Understanding that being a writer wasn't about some innate talent that you either had or didn't. It was about showing up and doing it.

The thing is, I'm still angry at Ms. Chen sometimes. Not angry like I'm holding a grudge but angry like I'm grieving the three years I lost to her one comment. I wonder who I would be if she'd written something slightly different. Something encouraging instead of dismissive. I wonder how many other kids just accepted her diagnosis and gave up.

But I'm also grateful to Mr. Patterson for saying something different. For suggesting that being not-naturally-good-at-something didn't mean I shouldn't do it. That's the thing I'm trying to hold onto now - that my identity isn't determined by my natural talents. It's determined by what I choose to do anyway.

meta.topic: a teacher who told them they were not a writer

text:
I keep the ribbon from that tournament in my desk drawer. A small tricolor thing that says County Champions 2022. When you debate competitively, you get used to winning. You prepare for months, practice every weekend, memorize arguments until they're part of your operating system. You stand at the podium and your brain produces evidence at the right time and the judges vote for you and it feels inevitable. Like you were always going to win.

That tournament was at a school about two hours from mine, in a gym that smelled like old basketball and new carpet. I was defending the resolution that private prisons should be illegal. I'd spent three months researching incarceration statistics, building affirmative cases, practicing responses to every argument I'd ever heard. I was good. I was genuinely good. My teammates knew it. My coach knew it. And I knew that I knew it, which is different from actually being good.

The debate round itself went smoothly until it didn't. My opponent made this argument about government inefficiency that I'd prepared for, but she made it in a way I hadn't. She connected it to something I said in my opening statement - something I'd basically forgotten about by the time rebuttals came around. She had three minutes to talk and she spent all three of them building this one idea where my position actually contradicted itself. It wasn't even particularly clever. It was just correct.

I had ten minutes to respond and I spent nine of them trying to find evidence that disproved her instead of just acknowledging the actual problem with my argument. I ran it three different ways. I added new statistics. I found a study about a completely different scenario that I tried to force into relevance. Every second I spent pretending I was right instead of admitting I was wrong, the judges were checking boxes on their ballots. I lost by two points. Not close enough to feel like a fluke. Close enough to know exactly where it broke.

Afterward, I read the judge's comments. She wrote that I had excellent research and strong advocacy skills but that I seemed unable to abandon a losing position. She said the moment I realized my initial framework was compromised, I should have pivoted to arguing something different - not better evidence for the same broken case. She said good debaters know when to change their minds.

The worst part was that she was right. I'd been so focused on winning that particular round that I'd forgotten the actual point of debate, which is figuring out what's true. Or at least what's more true than the alternative. I spent the ride home not even thinking about the other kids whose teams had won. I just kept replaying the moment when I could have said something like yeah, that's actually a legitimate problem with my case, let me address it differently. But I didn't. I just pushed harder.

I don't keep that trophy anywhere. But I keep the ribbon. Every time I'm in a conversation with someone I disagree with, every time I'm building an argument in a class or a meeting or just my own head, I think about that moment. I think about how much worse the loss felt than any loss ever has, not because of the points but because I'd earned it by refusing to listen to what the other person was actually saying.

I still debate. I still win most of the time. But I'm better at noticing now when I'm just trying to win instead of trying to understand. That moment taught me something about myself that no trophy ever could have.

text:
The library had a card catalog. This is the first thing you absolutely need to understand about this particular library. Not a digital system. Not a computer database or anything modern. A card catalog. Actual wooden card catalog cabinets that held thousands of handwritten index cards organized by the Dewey Decimal System. It was beautiful in an archaic way, genuinely beautiful to look at, and it was also completely useless because nobody knew how to use it and nothing in it was accurate anymore.

The school librarian, Mr. Hammond, asked me to reorganize the library in my junior year. I was the kind of student who read a lot and seemed organized and didn't mind spending time in the library during lunch. That made me, in his mind, the perfect person for the job. He said he wanted to update the system. He wanted the card catalog to actually reflect what books were in the building, because apparently the previous librarian had stopped updating it in 2007. Books had been donated. Books had been lost. Books had moved. The index was years out of date.

He gave me a hand-written list of the current inventory and told me I could work on it piecemeal over the semester. A few cards a day. No pressure. He said he'd pay me minimum wage for my time, which was generous, except the job took about three times longer than either of us anticipated.

The first thing I realized was that the card catalog was a fascinating artifact. Each card was handwritten, some in ink from the '80s, some updated in pen. You could see the history of the library through them. You could see what books were popular at different times based on the wear patterns on the cards. You could see where someone had crossed something out and written the correction. It was tactile history. It was beautiful.

The second thing I realized was that updating it was going to require me to actually interact with the books. To physically go into the stacks, find them, confirm they existed, update the information. The library had grown since anyone had properly organized it. The organization had become almost intentional in its chaos. Some books were shelved where they were supposed to be. Some books were just on a shelf somewhere. Some books that were in the inventory didn't actually exist anymore. Some books that existed weren't in the inventory at all.

I started creating a system. I'd work through each call number section and physically verify every single book. I'd update the cards. I'd note books that needed to be ordered. I'd find books that were missing from the catalog and create new cards for them. It was tedious and meticulous and it took forever.

But here's what actually happened. As I worked through the library section by section, systematically and methodically, the entire building became familiar to me in a completely different way than it had ever been. I knew where everything was. I understood the logic of the Dewey Decimal System not as an abstract concept you learn in a class but as something deeply functional - how it grouped knowledge together, what kinds of books ended up next to each other, how the system reflected the actual way human beings categorize and organize their understanding of the world.

I also got to know Mr. Hammond. We'd talk about books while I worked. He'd come check on my progress and we'd end up having these conversations about why organizing information matters, about how libraries are about more than just storing books. He talked about the library as a democratic institution, a place where knowledge was supposed to be accessible to everyone. He talked about how outdated systems become useless systems, no matter how beautiful.

By the end of the semester I hadn't finished the entire catalog. But I'd reorganized three-quarters of it. I'd created a new system where the physical shelves actually reflected the index. I'd discovered books nobody knew existed. I'd learned what work felt like when it was meticulous and kind of boring but mattered.

What I grew from was understanding that some accomplishments are quiet. That organizing a library catalog is not glamorous or impressive to other people. But to Mr. Hammond, who suddenly had a usable system, and to the students who could actually find books they were looking for, it mattered. And doing something that mattered, even in a small way to a small group of people, changed how I thought about what kinds of work were worth doing.

That card catalog taught me that meaning doesn't have to be big to be real.

text:
The email came on a Tuesday in March with an automated response. Nobody had subscribed. I sat in the empty broadcast room staring at the mic, which I'd polished so many times the reflection was starting to smudge. My first episode had been perfect in my head - three hours of carefully selected indie tracks, live weather updates, my own rambling thoughts about why we should care about cloud formations. I'd recorded it the week before and uploaded it to every platform I could find. Zero listeners. Zero comments. Zero reason to keep going.

But there was this one thing: my grandmother's old radio. Not the equipment in the broadcast room, but the actual radio from her apartment, the one she'd brought from 1983 and never replaced. She'd given it to me six months earlier, right before we cleared out her place. It was brown plastic, heavy, with a dial that stuck and a sound so tinny it made AM stations sound like they were calling from underwater. She used to let me mess with it as a kid, turning the dial between stations just to hear the static.

I brought it into the broadcast room one afternoon and sat it on the control console where I could see the face of it, really see it. The dials. The ancient preset buttons that still had pencil marks from the 1980s with station names faded to ghosts. I thought about her turning that dial every evening, listening to the same three stations, the same evening news at six, the same host's voice for fifteen years. She never once needed anyone else to listen. She didn't need an audience. She just wanted the voice there.

So I started over. Same studio, same setup, same terrible equipment. But different. I stopped trying to make it perfect. I started talking about things I actually thought about - why my school's cafeteria smelled like burnt plastic, what it feels like to walk home on a day when the light hits the buildings exactly right, whether anyone else felt like they were pretending in geometry class. I played whatever I wanted. Sometimes I played nothing and just read from a book I liked. I gave it a stupid name. I told exactly three people about the stream.

One of them actually listened. Then two more. By the end of the year we had maybe fifteen people who tuned in on Thursday nights when they got bored. Some of them never talked to me at all. But they were there. The numbers never got big. The show never went viral. But that wasn't the point anymore. The point was that my grandmother's radio is sitting next to mine now, and I don't need permission to keep going. I don't need thousands. I don't need validation. I just need the person turning the dial to know someone is speaking.

text:
The metronome is the thing I notice first when I open the box. It's small and red and still ticking faintly, even though I shut off all the power years ago. The batteries probably died inside it. I haven't opened this storage box in three years, not since I stopped piano lessons. I'm not sure why I opened it today, except my mom asked if I wanted to sell the pieces to make room in the garage.

I remember that metronome perfectly. It started clicking when I was six and never stopped. 240 beats per minute. I knew that number like I knew my own birthday. My teacher used to set it and say play through this twice and then we'll move on to the next piece, always forward, always faster. The clicking drove me insane by the time I was thirteen. I used to mute it by covering it with my hand or stuffing it under the piano bench. But it would still tick, muffled and determined, and I'd feel like it was mocking me for not being disciplined enough to just accept it.

Opening this box now, I pick up the metronome and it stops. The mechanism is finally dead. And I feel this strange thing in my chest that I'm not expecting - not quite relief, but not sadness either. It's something like recognition.

When I quit piano at sixteen, I told myself it was because I didn't love it anymore. That was true. But it was also because I was tired of measuring myself against that click. Tired of knowing exactly how I stacked up to professional performances I'd listened to. Tired of practicing scales while my friends were outside doing literally anything else. My teacher cried when I told her I was stopping, which made me feel guilty but also angry. She said I had real talent, real potential. I said I had other things I wanted to do. We were both right.

The thing is, quitting taught me something that the metronome never could have. When you stop measuring yourself against an external standard, you have to learn to listen to yourself. I spent the next two years doing almost nothing musical, which felt like betrayal. But then I started playing random things on my friend's ukulele, not because I was any good but because it was quiet and I could do it at my own speed. I started writing weird little songs that nobody would ever hear. I learned that I actually did care about music. I just didn't care about being perfect at it.

I'm taking piano lessons again now, actually. Just one a month, not the weekly performance prep that used to define my life. My new teacher doesn't use a metronome. We talk about pieces I actually want to learn. Sometimes I nail it, sometimes I don't. Nobody's keeping score.

I put the dead metronome back in the box. I don't think I'll sell the piano.

meta.topic: quitting piano after eleven years

text:
My mom has not really forgiven me, and I don't think she ever will, which is the point I'm trying to explain here.

I stopped speaking Spanish at home when I was fourteen, right around when I started caring about fitting in at school. Everyone else spoke English. Their parents spoke English. Nobody had to think about what language to use - it was just the default, the neutral option, the American one. Spanish was the thing that marked you as different, and I was tired of being marked.

It started small. I'd answer my mom in English when she spoke to me in Spanish, and she'd sigh but repeat herself in English so she could get a response. I'd text my younger brother in English and he'd text back in English, and eventually we'd forgotten how to have certain conversations in Spanish because we were doing it all in English now. My dad had always been more English anyway, so he didn't care. But my mom cared.

We fought about it exactly once, clearly, when I was fifteen. She said I was forgetting where I came from and I said I wasn't forgetting anything, I was just choosing who I wanted to be. I remember her face when I said that. She looked like I'd told her I was choosing to erase her. I didn't mean it that way, but I also kind of did. I meant that I was choosing to not be the kid whose mom sent her to school with weird food and whose last name didn't fit the way other last names fit. I was choosing to just be American, which is what I was, mostly, anyway.

She stopped trying after that. She spoke to me in English even though I could see it cost her something, some small humiliation of having to accommodate her own child. My little brother kept speaking Spanish at home, and I'd listen to them talk and feel this weird mix of being outside the family and also being exactly where I wanted to be.

Three years later I'm taking Spanish classes again at school, and I'm angry about how hard it is to remember something I used to speak fluently. I'm angry that I let myself become the kind of person who needs to take a class to speak the language my mother used to sing me lullabies in. And I'm angry at my mom for not fighting harder to keep me speaking it, even though I know that's completely unfair. She tried. I refused. I was the one who shut the door.

I've tried talking to her about it since then. I've tried apologizing. She says there's nothing to apologize for, which is how I know she hasn't forgiven me. She says it very gently, like I'm still the person I was then, the one who wanted to escape her too much to care about our language. And maybe she's right. Maybe something in that choice was permanent.

My Spanish is getting better. It's coming back slower than I expected. But the thing that's hard isn't the grammar or the vocabulary. It's knowing that my mom is speaking English to me now because I taught her to, and that I can't really teach her back.

meta.topic: the year they stopped speaking their first language at home

text:
It was problem seven on the midterm. A block on an inclined plane with friction, a pulley, and a second mass hanging over the side. Standard physics problem. I looked at it and immediately understood the setup. I drew the free body diagrams. I identified the forces. I applied Newton's second law. I solved for the acceleration.

I got it wrong. According to the answer key, my final answer was off by a factor of two. Not just a calculation error - something fundamental in my approach was incorrect. I stared at my work and I couldn't see where I'd gone wrong. My teacher couldn't quite explain it either when I asked her. She said "your method is correct but you're missing something." She wouldn't tell me what.

That was three years ago. I'm serious. Three years. I think about that problem sometimes when I'm trying to fall asleep. I lie there and I mentally reconstruct the diagram and I try every possible configuration of forces and I still can't see what I missed. It's like an itch I can't scratch.

The frustrating part is that the problem itself doesn't matter. I'm not going to be a physicist. I got an A in the class. The midterm grade doesn't follow me anymore. I've taken higher-level physics. I understand calculus and vectors and electromagnetic fields. There's no good reason that a single wrong answer from three years ago should still occupy my brain space at all.

But there's something about being wrong in a way that you can't understand that really gets to me. It's not like making a simple calculation error. I can see those and fix them. It's not like misunderstanding a concept. I can learn those. It's this specific thing where I did everything right and still got the wrong answer, and I don't know why. And my teacher didn't know why. And the answer key just gave me a number without showing the steps.

I've tried looking it up online. I've reconstructed the problem from memory multiple times. I've asked other people about it. Everyone tells me to just move on. It's not important. You don't need to understand every problem you've ever encountered. That's reasonable. That's mature. But I can't stop thinking about it anyway.

What I did next, when I first got it wrong, was not really anything useful. I asked my teacher for help and got non-answers. I studied harder for the next test and did fine. I moved on to other classes and other problems. I essentially did all the things you're supposed to do when you encounter something you don't understand. I accepted that sometimes you don't understand things and that's okay.

Except I didn't actually accept it. I just pretended to. The problem stayed in my head like a splinter. Every few months something will trigger the memory - I'll see an inclined plane or a pulley in real life, or someone will mention physics, and I'll think about it again. And I'll spend twenty minutes trying to figure it out, knowing in advance that I won't be able to, and then I'll give up again.

Maybe the point is just that I'm the kind of person who can't let things go. That I need to understand everything, even unimportant things. Or maybe I'm just stubborn in a way that's not particularly productive. Either way, I've learned something from that wrong answer even though I never figured out why it was wrong. I've learned that there are some questions my brain won't stop asking even when they stop mattering. And I'm not sure if that's a strength or a limitation.

meta.topic: the physics problem they could not stop thinking about

text:
The keyboard was sticky. I pressed the same note again, and this time my grandfather's name hung in the air with it. He had died two years before I was born, so I only knew him through the harmonium - a wooden instrument that sat in our living room like a piece of furniture nobody touched. My mother said it was too delicate, that it had cost more than a motorcycle, that it needed to be left alone. She meant the way rich people leave paintings alone, as if looking too hard might damage them.

One afternoon I sat down in front of it anyway. My fingers found the keyboard in the dust. The ivory was yellowed and some keys had turned to cream, which made a map of the harmonium's age more than any calendar could. I pulled the bellows toward me and the mechanism groaned, a sound like someone waking up after decades of sleep. I pressed a note and it sang back to me, strange and nasal but utterly real. There was a harmonium and there was a note. There was no space between thought and sound.

I started going back without telling anyone. I didn't know how to read music. There were no videos of my grandfather playing, no recordings, no instructions in the bench. I could only experiment - try combinations until something felt right, press keys by proximity and intuition. My fingers learned the keyboard's temperament, its quirks. Some keys stuck if you didn't press them hard enough. The middle octave had a sweetness to it that the higher notes lost. If you held the bellows open too long, the tone became thin.

Weeks into this, I played something that sounded almost like a melody. It wasn't my grandfather's style, because I had no reference for his style, but it was mine. That seemed to matter more than I expected. I wasn't learning his way of playing or approximating what I thought a classical instrument should sound like. I was finding my own way on something that had belonged to someone else, using tools that carried their history but making something new.

My mother came downstairs one day while I was playing. I thought she would tell me to stop, to protect the delicate thing from my untrained hands. Instead she sat on the edge of the sofa and didn't say anything. When I finished, she told me my grandfather had learned the same way, alone, by ear. He never had a teacher either. He taught himself first, and after many years, he helped his sister do the same.

I kept playing after that, not because anyone encouraged me, but because the instrument had stopped feeling like a monument. It felt like a conversation.

meta.topic: learning to play a grandfather's harmonium
meta.prompt: What is something you have taught yourself, and what did learning it without a teacher show you?

text:
My father said it was a waste of space. He said a lot of things, actually - that balconies were for decoration, that growing food in pots meant the soil became exhausted and you'd get nothing worth eating, that if I wanted chillies I should buy them from the market like normal people. He said this as he stood over my small collection of pots, watching me pour water into the soil one morning before school.

I had been reading about agriculture. Not in textbooks for class, but actually reading, staying up too late with articles about urban farming and soil regeneration. My father saw this as peculiar. He's an accountant who trusts numbers and systems, and there was nothing systematic about my half-dozen pots arranged in no particular order on our balcony in Mumbai. The idea that I could take seeds and sun and water, and that something edible would come from this, seemed to him like fairy tale logic applied to real life.

But I started anyway. I planted three varieties of chilli seeds in recycled containers, and for weeks nothing happened except my father's sideways looks whenever he passed through the kitchen. Then the first seedlings emerged, thin green threads that looked impossibly fragile. I watered them carefully, moved them when they seemed to need more sun, talked to them in the morning before anyone else was awake. My father made a comment about how I was throwing away water that could have gone to actual plants in the building's garden.

This part still bothers me. This part is where I pushed back in a way that made the space between us wider. I told him he was stuck thinking about agriculture the way his generation always did - with big fields and old methods, never questioning whether there was another way. I said just because he didn't understand something didn't mean it was foolish. I remember the exactness of how this came out, designed to hurt a little.

The chillies grew. By August, the plants were flowering. By September, small green peppers were forming. My father didn't apologize, and I didn't expect him to. But he stopped with the comments. What he did instead was different - he started bringing up the plants in passing, asking me practical questions about them. "Did you change the soil yet?" "What's the pH supposed to be?" He researched regeneration too, I think, though he never said so directly.

By November, I harvested the first batch. They were small and intensely spicy, more so than anything from the market. I gave some to my mother, some to our downstairs neighbor who had always been kind to me. I kept one pepper and showed it to my father. He looked at it the way he looks at a balance sheet - as evidence that something worked according to principle.

We still haven't resolved it entirely, that disagreement about what's possible. He still doesn't think growing food on a balcony makes economic sense. I still think there are ways of living that matter beyond what the numbers show. But now he waters the plants sometimes when I'm at school, and last week he asked if I wanted more pots for next year. We haven't said any of this to each other directly. We're just both choosing to live with the question open.

meta.topic: growing chillies on a balcony
meta.prompt: Reflect on a time when you questioned or challenged a belief or idea. What prompted your thinking? What was the outcome?

text:
The clipboard sits on the bench next to me, and right now I'm staring at it instead of at the game. It's a white board with a metal clip, nothing special, and the formations I've drawn with a dry-erase marker are probably smudged and barely legible. Nobody else seems to be looking at it, but I keep it there every Saturday because it represents something I can't quite explain to the parents who stand along the sideline and shout instructions at their kids.

I started coaching this under-eleven football team last year when the previous coach left and there was nobody else to take it. I was only sixteen myself. The league allowed it because it's a community team and it was that or the program shut down. I said yes without thinking through what this meant. What I got was eight kids aged nine to eleven, a field at a park that's usually occupied by people walking dogs, and the responsibility of teaching them a sport I played but had never tried to teach before.

The clipboard became my anchor. On it, I draw formations. We do drills. We talk about positioning and strategy, about how to move as a unit, about the difference between just kicking the ball and moving toward a goal. It's a simple diamond shape I usually go with, or sometimes a four-three-three spread, depending on the week. I spend time on Thursday nights drawing these out, thinking about how to explain them. The clipboard matters because it means I'm taking this seriously.

What surprised me is that the kids took it seriously too. I expected them to want to just run around kicking the ball, but they looked at the formations. They asked questions. One of the smaller kids, Priya, started asking if she could write in ideas of her own. Soon they were all contributing. The clipboard stopped being my tool and became something they owned. They'd gather around it before games and trace through what we'd talked about, and I could see them thinking through how their position related to everyone else's.

The field became the place I felt most myself without realizing it was happening. On other days I'm managing school and friendships and expectations and all the small politics of being sixteen. On Saturdays, the field is simpler. The goal is literally a goal. The team is eight kids who need me to help them understand how to work together. There are no ambiguities about what success looks like. If you move the ball into the net, you have succeeded. If you don't, you haven't. The clipboard keeps me honest about the strategy of how to make success possible.

There's one Saturday that sticks with me. We were playing a team that was clearly better - they had more coordination, better equipment, more confident kids. At halftime we were losing three to nothing. The other team's coach had actual credentials and experience. I sat with my clipboard and felt completely inadequate. But the kids didn't care. They gathered around to see the clipboard. One of the boys said he thought if we pushed the line forward more, we'd have a better chance at cutting off their passes. We adjusted. We didn't win the game, but we held them to four to one and scored our first real goal as a team. I remember Priya's face when the ball went in. I remember the other kids running to hug her. I remember that the clipboard, sitting on my lap with its smudged formations, had been part of that.

The field is where I understand myself. I'm someone who can take eight kids who don't know each other well and help them see how they fit together. I'm someone who can draw plans and hold them in my head and explain them until they make sense. I'm someone who matters to these kids in a specific way - not as a friend or a family member, but as someone who believes they can do something hard and helps them find the way.

I still have that clipboard. It's covered in the marker lines from a hundred different formations, strategy notes, starting lineups. It's battered and barely functional. But when I stand on that field on Saturday mornings, when I watch these kids arrange themselves into a formation we've practiced, into the shape we drew together on the worn white surface of the clipboard, I'm exactly where I'm supposed to be. The place where I know who I am and what I'm capable of.

meta.topic: coaching a under-11 football team
meta.prompt: Describe a place where you feel most yourself, and why.

text:
I was nineteen lines into the code when I realized I had no idea what I was doing. Not the syntax - I had looked that up in the tutorials. I meant the architecture. I had decided to make a game for my cousin Sanjay, who was eight and constantly told me he was bored with the games he already had. The game was a simple side-scroller, just something to move him around a screen and have him collect things. In my head it was clear. On the screen, it was a mess.

The problem was I had started coding without planning. I had jumped straight into writing the player movement because that was the exciting part. I wanted to see the character move. I wanted Sanjay to come over and see something playable immediately. What I didn't do was think about how the player interacted with the world, how gravity worked, what happened when he touched a wall. These things weren't exciting to plan. They were just logical scaffolding. So I had skipped them.

I spent two weeks fixing things that should have been set up from the start. A wall that should have been solid wasn't. The character clipped through platforms. When you collected items they disappeared but also sometimes didn't, and I couldn't figure out why. Every time I tried to fix one problem I created three more. The code was getting longer and messier. I was reading forums and Stack Overflow posts trying to debug things that experienced programmers said were fundamental problems - problems that wouldn't exist if I had planned.

When Sanjay finally played it, he was kind. He played for maybe five minutes and then lost interest. The game was janky and confusing. The character moved in a way that felt wrong. There was no feedback for what he was supposed to do. It wasn't fun. He went back to his old games without saying anything, and I felt the specific shame of someone who had gotten a commission from a child and failed to deliver.

What gets to me is that I knew better. I had read about game development. I understood that architecture mattered. I just didn't want to do the boring part. I wanted to jump to the part where things worked. I wanted to be a person who made games without being a person who thought through how games should work.

I did it differently the next time. I planned everything before writing a single line. I drew out the structure, thought through the physics, decided what would happen in different scenarios. It took a week of planning. It felt like the game was already finished before I started coding, which seemed wrong somehow. But when I actually coded it, things went smoothly. The architecture held. When I fixed a bug, it stayed fixed. When I added features, they integrated cleanly.

I asked Sanjay to try again. This version he played for twenty minutes. He asked questions about where to go next. He actually cared whether he won or lost. It wasn't a good game - I'm not claiming that. But it was a real game.

The thing about that first failure is I still think about it. Not with shame anymore, but with the understanding that the invisible work is the most important work. Every game Sanjay plays or every piece of software I use is mostly planning that nobody sees. The exciting part is the smallest part. I learned this by failing to do it, by trying to skip to the good part and discovering there is no good part without the boring part first.

meta.topic: learning to code to make a game for a younger cousin

text:
The notebook is blue and narrow-ruled. I've been using it for two years as a scribe for a blind student named Pradeep who is in three of my classes. The notebook is where I write down what he tells me to write, which is his way of taking notes. It's simple in concept - I write, he listens, he remembers - but it has meant something to both of us that goes beyond the practical.

Pradeep didn't ask me to be his scribe. The school provided an official scribe who was there during tests and in some of his classes. But he asked me one day if I would take notes in his math class because the official scribe wasn't available that day. I said yes. I just did it. The next day he asked if I would do it again. I said yes. Eventually the official scribe became backup and I became the regular scribe.

What I realized is that I'm not just writing down the material he needs to know. I'm writing down his understanding of it. When he tells me to take a note, he's already processed the information. He's already decided what matters and what doesn't. I'm not just transcribing. I'm recording the way his mind works.

This changed how I took notes. I had to listen more carefully because he needed clarity, not just speed. I couldn't scribble shortcuts. Everything I wrote had to make sense. This meant I was actually learning the material better while I was writing it for him. I was thinking about what mattered while I was writing. I was engaging with the content instead of just creating a record of it.

The blue notebook sits on my desk now as a completed thing. It's full of notes from this past school year, and I'm starting a new one for next year. Looking at it, I can see the progression of how I write. Early pages are messy, full of abbreviations and unclear phrases. By the middle, my handwriting has settled. By the end, I've developed a system where everything is clear and organized.

What changed for me is that I understood what attention means. Pradeep couldn't check the notes immediately like other students could. He had to trust that what I wrote was accurate and clear. That responsibility made me a better student, not just for him but for myself. If I'm going to write something down, it needs to be worth writing. It needs to be true and clear and useful.

Pradeep has never told me that this meant a lot to him. We don't talk about it much. I just show up and take notes and I hand him the notebook and he goes home and studies. It's practical. It's also something else - a relationship based on trust and attention. He's trusting me to care about the accuracy of what I write. I'm paying attention to his education in a way I wouldn't if I wasn't responsible for his notes.

I think often about how small this thing is. It's one class, one notebook, one student. But it's taught me something important about what it means to be useful to someone. It's not about grand gestures. It's about showing up consistently and caring about doing the work right. It's about understanding that the thing you think is simple might be essential to someone else's life.

The notebook is just paper and ink. But it's also a record of learning together, of paying attention, of being responsible to someone else's future. That's something worth showing up for.

meta.topic: working as a scribe for a blind student
