text:
I have sung in my church's choir every Sunday for four years, and I have not believed in God for almost three of them. I've never told my grandmother this, and I don't know if I ever will, which is its own kind of unresolved argument, the kind that happens entirely in my head because I've never had the nerve to have it out loud.

The choir is a real community, not the vague kind people mean when they use that word in an essay. It's Mrs. Adeyemi, our director, who has no patience for sopranos who rush the tempo. It's the two Nguyen brothers, one bass and one tenor, who argue about basketball during every rehearsal break. It's the smell of the church basement, coffee and old carpet, and eight-part harmony landing exactly right after weeks of it not quite landing. I know these people better than I know most of my classmates.

What I don't have anymore is the belief that supposedly holds the whole thing together. It slipped away gradually, somewhere in tenth grade, through science classes and just thinking too hard during sermons. I didn't quit the choir when it happened. Some of it is honest - I love the music itself, independent of whatever it's supposedly praising. Some of it, if I'm being fully honest, is cowardice. Quitting would mean a conversation with my grandmother that I have rehearsed and abandoned probably twenty times.

My grandmother is the one I love and disagree with here, though we've never actually had the argument. She got me into the choir when I was ten, and she still watches from the third pew every Sunday with an expression I can only describe as complete faith, not just in God but in me. I know that if I told her the truth, she wouldn't yell. She'd be hurt, quietly, in a way that would be worse than yelling. So instead I sing the words and let her assume they mean to me what they mean to her, and I hate that this feels like the kinder choice, because it also feels like a lie I tell her every week without saying anything false out loud.

My place in this community is complicated in a way I haven't resolved for myself. I am fully present in the choir loft and fully absent from the belief that supposedly explains why I'm standing there. I don't know if that makes me a fraud or just someone who found a community worth keeping after losing the reason he first joined it. Some Sundays I think it's the second thing. Other Sundays, watching my grandmother mouth the words beside me, I think it might be the first.

meta.topic: the church choir they sang in but did not believe in
meta.prompt: Describe a community you belong to and your place within it.

text:
For the first five weeks of my internship at the Millbrook planning department, my main function was to exist near a photocopier. I had applied expecting to help draft actual reports - I'd read about zoning variance data, I'd practiced explaining floor-area ratios to my very patient dad - and instead I got a badge, a desk nobody had used since a retirement, and roughly four hours of real work spread across two hundred hours of sitting. I reorganized a supply closet twice. I read the entire zoning code cover to cover out of boredom, which turned out to matter later in a way I couldn't have predicted. I spent a lot of that time deciding I didn't belong there, that whatever community existed in that building had already filled every role it needed and mine was decorative.

I want to explain the moment that stopped being true, because it happened on a Tuesday I almost skipped.

There was a public hearing that evening about a proposed apartment complex on Chandler Road, the kind of meeting that draws maybe thirty residents and two reporters and lasts far longer than the agenda promises. My supervisor, Denise, asked if I'd help set up chairs, which was about the level of task I'd come to expect. An older woman named Mrs. Okafor arrived forty minutes early, holding a notice she'd gotten in the mail, clearly confused about whether the meeting was about her own property or the one three lots down. Everyone who could have explained it to her was busy - Denise was on the phone with the fire marshal's office, the planner was rehearsing his presentation, the clerk was fighting with the sign-in sheet. I was the only person in the room with nothing scheduled. So I sat down next to Mrs. Okafor and walked through the notice with her, line by line, using the exact vocabulary I'd absorbed from five weeks of having nothing better to do than read every document that crossed my desk twice.

It took maybe fifteen minutes. Afterward Denise thanked me in a way that felt different from her usual politeness, and the following week she started routing me toward the front desk whenever a resident came in confused, not because I had any authority, but because I was reliably available and had absorbed enough of the department's language to translate it. I hadn't changed. The work hadn't changed. What changed was my understanding of what my place in that office actually was.

I'd been measuring my belonging by whether I produced anything with my name on it - a memo, a report, a line in a staff email. I don't think that's a bad way to measure most jobs. But it was the wrong measure for a room like that one, where half the actual function of the department is translation between technical process and worried, half-informed residents, and where the person with unscheduled time turns out to be structurally necessary rather than incidental. I stopped resenting the empty hours once I understood they were the raw material of the thing I ended up being useful for. Nobody had assigned me the role of "person residents can find," and it took a confused woman with a mail notice to show me that the role existed and that I already had it.

I finished the summer still without a report bearing my name, and I no longer think that's the honest measure of what I contributed. My place in that community turned out to be the empty chair nobody thought to fill, which was apparently exactly the chair the room needed someone sitting in. I think about Mrs. Okafor sometimes when people ask what I did all summer, and I've stopped giving the shorter answer just because it's easier to explain.

meta.topic: an internship where they were given nothing to do
meta.prompt: Describe a community you belong to and your place within it.

text:
My mother thinks I go to the retention pond behind Value Foods because I'm avoiding grief, and every time she says it we end up in the same half-argument, standing in the kitchen with the dishes not yet done, both of us too tired at six in the morning to actually finish the fight. She isn't wrong, exactly. My grandfather taught me to bird two winters before he died, standing in that same weedy stretch of cattails and shopping-cart wheels with a pair of Bushnells that now live around my neck every school morning by 5:50. What she gets wrong is the rest of it - that going out there is a way of staying stuck, that a seventeen-year-old should not be spending her mornings alone with a bird app and a notebook when she could be sleeping, or eating breakfast at the table like a person in a family. We have never once agreed on this. I don't think we ever will.

Here is what actually happens out there. The pond is not beautiful. It exists because a strip mall needed somewhere to put its runoff, and the water carries a faint gasoline sheen some mornings, and a shopping cart has rusted into the far bank for as long as I can remember. But a green heron nests in the willow scrub on the north side every April, and in October the pond fills up with ring-necked ducks stopping over on their way somewhere better, and once, in January, I watched a Cooper's hawk take a mourning dove out of the air four feet from my face and felt my whole body go still in a way it never does in a classroom. My grandfather used to say the best birding happens in ugly places nobody else bothers to look at twice, and I think about that sentence more than almost anything else he told me.

My mother knows all of this. I've told her about the heron, shown her photos of the ducks, tried to get her to come once, and she said maybe and never did. The argument isn't really about birds. It's about what it means that I'd rather be alone with a dying man's binoculars at dawn than sitting across from her, and neither of us has found a way to say that plainly, so instead we argue about sleep schedules and whether I'm avoiding something, and I always leave for the pond a little too fast, the way you leave a conversation you're afraid of finishing.

What I would bring to a campus is that same stubborn attention, turned outward instead of used to dodge my mother at the breakfast table. I notice what's easy to walk past - a heron in a drainage ditch, a rare warbler blown off course into a courtyard hedge, the kid who's been eating alone in the dining hall for three weeks. I keep a list. I go back. I have never once managed to explain to the person I love most why an ugly pond full of shopping carts matters to me, but I can promise that whatever patch of scrub or forgotten courtyard exists on your campus, I will find it, and I will notice things about it that everyone else stopped seeing months ago. My mother and I still haven't finished our argument. I don't think either of us wants to, really - it would mean admitting the other one might be a little bit right.

meta.topic: birdwatching alone before school
meta.prompt: What would you contribute to our campus that would not be here if you were not?

text:
Every night for the eight months before regionals, I wrote down what had gone wrong that day. Not what had gone right - I didn't have a habit for that - just the failures, in a green spiral notebook I kept in my backpack, half-illegible because I usually wrote it at eleven at night after four hours in the robotics lab. "Claw drops object 1 in 6 times." "Autonomous routine drifts left, unknown cause." "Battery voltage sags under load, check connectors." It wasn't glamorous. It was closer to a confession.

I started the notebook by accident, honestly, because our team lead made us log bugs for the mentors to review, and I was the one who volunteered to keep it since nobody else wanted the job. But somewhere around week three I noticed I was writing more than the assignment required. I'd add little theories in the margins, sketches of the gripper mechanism, arrows connecting one failure to another failure from two weeks earlier that I was suddenly sure was the same root cause. I'd lose entire evenings to it. My mom would knock on my door to ask if I knew what time it was, and I genuinely wouldn't.

That's the strange thing about debugging that people who haven't done it don't believe: it is not tedious, it is completely absorbing, in the way I imagine a puzzle is absorbing to someone who loves puzzles, except the puzzle fights back and changes shape every time you touch it. A robot that isn't working is a small, solvable mystery with real physical evidence, and I found I would rather sit on a concrete floor at ten p.m. tracing a wire with a multimeter than do almost anything else. I liked that the answer was always in there somewhere, in the machine, waiting to be found, and that finding it required nothing except attention and enough patience to write down what I'd already ruled out.

At regionals, none of it mattered, or that's what it felt like at the time. Our robot's arm seized up thirty seconds into our first match, in front of judges, in front of the other forty teams, in front of my parents, who had driven four hours to watch. It never moved again that day. We didn't place. I remember sitting behind the pit table afterward, not crying exactly, just very quiet, holding the green notebook like it had failed me personally.

It took me a few weeks to understand what actually happened, which was that the seized arm was a wiring fault we'd genuinely never seen before, a one-in-a-hundred failure that had nothing to do with anything in my notebook - and that the notebook was still the reason I could diagnose it that fast once we got the robot back to the shop, three days later, in about twenty minutes. Every failure I'd logged all season had built a kind of map in my head of how the machine failed, so when a new failure showed up, I already knew what it wasn't.

I still keep the habit. New robot, new season, same green-covered notebooks, now four of them deep. I don't think I'm chasing the stage moment anymore, the one where everything works and the crowd claps. I think I'm chasing the two hours before that, alone with a multimeter and a problem that hasn't given up its answer yet, writing down exactly what's wrong so that next time, whatever breaks, I'll already recognize it.

text:
My grandfather had a stroke the winter I was fifteen, and it left the right side of his mouth slower than the left, so that words he'd said his whole life without thinking now came out thick and delayed, sometimes wrong, a name swapped for another name, a year that didn't match the story. He grew up in a village called Barhona that doesn't exist anymore, swallowed decades ago when the coal operation on its border expanded and the whole settlement was relocated, houses and wells and a school and all, to make room for the pit. He used to tell me about it constantly when I was small, and I used to only half listen, the way you half listen to anything that seems like it will always be available to you later.

After the stroke, I was afraid it wouldn't be. That's the honest obstacle here, not the stroke itself, which he recovered from well enough, but the specific fear that the stories I'd never bothered to actually absorb were about to become permanently harder to reach, garbled by a mouth that didn't work the way it used to, and that I had wasted twelve years of easy access to something I could no longer take for granted.

So I started a habit that felt almost too small to count as anything. Every Sunday after lunch, I'd sit with him on the porch for exactly as long as he had energy for, which usually wasn't long, fifteen or twenty minutes before his face would start to look tired in a way I learned to recognize. I brought a small notebook, not a recorder, because I noticed early on that a recorder made him self-conscious about how slowly he spoke, and a notebook let me just write while he talked without either of us watching a machine measure the gaps. I gave myself one rule: write down one full sentence, just one, that felt true. Not a summary. An actual sentence, in something close to his words.

Some Sundays that was easy. Some Sundays he'd stall on a name for a full minute and I'd sit there not filling the silence for him, which was its own kind of discipline I had to teach myself, because my instinct was always to guess the word and finish his sentence, and I learned that finishing it for him usually meant losing whatever he'd actually been about to say.

I have sixty-one sentences now, one notebook, less than a page for some months and more for others. It doesn't read like a story. It reads like fragments: the well was deeper than any well after it. My mother sold milk to the overseer's wife on Tuesdays. The school bell was actually a piece of rail track someone hit with a hammer. None of it would mean much to a stranger. But when my younger cousin needed something for a family history project last spring, that notebook was the only written record of Barhona that exists anywhere, and I handed it to her without hesitation, sixty-one small true things, collected on purpose, one sentence a week, because I was scared of losing something I'd never actually thought to value until it was almost gone.

I still go on Sundays. I don't need the fear anymore to keep doing it. That part surprised me most.

meta.topic: a grandfather's stories about a village that no longer exists
meta.prompt: The lessons we take from obstacles we encounter can be fundamental to later success. Recount a time when you faced a challenge, setback, or failure. How did it affect you, and what did you learn from the experience?

text:
I promised the county food bank two thousand cans. I'd done the math on a napkin at their intake desk, multiplied by the number of homerooms at my school and a number of cans per homeroom that seemed reasonable, and a woman named Denise had written "2,000" on a form and thanked me for the commitment before I understood that a napkin estimate and a commitment are not the same thing.

We collected six hundred and eleven cans. I know the exact number because I was the one who counted them, alone, in the equipment room behind the gym, on the last Friday of the drive, and I remember sitting on the floor afterward doing arithmetic I didn't want to do, the kind where every version of the equation still comes out short.

What I haven't said yet is the part that actually matters, which is that every morning of that six-week drive, a little before first period, I checked the bin outside the office before anyone else did. That was the routine. It wasn't strategic. I told myself I was checking so I could report numbers at the Wednesday assembly, but really I think I just wanted to see the level rise, the way you check a jar of coins even when you know exactly how much is in it. Some mornings it hadn't moved at all. Some mornings there'd be four or five cans, always the same brands, always stacked a little too neatly to have been dropped in carelessly.

It took me until the fourth week to notice that the neat stacking was a pattern, and another week to figure out whose pattern it was. Mr. Aroyan ran the loading dock for the cafeteria and I'd probably said ten words to him in three years, mostly "thanks" when he propped the side door for late buses. He'd started buying a few cans himself, out of his own paycheck, on his way in every morning, and setting them in the bin before the halls filled up, because he'd heard the announcement about the drive and, in his words when I finally asked him, "a food bank running short felt like something worth six dollars a week."

Six dollars a week doesn't fix a drive that fell fourteen hundred cans short of what I promised. I want to be clear that it didn't. Denise was gracious about it in the way adults are gracious when they've clearly seen this exact disappointment from a teenager before, and I still had to write an email admitting the number, and it still stung to send it. But finding out about Mr. Aroyan changed what the whole six weeks had actually been, in my memory of it. I had built the drive around a promise I made to impress a stranger with a clipboard, and it turned into something else entirely, a habit two people kept without discussing it, one checking a bin every morning out of something between hope and dread, the other quietly making sure the checking wasn't for nothing.

I don't think I'd have noticed any of that if I'd hit my number. A successful drive ends with a big total and a photo for the newsletter, and you move on. A drive that falls short forces you to sit with the smaller true thing underneath it, which in my case was a man on a loading dock who decided, for reasons that had nothing to do with me, that showing up mattered more than whether the goal got met. I still check bins now, at other drives, for other causes, mostly out of habit. I'm not chasing the total anymore. I'm checking to see who else is quietly there.

text:
Mrs. Novak was the first adult outside my family who ever seemed to really see me, which is probably why I believed her so completely when she sat my parents down in the fall of fourth grade and told them that if they wanted my reading scores to catch up, we should speak English at home from now on. She was my ESL teacher, and she had a way of crouching down to eye level when she talked to you that made you feel like the only person in the building. My parents were skeptical. I was not. I remember sitting between them at that conference table, ten years old, translating her advice into Vietnamese for my own mother because I already understood English better than she did, and feeling, for the first time, like I was the expert in the room.

I pushed for it harder than my parents did. My bà ngoại, who lived with us and had opinions about everything, told me flatly that this was a mistake, that a language is not a subject you drop when it becomes inconvenient, that I would regret it. I respected her more than almost anyone, but I was ten and certain, and I told her that Mrs. Novak knew about school in a way she didn't. We went English-only within the month. My Vietnamese, which had been clumsy but alive, started going quiet almost immediately - first the complicated words, then the ordinary ones, until by seventh grade I could understand my grandmother perfectly and answer her only in English, a strange lopsided conversation we had every single day without either of us commenting on it.

For years I didn't think about the disagreement again. My reading scores did climb, and I told myself that settled it, that Mrs. Novak had been right and my grandmother's objection was sentimental in a way that didn't hold up against evidence. The turn happened on a Tuesday in March of last year, in a hospital hallway, when a nurse asked if anyone could help translate for my grandmother, who'd had a stroke that had taken most of the English she'd picked up over twenty years and left her only the Vietnamese she'd started with. I said I could. I walked into that room and opened my mouth and nothing came out that was worth anything - I had the grammar of a small child and none of the vocabulary for what a stroke does to a person, what a doctor needed to know, what she needed to hear from me. My mother had to take over. I stood in the corner of that room and watched my own mother comfort my grandmother in a language I had once decided, on a stranger's advice, that I didn't need.

That's the moment I stopped agreeing with Mrs. Novak, four years too late to do anything but notice it. I don't think she was malicious, or even wrong about the reading scores. But I understand now that she was giving advice about a child's test performance and calling it advice about a child's life, and I was too young and too flattered by her attention to hear the difference. I've spent the past year relearning Vietnamese from my grandmother in the hours she has energy for it, badly, slowly, writing words on index cards like I'm ten again but without the confidence I had back then. She corrects my tones and doesn't bring up the argument we had, though I think about it every time I get a word wrong. I still respect Mrs. Novak. I just don't think I'll ever again mistake someone's confidence for their being right, especially not about something as permanent as what a ten-year-old is allowed to keep.

meta.topic: the year they stopped speaking their first language at home

text:
The route was my brother Miles's before it was mine, forty-one houses along Delford and Grantham and half of Kessler, and when he left for community college he handed it to me along with the same canvas bag he'd used for six years, the strap gone stiff with salt from a hundred winters of sweat. I was thirteen. I did not expect the route to become the thing that decided what I wanted to study, but it did, and it happened because of a habit I picked up in my first week that I never dropped.

Before I loaded the papers into the bag each morning, I'd sit on the porch steps of the distribution stop and read the "Yesterlands" column on page four of the Cutchogue Herald, a little box that ran a clipping from the paper exactly one hundred years earlier. It was supposed to take thirty seconds. I was supposed to be riding. But that column was where I first read about the fire that took the old cannery in 1924, and the fight over whether to pave Grantham Street in 1911, and a missing-persons notice for a girl named Adeline Voss who was never found, printed in 1923 in the same clipped, uncertain type as everything else that week, as if the paper had no idea it was printing a mystery that would outlive everyone involved. I started getting to the stop ten minutes early just to have time to read it before my bag got too heavy to sit comfortably.

I lost track of time on that porch more mornings than I can count, which is a strange thing to say about a job where being late means forty-one people don't get their paper before work. But something about reading a hundred-year-old fragment of my own streets, delivered to me for free every single morning, made the town feel like it had a floor underneath it I hadn't known was there. Grantham Street wasn't just the street with the pothole by the Merricks' driveway. It was a street people had once argued about hard enough to fill a column. Adeline Voss wasn't a name. She was a person whose disappearance I couldn't stop thinking about on a Tuesday in October, ninety-nine years after the fact, while pedaling past the exact intersection where she was last seen according to the clipping.

Eventually I did what anyone that obsessed does - I biked, on a non-route day, to the Cutchogue Historical Society, which turned out to be one room above the library staffed three afternoons a week by a woman named Ruth Petrosky who has been answering my questions for almost three years now. She's the person I go to when a name from the column doesn't turn up anywhere else. She showed me the actual bound volumes the "Yesterlands" clippings are pulled from, let me sit with them, and eventually let me write two of the columns myself, both about the cannery fire, both fact-checked against fire department records she keeps in a drawer that smells like the inside of an old church.

I still have the route. Miles is finishing his degree now and asks about it less than he used to, which is fair. But I've never told him that the bag he handed me turned into the reason I want to study history and archives instead of whatever I assumed I'd study at thirteen. Some mornings I still get to the stop early, sit on the same steps, and read whatever hundred-year-old fragment the paper decided to print that day, before I ever open the bag.

text:
Nobody at WKPR, the public radio station where I interned last summer, had actually planned for an intern. I found this out my first morning, when the program director realized there was no desk, no assigned task list, and no real use for a sixteen-year-old who couldn't legally operate the board alone. For the first three weeks I did almost nothing. I alphabetized a CD archive that hadn't been touched since the station switched to digital. I sat in on pledge-drive planning meetings where nobody asked my opinion. Around 4:45 every afternoon, the staff would start packing up for the day, and I would sit alone at the front desk for the last hour of my shift with genuinely nothing assigned to do.

I started answering the phone during that hour, not because anyone asked me to, but because it was there and I was bored. Almost nobody calls a small public radio station after five in the evening. Most days the phone didn't ring at all. But it turned out one person did call, most evenings, around 5:15 - a man named Mr. Halvorsen, eighty-one years old, who listened to the station religiously and had strong, specific opinions about the afternoon jazz program that he had apparently been trying to share with staff for years without much luck, since nobody was ever at the front desk that late to pick up.

I picked up. The first time, I mostly just listened, because I had no idea what else to do with a stranger telling me in detail why the Tuesday host played too much bebop and not enough swing. I could have transferred him to voicemail, which is clearly what the system was built for. Instead I started taking actual notes, and then I started calling him back the next day if I hadn't understood something, and by the second week I was doing this every single afternoon at 4:45, treating it like a real part of the job even though it appeared on no schedule anywhere and nobody had assigned it to me.

It became a genuine routine, the kind you don't notice reshaping you until it already has. I learned the names of six or seven regular late-afternoon callers that summer, people the station had effectively lost as a channel of contact once they stopped hiring anyone to sit at that desk after four. I started keeping an actual log - dates, names, what people said, which shows they were responding to - because it seemed wasteful not to write any of it down. By July, the program director noticed the log sitting on the desk and asked to read it, and by August she'd used three separate entries from it to make actual programming decisions, including moving the jazz block twenty minutes earlier because four different callers, independently, had mentioned missing the start of it on their drive home.

None of this was in my internship description. I wasn't hired to build a listener-feedback pipeline out of a dead phone hour; I was hired, loosely, to learn what a radio station does, and instead I discovered that a huge and completely unaddressed need - actual human contact with the people the station serves - was sitting in an unstaffed hour every single day, waiting for someone bored enough and stubborn enough to keep answering a phone that almost never rang.

That's the habit I'd bring to a campus that wouldn't otherwise be there: the willingness to occupy an unglamorous, unscheduled hour on the theory that something real might be happening in it that nobody's paying attention to. I don't think I'm unusually talented at any one thing. What I am is the kind of person who will sit at the empty desk during the dead hour, and answer the phone anyway, and keep a log nobody asked for, for long enough that a pattern shows up that everyone else was too busy to notice. WKPR still has that late log, kept now by whichever intern comes after me, because I asked that it become a real part of the job before I left. I like to think Mr. Halvorsen still calls at 5:15, and that somebody is still writing down what he says.

text:
The server is called Sprout, and it started three years ago as a place for people to post half-finished games from a weekend jam nobody remembers the theme of anymore. There are about four hundred of us now, mostly fourteen to nineteen, scattered across time zones that mean somebody is awake at any hour to answer a question about collision detection or why a sprite keeps flickering at the edge of the screen. I found it the way I imagine most people find the thing that ends up organizing their week: by accident, searching for help with a problem I didn't have the vocabulary to describe yet.

My place in it isn't glamorous. I'm not the best programmer on the server, not close. What I am is the person who answers beginner questions at eleven at night when the actual experts are asleep, because I remember exactly what it felt like to post something and watch it sit there unanswered for six hours. I got good at explaining things badly-explained tutorials had explained badly to me first, which is its own kind of expertise. People started tagging me. Somewhere along the way "ask the person who explains it twice" became a real reputation, small as it is, and I've built almost my whole understanding of who I am as a builder of things around being useful to people who are stuck.

I started learning to code at all because of my cousin Milo, who is eight and was diagnosed with leukemia the year I turned fifteen. He spent most of that year in and out of a hospital forty minutes from us, and then most of the year after that at home but still not really able to go anywhere, still tired in a way that scared everyone even after the doctors said the numbers looked good. I wanted to make him something. Not a card, not a stuffed animal, something he could actually do, so I taught myself to build a small game where you play a knight collecting the exact eight kinds of dinosaurs he was obsessed with that year. It took me four months and it is, by any real standard, not a good game. He has played it probably three hundred times.

My aunt has never liked this. She's Milo's mother, and she loves him more carefully than anyone I know, and she has told me, more than once, in the specific tired voice she uses when she's decided not to raise her voice instead, that a screen is a screen, that what he needs is people in the room with him and not another glowing rectangle, that I am solving my own discomfort with his illness rather than actually helping him. I don't think she's wrong that some of it is about my own discomfort. I don't think she's right that the game is nothing. We have had this conversation four or five times now and it always ends the same way, with both of us a little hurt and neither of us saying anything else about it, because we both know the other one loves him and we can't find the seam where her version of love and mine actually disagree.

I still build Milo new levels. I still don't know how to explain to my aunt why it matters to me the way it does, why sitting in his room while he plays something I made feels like a form of presence and not an escape from it. On Sprout I can explain almost anything to almost anyone. I have never once managed to explain this to her, and I don't think either of us has given up trying, which might be the truest thing I can say about what family actually is.

meta.topic: learning to code to make a game for a younger cousin

text:
The water is down almost five feet this year, and my grandfather is already unlacing his shoes before I've finished parking the car. "Kohlua is close today," he says, like the village is a person who sometimes comes near the shore and sometimes doesn't, and by then I'd heard him say the name Kohlua so many times across so many dinners that I'd stopped actually hearing it, the way you stop hearing a clock once you've lived with it long enough.

He'd told the stories my whole life. The mango tree outside his father's house that took four children holding hands to circle. The well that never ran dry even in the worst summers, right up until the year the engineers came with their surveying poles and told everyone in the valley they had eighteen months. The temple with the cracked bell that rang wrong, a half-tone flat, and how the whole village claimed to like it that way better than a bell that rang true. I'd heard the mango tree story probably forty times. I used to time how long it took him to get to the part about the bell, and I am ashamed, now, of how bored I let myself look while he told it.

That afternoon, the reservoir was low enough that you could see it. Not imagine it, not take his word for it. See it. A ridge of stone poking through brown water that he said, without any drama in his voice at all, was the temple's outer wall. We stood there for maybe twenty minutes while he pointed at flat, unremarkable patches of water and told me what used to be under each one, the well, the courtyard, the lane his mother walked to the river every morning, and I realized somewhere in those twenty minutes that I was the only other person standing on that shore who had ever heard any of it. Not the only person who could have. The only person who had.

There is no village left to visit that isn't underwater nine months a year. There is no archive, no marker, no plaque the state ever put up, because a submerged village of eleven hundred people from sixty years ago isn't the kind of history anyone thought worth funding. There is a ninety-one-year-old man who still unlaces his shoes at the shoreline like he might wade in, and there is me, and after that afternoon there is a phone in my pocket I now actually use, recording him telling the mango tree story for the forty-first time, and the bell story, and one about a flood in nineteen-sixty-something that I'd genuinely never heard before because I'd always tuned out before he got that far.

I have eleven hours of him now. Some of it repeats. He tells the mango tree story slightly differently each time, the number of children changes, six once, four another time, and I've stopped trying to correct it into a single fixed version, because I think the drift is part of what's true about it. A place that only exists in memory doesn't hold as still as a place you can still walk through.

What I want to bring with me is not a finished archive. It's the habit itself, the recorder in the pocket, the willingness to sit through a story for the forty-second time in case this is the telling where a new detail surfaces, in case this is the last year the water goes down far enough to see the wall at all.

text:
In the semifinal round of state, a sophomore from a school I'd never heard of took my case apart in four minutes using almost nothing but questions. I was arguing that mandatory minimum sentencing should be abolished, a position I'd defended maybe thirty times that season and had genuinely stopped listening to, in the sense that I knew all its moves so well I'd stopped hearing what it actually claimed. She asked me, calmly, what I would replace it with, and I gave the answer I always gave, judicial discretion, and she asked how I'd stop that discretion from reproducing the exact racial disparities the mandatory minimums were originally written to prevent. I didn't have an answer. I had a rebuttal, which is a different thing, and it showed.

I lost that round on a two-to-one decision, and one judge's ballot said something I still have taped inside my binder: "Confident delivery of a case that never met its strongest objection." I'd been coached for three years to build cases that were hard to attack. Nobody had taught me to build a case that survived actually being right about something I'd rather not be right about, which is what she'd done to me.

What I'd bring to your campus is the version of arguing I built after that loss, which starts from the opposite instinct than the one I walked in with. Before every round now, before I write a single line of my own case, I write my opponent's best question first, the one I'm most afraid of, and I make myself answer it honestly before I'm allowed to write anything persuasive. Some of my current teammates think this is slower than it needs to be, and they're right that it is slower. I've tried to bring it into our club's practice rounds anyway, not as a rule, just as a habit I model, because I think most debate teaches people to be unbeatable and I'd rather learn to be correct, which sometimes means losing well instead of winning badly.

I still think about that sophomore's question more than I think about almost anything else from four years of tournaments. Not because losing to her hurt, though it did, but because she'd clearly built her whole case by imagining mine first and taking it seriously. I want to bring that discipline into rooms where it currently isn't the norm, classrooms, clubs, wherever people gather to disagree, because I've learned the hard way that being persuasive and being right are not the same skill, and only one of them is actually worth teaching yourself.

text:
The turbidity tube lives in a shoebox under my bed now, but for eleven months it lived in my backpack, wrapped in a hand towel so the acrylic wouldn't crack against my textbooks. It's a clear plastic cylinder about sixty centimeters long, open at the top, with a small drain valve at the bottom and a black-and-white pattern - like a tiny archery target - printed on the inside floor. You pour creek water in until the pattern disappears from view, drain a little out, look again, and keep going until you can just barely make out the rings. Whatever depth the water sits at when the pattern reappears is your turbidity reading, and that one number, more than anything else I measured that year, is what kept me up until midnight in a county extension office that smelled like pond water and printer toner.

I got the tube from Mr. Halloran, who ran the water quality program out of the extension office two towns over and who I called so many times about Sugar Creek that his assistant started recognizing my voice. My project started as something small - I wanted to know whether the creek behind the Tractor Supply, the one that ran orange after storms, was actually worse off than the creek near my grandmother's, which ran clear even in August. I figured I'd take a few samples, make a chart, be done in a month. Instead I found myself standing in that creek every Saturday from September to July, sometimes in waders that let in water anyway, holding the tube up to the light and squinting at a target pattern like it was going to tell me something about my own life.

In a way it did. The tube doesn't care what you want the water to say. You can hope the numbers are good, the way I hoped every week that Sugar Creek would clear up, and the tube will still show you thirty-eight centimeters of visibility after a hard rain, which is bad, full stop, no matter how much you were rooting for the creek. I think that's what captivated me about the whole project - not water chemistry exactly, though I did fall in love with nitrate test strips and dissolved oxygen kits along the way, but the particular honesty of a measurement. A number from a stream doesn't perform for you. It doesn't care if your hypothesis was elegant. It just sits there in the tube, at whatever centimeter it landed on, and you either report it accurately or you're not really doing science anymore.

By spring I had four sites, forty-one weeks of readings, and a working theory that the runoff from a hog operation upstream, not the parking lot everyone blamed, was the real driver of the worst turbidity spikes - a theory Mr. Halloran initially doubted and then, after I showed him three storms in a row where the numbers only made sense his way, started taking seriously enough to mention to the county. That felt bigger than any ribbon the project could have won, and it did win a ribbon, though by the time regionals came around I cared much less about the placard than about whether site three was going to clear up before the fair even happened, which it did, barely, the morning of.

I still have the tube. I take it out sometimes, not because I need it for anything anymore, but because turning it in my hands still makes me want to know what the water looked like the week before, and the week before that. Mr. Halloran is the person I call when I don't understand a reading. The tube is the thing that taught me to trust a number over a hope, and I don't think I've stopped being the kind of person who'd rather wade into a cold creek in October than guess at an answer from the bank.

text:
There's a microphone in my closet that doesn't work anymore, hasn't worked in about a year, and I still won't throw it out. It's a cheap Behringer, the kind you'd buy for a podcast you never finish, silver mesh gone a little tarnished on one side where I dropped it on the studio floor sophomore year. My mom asks about it sometimes. Why do you still have that thing. I don't have a great answer.

I started the radio station - well, "station" is generous, it was a closet off the library that used to store textbooks, plus one ancient mixer someone's uncle donated - because I'd gotten it into my head that our school needed one. Not needed like a real need. Needed like I personally couldn't stop thinking about it. I spent the whole summer before junior year writing a pitch, getting the principal to sign off, begging the AV teacher for equipment, and I was so sure, so completely sure, that once it existed people would just show up.

They didn't. First broadcast, I think four people listened, and two of them were my friends who I'd basically ordered to tune in. I remember sitting in that closet with dead air on the mic for what felt like forever because I hadn't planned enough content and figured people would just want to hear us talk. Nobody wants to hear you just talk. I learned that the hard way, more than once.

Here's the part I actually got wrong, though, and it's not the small stuff. I thought the problem was marketing - so I made flyers, did announcements, begged the student council for airtime during assembly. All fine. All fairly reasonable moves. But the real mistake was that I built the whole thing around what I wanted to hear. Music I liked. Topics I found interesting. I didn't ask a single other student what they'd actually want from a school station before I opened it, and by the time it was up and running, changing direction felt like admitting the whole idea was broken from the start. So I didn't change it. I just kept making the thing I wanted and getting quietly hurt that nobody else wanted it too.

It got better eventually - a sophomore named Priya started doing a segment where she read anonymous confessions people submitted through a Google form, and that thing blew up, relatively speaking, forty or fifty regular listeners by spring, which felt enormous to us. But it blew up because of her idea, not mine, and it took me embarrassingly long to hand her the reins instead of trying to fold her segment into my vision for the station.

I keep the microphone because it was there for the bad months, the four-listener months, and I don't want to pretend those didn't happen just because things worked out okay later. It sits on a shelf and it's basically junk and I still catch myself looking at it when I'm annoyed at myself for doing the same thing again in some other group project - deciding I know what people want before I've asked them. I'd like to say I fixed that about myself. I haven't, not all the way. I just notice it faster now, usually around the point where I've already made the flyers.

I don't know exactly what I'll do with the mic. Maybe nothing. It's not sentimental in a nice way, if that makes sense - it's more like a reminder I keep somewhere I'll actually see it.

meta.topic: starting a school radio station nobody listened to at first
meta.prompt: Write about an object that is important to you.

text:
There's a notepad by our toaster. It's nothing special to look at - spiral bound, about the size of a coaster, the kind you'd buy in a three-pack at the drugstore without thinking twice. My mom writes one Korean word on it every morning, has for as long as I can remember, and for a stretch of years I barely looked at it. I want to explain why that stretch happened and why I look at it now.

I was twelve when I decided we should speak English at home. Nobody made me decide this. I just got tired, I think, of the half-second lag before I answered a friend on the phone because I'd been mid-sentence in Korean with my mom, tired of feeling like two different kids depending on which room I was standing in. So I asked. Not even asked, really - I sort of announced it, the way twelve-year-olds announce things, like the decision had already been made somewhere above my head and I was just the messenger. My parents went along with it faster than I expected. Looking back, I think they'd been waiting for permission to stop working so hard at something that clearly embarrassed me.

For the next four years, our house ran in English. Not perfect English - my dad still counts in Korean, still yells numbers at the TV during soccer games without noticing he's doing it - but the day-to-day stuff, dinner, homework, arguments about curfew, all of it switched over. I got good at English fast, better than I already was, which I guess was the point. And somewhere in there, without me clocking it, my Korean started going soft around the edges. Words I used to grab without thinking started needing a half-second search. I stopped noticing the notepad by the toaster the same way you stop noticing a clock ticking in a room you sit in every day.

Except my mom never stopped writing on it. Every single morning, before anyone else was up, one word. Sometimes a simple one, sometimes something weird and specific, like the word for the smell right before rain. I didn't ask her why she kept doing it during the years we weren't even speaking the language at the table. I think I assumed it was just a habit she hadn't gotten around to dropping, like a nail-biting thing, not a decision.

It took me embarrassingly long to understand it as a decision. Sometime last winter I picked the pad up off the counter, mostly out of boredom, and started flipping back through old pages she'd torn off and kept in a drawer instead of throwing away - hundreds of them, rubber-banded, going back years. Years I hadn't spoken more than ten words of Korean to her. She'd kept writing anyway. Not to teach me, not really, since I wasn't reading them. More like she was keeping a door propped open in case I ever wanted to walk back through it, even if that meant propping it open alone for a really long time.

I read one word off that pad every morning now. I say it back to her, badly, and she corrects me, and some mornings that's the only Korean either of us speaks all day, which still isn't much. But it's not nothing. That notepad is maybe forty cents' worth of paper and it sat by our toaster through four years of me deciding our first language was something to leave behind, and it was still there when I decided otherwise. I don't think I'd have found my way back at all without it just sitting there, boring and small and stubborn, waiting.

meta.topic: the year they stopped speaking their first language at home
meta.prompt: Write about an object that is important to you.

text:
I keep a cracked yellow lid from a peanut butter jar on my key ring, and it has gotten me more questions at airport security than anything else I carry, mostly because there is no obvious reason a seventeen-year-old should be sentimental about a piece of plastic with a hairline fracture running through the middle of it. The reason is a dog named Ranger, who three trainers and two shelters had already given up on by the time he came to live in our garage.

Ranger was a shepherd mix who'd been surrendered twice and returned once, and the intake notes said he was hand-shy, food-aggressive, and unsuitable for a first-time foster, which is exactly the kind of warning my mother, who runs a small rescue out of our house, tends to ignore. He would not take a treat from anyone's fingers. He'd flinch and sometimes snap, not out of meanness but because somewhere before us a hand reaching toward his mouth had meant something bad, and every trainer who'd tried the standard approach - lure with a treat, mark the behavior, reward - had run headfirst into that flinch and eventually written him off as untrainable.

I didn't have a better method. I had a peanut butter jar that had just gone empty, and a dog who wouldn't come near my hand, and an afternoon with nothing else to do. I smeared the inside of the lid, set it on the garage floor a few feet from him, and waited. It took him four days to walk over and lick it without bolting. It took another week before he'd touch the lid with his nose, dry, no peanut butter at all, just because I clicked a sound he'd started to associate with something good happening a few feet away from my hands rather than in them. That lid became the whole hinge of his training. I could ask for a nose-touch to the lid from any distance, any direction, and build everything else - sit, stay, walking calmly past another dog - off a behavior that never once required him to trust a hand near his mouth. The trainers hadn't been wrong about the method. They'd just assumed the method was the only door into the room, when Ranger needed a completely different one.

He was adopted eleven months later by a retired postal worker who still sends my mother photos, and in every one of them, taped above the guy's desk, is that same lid, kept as a kind of relic in his house too. I asked to keep the original, and he mailed me a plastic sandwich bag with it wrapped up like something precious, which by then, to both of us, it was.

What I'd bring to a campus is the instinct that lid represents, which is not patience exactly - patience makes it sound passive, like waiting something out - but a working belief that when a standard method keeps failing on someone, the answer is rarely more of the same method delivered more forcefully. It's usually the wrong door. I've carried that instinct into tutoring a freshman who couldn't sit through a normal reading assignment but could absorb an entire chapter listened to at double speed while pacing the hallway, and into a robotics team where our best engineer thinks in sketches, not spec sheets, and needed the whole group to stop insisting on written documentation before her ideas got taken seriously. I notice, fairly quickly, when a system is failing someone not because the person is failing but because the system only has one door built into it. Then I go looking for the lid - whatever the equivalent turns out to be - because I've watched what happens when you find it. A dog nobody could place ends up asleep on a postal worker's couch, and a piece of cracked yellow plastic ends up meaning more than anything I've ever been formally taught.

meta.topic: training a rescue dog that could not be trained
meta.prompt: What would you contribute to our campus that would not be here if you were not?

text:
My dad and I still argue about the motorcycle, and I don't think either of us is going to win, mostly because we're not actually arguing about the motorcycle.

It was my grandfather's, a 1978 Honda CB400 he bought used in the eighties and never quite finished fixing before he died two years ago. It sat in our garage under a tarp for a year after that, and my dad kept saying he was going to sell it to a guy at his work who restored bikes, get it out of the way, stop tripping over it every time he looked for the leaf blower. I asked if I could try fixing it myself instead. He said sure, mostly, I think, because he assumed I'd lose interest by June.

I did not lose interest by June. I spent basically that whole summer out there - carburetor cleaned three times before I got the jetting right, a new battery, a seat I reupholstered badly and then less badly, hours on forums trying to figure out why the electrical system kept grounding out. My hands smelled like gasoline for three months straight. My mom made me take my shoes off before coming inside.

My dad would come check on me sometimes, and at first it was fine, even good - he knew more than he let on, and he'd point out things, show me how to bleed a brake line. But somewhere around July it turned into something else. He started saying things like "you know he never actually got that thing running, right, in like fifteen years," which is true, and which I think he meant as a warning, but which I heard as him telling me to quit. I'd say something back about how that wasn't the point, and he'd say everything's the point of something, Jake, and we'd both go quiet and do something else for a while.

We never really settled what the bike meant to either of us, which I think is the actual disagreement, underneath the one about torque specs and whether I was wasting my summer. I think my dad needed it gone because looking at it half-fixed in the garage was like looking at his father half-here, and finishing it, or worse, making it run, wasn't going to bring anyone back, so what was the point. I think I needed the opposite - I needed to finish something my grandfather started, because I'd barely known him, honestly, he died when I was fourteen and lived two states away most of my life, and the bike was the closest thing I had to actually meeting him.

I got it running in August, the night before I had to go back to school. I rode it around the block twice, badly, stalling once at the stop sign. My dad watched from the driveway with his arms crossed and didn't say much, and I couldn't tell if he was proud or just sad in a way he wasn't going to explain to me. He still brings up selling it sometimes. I still say no. Neither of us has really said the real thing to the other, the thing about grief looking different for two people who loved the same man in different ways, and I don't know if we ever will. But the bike runs now, and some nights he comes out and looks at it with me, quiet, and that's not resolution exactly. It's something close to it.

meta.topic: a summer spent restoring a broken motorcycle

text:
I quit piano on a Tuesday in October, told my teacher I wasn't coming back, and felt, for about three weeks, an enormous relief, like I'd put down something heavy I hadn't noticed I was carrying. Eleven years of lessons, competitions, juries, a wall of certificates my mom insisted on framing. Gone, just like that, over a five-minute conversation in a parking lot.

Here's what I got wrong, and I didn't figure it out for almost two years: I told myself I was quitting music. I wasn't. I was quitting the specific, narrow, competitive version of music I'd been handed since I was six, the one measured in points off a judge's sheet and rankings posted on a corkboard, and I mistook my exhaustion with that structure for exhaustion with the thing itself. I stopped touching a piano almost entirely for a year and told anyone who asked that I was "done with music," said it flatly, like a fact about myself, the way you'd say you're done with a sport after an injury.

What actually happened is I got a cheap laptop for my sixteenth birthday and, out of boredom more than anything, downloaded a free version of some music software a friend used for a class project. I wasn't trying to compose. I was mostly trying to make a weird beat to annoy my sister through the wall. But I stayed up until two in the morning that first night, layering a bass line under a chord progression I half-remembered from a Chopin piece I used to hate practicing, and I looked up and it was two a.m. and I genuinely didn't know where the time had gone. That hadn't happened with piano in years, not since I was small and lessons were still new.

It's the same underlying thing, I think, that used to captivate me before competition flattened it - the way a chord can almost resolve and then doesn't, the way silence between two notes is doing as much work as the notes themselves, the actual architecture of why a piece of music makes you feel something specific instead of something general. I used to feel that as a kid banging around on the keys before anyone was grading me on it. I'd just forgotten, or buried it under eleven years of being told exactly how to play things correctly.

Now I lose hours to it constantly, in a way that worries my parents a little, honestly, because it's not attached to any external reward the way competitions were. Nobody's handing me a plaque for a three-minute track I made at midnight. I don't care. I go down forum rabbit holes about mixing technique, I rewatch the same twenty-minute video on modal interchange four times until it clicks, I have a Discord server full of people twice my age who make music in their bedrooms and who answer my dumb questions at eleven p.m. without any condescension at all. There's a guy who runs a tiny studio near my house, Marcus, who lets me sit in sometimes on Saturdays and watches me work without correcting anything unless I ask - which is the opposite of every piano lesson I ever had, and it turns out that's exactly what I needed.

I don't regret quitting, even knowing what I know now. If I hadn't quit, I don't think I'd have found my way back to the actual thing underneath it, the part that had nothing to do with rankings. But I do think about the eleven years sometimes and wonder what I'd have made of them if someone had told me, early on, that being done with competition wasn't the same as being done with music. I might have believed that competitive piano version of me could disappear and something truer would still be standing underneath. I didn't believe it then. I do now, mostly because I've watched it happen to me at midnight, more than once, with a laptop and headphones and no judge anywhere in the room.

meta.topic: quitting piano after eleven years
